By: Aja Dorsainvil Posted and last updated BOCA RATON, Fla. — Authorities are investigating after a woman's body was found in the ocean about 2 miles off the coast of Boca Raton Tuesday morning. Just after 8 a.m., a boater reported the body in the water east of 2500 N Ocean Blvd., Boca Raton police said. Police responded to the scene, with the dive team recovering the woman’s body in the water, authorities said. The woman is described as being white, between the age of 40 and 50 years old, with brown and gray hair and was wearing a blue T-shirt. Police said Boca Raton Fire Rescue and the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission are also involved in the investigation. Anyone with information on this case should call call Detective Lima at (561) 620-6246.

As cranes fill the skyline and major projects continue rising across downtown West Palm Beach, leaders and residents in Palm Beach say the explosive growth happening across the Intracoastal is no longer just a West Palm Beach issue.During a recent Palm Beach Town Council meeting, officials reviewed more than 100 projects planned, approved, under construction, or completed in downtown West Palm Beach — including thousands of residential units, multiple hotels, and more than 2 million square feet of commercial development.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:Traffic quickly emerged as the biggest concern. “I’m horrified because of our traffic issue with this much going up,” one councilmember said during the meeting. “We just don’t have the road capacity.”Palm Beach officials stressed they cannot stop or veto projects in West Palm Beach because each municipality operates under its own home rule authority. Instead, council members said their best option is to stay engaged, attend meetings, and advocate for balanced growth.“We just can’t sit around anymore. We can’t say, ‘I’m from Palm Beach and you’re not,’ anymore,” one council member said. “We are now a part of a regional superstructure.”Planning staff member Jennifer Hofmeister presented the council with updated GIS mapping data showing projects clustered largely along Flagler Drive and south of Palm Beach Lakes Boulevard — areas officials said could have the greatest impact on traffic heading to and from the island.Residents on both sides of the Intracoastal say the traffic problem is already difficult.“We keep getting stuck everywhere,” West Palm Beach resident Eva Sherwin said. When asked to describe the city’s traffic situation in one word, resident Michael Jones responded: “Tragic.”For Mark Maller, getting off Palm Beach Island can already feel like a commute before his drive even begins.“When Trump is in town and A1A is closed, my office is just a block away from here,” Maller said. “It can take me 20 minutes, 25 minutes just to get to the bridge, where it should take three or four minutes.”Maller said he fears the thousands of new residents expected from West Palm Beach’s building boom will make an already difficult situation much worse. “I can’t imagine when all those are built up, what the traffic is going to be like,” he said. It’s going to be a nightmare.”He worries future commutes during road closures or busy season could stretch to nearly an hour for trips just a few blocks long. “Once all that construction’s done, that commute when Trump’s in town as well is just going to be tenfold,” Maller said.Longtime resident Mike Tyler, who said he was born in 1941, also believes the pace of development has outgrown the region’s infrastructure. “The construction and real estate industry has gotten out of hand,” Tyler said.Tyler said routine trips have become increasingly difficult, especially during season. “I have been here at 3:30 trying to get off the island,” he said. “Don’t try that during the busy season.”Council members also voiced concern about proposals tied to West Palm Beach’s Downtown Master Plan, including past discussions about potentially closing portions of Flagler Drive for future waterfront development. “That is something we all need to keep an eye on,” one council member said, warning traffic could become “absolutely insane” if major roadway changes move forward.The Downtown Master Plan is currently paused following pushback from West Palm Beach residents, some of whom have voiced concerns about overdevelopment and density. “We do not want Wall Street South,” resident Draana Conetan said during a meeting.In response, West Palm Beach created a resident-led coalition involving roughly 30 neighborhood organizations meeting weekly with city staff.“I think they’re finally starting to listen,” resident Patty Wilmoth said.Regarding the coalition, the city says:The City's Resident Partnership Initiative is underway as a collaborative effort that brings together representatives from participating neighborhood associations across West Palm Beach. Representatives have already begun meeting weekly and are participating in structured working sessions with City staff. The initial series of sessions focuses on the Downtown Master Plan Update, providing neighborhood representatives with a deeper understanding of the City's planning process and the work of departments including Utilities, Engineering, Transportation, Public Works, and others. These sessions also provide opportunities to review technical information, ask questions, and provide feedback from their neighborhoods that helps inform the planning process. The initiative is designed to strengthen two-way communication between the City and residents by ensuring neighborhood representatives have timely, factual information they can share with their communities while bringing neighborhood questions and feedback directly to City staff.Palm Beach leaders say they plan to continue monitoring development discussions, join more regional transportation and planning committees, and encourage residents to stay informed about projects that could reshape traffic and quality of life across both communities. “It’s interconnected, so it’s going to create a much bigger problem here,” Maller said. “We don’t call it West Palm Beach now; it’s called Palm Beach West.”This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Tradition Lakes K-8 in St. Lucie County is set to open its doors on Aug. 10, offering much-needed classroom space for one of the county’s fastest-growing communities. Crews have worked throughout the summer to prepare the campus for its first group of students. Principal Latanya Greene said the school’s motto, "Traditions begin here," reflects the focus on building a foundation of achievements and accomplishments. Your neighborhood: Local coverage from WPBF 25 News "Throughout this process, we have talked a lot about traditions and accomplishments and the achievements that we want to build and grow at this school. Hence, our motto for the school year is that tradition leads K through eight. Traditions begin here," Greene said. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. Greene emphasized that months of planning have gone into creating an environment where students can grow academically and socially. "It's about being in an environment that you can grow and continue with great levels. But bigger than that, you begin to set the tone of creating those strong academics that move with you from year to year to year. You develop friendships," Greene said. The new campus comes at a critical time for the Tradition area, where population growth has led to overcrowding at nearby schools. District leaders expect as many as 1,600 students on opening day, with many families benefiting from the school’s convenient location. "We are busting at the seams in the south and the west. And this school is so conveniently located to families that we're going to have a tremendous number of students that are walking or even other parents dropping the kids off in a golf cart," said John R. Prince, superintendent of St. Lucie County Public Schools. As the first day approaches, Greene said success will be measured not only by academics but also by the sense of community created during the school’s inaugural year. "The academics component is going to be there, but it is going to be walking through this inaugural year and looking back on all the traditions that we have created as a team, as a family, and the strength of our culture, and how we just grow throughout the first year will be beyond the definition of success for us," Greene said. Tradition Lakes K-8 will officially open on August 10, marking the beginning of a new chapter for students and families in the Tradition area.

Indian River County firefighter-paramedic Geoffrey Lang was honored Tuesday morning at a memorial service held at The Community Church in Vero Beach, following his unexpected death last month. The room was filled with Lang's friends, family, and colleagues, while dozens of community members showed their support through the church’s livestream of the event. Bagpipes led the procession, followed by a prayer, setting the tone for a service focused on remembering Lang's life of service. Speakers described Lang as someone who dedicated himself to his community, sharing stories of his service, compassion, and the lasting difference he made in the lives of many. Your neighborhood: Local coverage from WPBF 25 News "He chose to serve alongside all of us. When there was a need, he met and exceeded, and throughout his career, as having a great honor of served alongside of him, he answered those calls with courage," said Dustin Hawkins, chaplain and firefighter with Indian River County Fire. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. "He was always a sweet soul and approached life with grace and accountability, humor inappropriate at times," Hawkins said. Lang's colleagues and family encouraged attendees to remember not just his loss but the example he set throughout his life and service, saying his contributions and memory will continue to be felt across the community.

Mauricio Pochettino is staying with the U.S. soccer team, agreeing Monday to a four-year contract to coach the Americans through the 2030 World Cup.The 54-year-old Pochettino, who took over the national team in October 2024, led the U.S. to the round of 16 at this year's World Cup, where the tournament co-hosts were eliminated in a 4-1 loss to Belgium.Still, he helped the seeded U.S. team to a pair of firsts in the expanded 48-nation tournament, clinching advancement from the group stage with a game to spare and winning three games in a single World Cup. The team captivated American fans with excited audiences in stadiums and record television viewers.RELATED STORY | US-Belgium match draws biggest soccer audience in US history"The magic thing that happened during the World Cup, the connection with the people, of course with the whole organization and everything was a key point," Pochettino said during a Zoom news conference from his home in Barcelona, Spain.Since reaching the quarterfinals at the 2002 World Cup, the U.S. has lost four round-of-16 games."What we learn(ed) is that we can compete, that we have the quality and we have the talent," Pochettino said. That gap with the best teams in the world is not too big."Pochettino said there is potential to make soccer in the U.S. "grow and grow and grow and be one of the important sport(s) in America, like it is in the rest of the world.""We have players and organization that can compete with the best organization in the world in that sport," he said. "We learned that the fans are amazing and when they were so excited to discover a sport that made our fans become crazy, no? The connection was amazing."Pochettino views the next cycle as a new start for a program lacking quality depth at goalkeeper and central defender."It is going to be important to provide the young kids that we really believe (in) that they have the potential to arrive in 2030, in four years," he said.Before taking the U.S. job, Pochettino coached Espanyol (2009-12), Southampton (2013-14), Tottenham (2014-19), Paris Saint-Germain (2021-22) and Chelsea (2023-24).When Pochettino replaced Gregg Berhalter two years ago, he signed an initial contract through the 2026 World Cup. Pochettino said ahead of the tournament that he had discussed a possible new deal with the USSF. He also said in May that his agent had spoken with AC Milan, a club that then hired Rúben Amorim.RELATED STORY | Senior FIFA official resigns over Infantino's World Cup sell-off planPochettino, who has homes in Spain and London, said he may move to the U.S. He intends to stay with the American team until 2030 but left himself an out."Four years time is a really long period. You never know what can happen in soccer," he said. "Today people really love you. In eight weeks time, maybe that change(s), that feeling."He has led the U.S. to 17 wins (including a penalty-kick victory), 13 losses and one draw. Twenty-three of 62 players to appear under Pochettino have accounted for the team's 57 goals."We know we have a lot of work to do to achieve our clear ambitions, including competing to win Men's World Cups and having soccer become the most played sport in every community," USSF CEO JT Batson said in a statement.Hedge fund manager Ken Griffin is again the lead philanthropic funder supporting Pochettino's contract with additional support by Scott Goodwin, Adam Freede and commercial partners. Pochettino earned just over $5 million in his first seven months as coach, according to the U.S. Soccer Federation tax return.U.S. coaches have not been successful when they remained for a second World Cup cycle.After leading the Americans to the 2002 quarterfinals, Bruce Arena was unable to get his team past the group stage in 2006.Bob Bradley helped the U.S. reach the round of 16 in 2010, then was fired a year later after the team lost the CONCACAF Gold Cup final.Jurgen Klinsmann took over and in December 2013 was given an extension through the 2018 World Cup. The Americans reached the round of 16 in 2014 but Klinsmann was fired in late 2016 after the U.S. lost its first two games in the final round of qualifying. Arena returned but the U.S. failed to qualify for the 2018 World Cup.Berhalter was hired in late 2018 and led the Americans to the round of 16 in 2022. Given a new contract in 2023, he was fired a year later after the U.S. failed to advance past the group stage at Copa America."We are going to demand more from them," he said of the players. "We are not going to be in some situation(s) not flexible like we were because before it was (for) the benefit of players, benefit of structures that were already built. But now it's about to start the house from zero."

Tom Garfinkel is stepping down as the Miami Dolphins' president and CEO after 13 years, the team announced Tuesday amid a handful of operational changes in the organization.He will remain part of the organization as vice chairman of the Dolphins and Hard Rock Stadium, as well as managing partner of the Miami Grand Prix, but is stepping away from day-to-day responsibilities.Also Tuesday, the Dolphins announced that Daniel Sillman, the son-in-law of owner Stephen Ross, will oversee football operations for the team, with head coach Jeff Hafley, general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan and executive vice president of football operations Brandon Shore reporting directly to him.Sillman was also named CEO of Ross Sports & Entertainment, a new company that will merge Ross' sports holdings — the Dolphins, Hard Rock Stadium, the Miami Grand Prix, the Miami Open tennis tournament and the Precision Drive Club — into one entity. Sillman is the co-founder and executive chairman of the sports and media rights company Relevent."Tom has had one of the most impactful executive tenures in professional sports history," Ross said in a statement released by the Dolphins. "When he joined our organization, we envisioned creating a world-class sports and entertainment company that would redefine what was possible for a franchise, a stadium and a community. Together we turned that vision into reality. Tom assembled an extraordinary leadership team and created an incredible foundation for continued growth. While he is stepping away from the day-to-day responsibilities of CEO, I am grateful that he will continue to play an important role as Vice Chairman and a trusted advisor to Danny and me."Since joining the Dolphins in 2013, Garfinkel spearheaded the business turnaround of the organization. He had a primary role in bringing Formula 1 racing to Miami through the Miami Grand Prix, securing the event through 2041. He also established a 30-year agreement to host the Miami Open tennis tournament at Hard Rock Stadium and won bids to host the 2020 Super Bowl, the 2021 and 2026 College Football Playoff National Championship games and seven matches during the 2026 World Cup."I love the Dolphins and the people here, but after 13 years it was just the right time for me to make this decision," Garfinkel said in a statement. "The business has never been in a better place and the team of people we have here is second to none in sports."

The developer of a proposed up-scale Marriott hotel, considered a linchpin of the downtown waterfront King’s Landing project, says it needs $15 million from the City of Fort Pierce to fill a financing gap it can’t meet. FORT PIERCE – The developer of a proposed up-scale Marriott hotel, considered a linchpin of the downtown waterfront King’s Landing project, says it needs $15 million from the City of Fort Pierce to fill a financing gap it can’t meet. Records show Mainsail Lodging and Development, the primary force behind the proposed downtown hotel, has already missed at least three deadlines in contracts with the city, including a requirement to have the hotel’s financing “fully and finally closed” by July 15. Several city commissioners have already indicated they are a “hard no” on the city contributing $15 million to keep the hotel project alive in exchange for a proposed 60 percent ownership in the hotel. However, a representative for Live Oak Holdings Group LLC–another player in the King’s Landing project– has proposed seeing if it can get $15 million worth of commitments from another set of potential investors to fill the financing gap. In an email to city officials, Bill Ware, Live Oak development manager, has asked the city for 180 days to see if Live Oak can find that capital commitment. King’s Landing is on tonight’s city commission agenda where officials are expected to decide if they are willing to grant the 180-day request, and consider setting a special meeting to discuss another amendment to the original development agreement or whether and how the development plan should be abandoned. City Manager Richard Chess also suggested another hotel developer could be identified to take over that part of the King’s Landing proposal. The city’s other option would be to end its King’s Landing development agreement and take back the downtown waterfront property due to the developer’s contract defaults. The roller coaster of development hurdles dates back more than five years when the city issued a request for proposals (RFP) from potential developers for a visionary, multi-use plan for the former H.D. A proposal from Audubon Development Inc., of Palm Beach, was given the nod to build six buildings by the end of 2025, including a hotel, condominiums, restaurants, retail and office space, single-family residences and apartments. So far, none of the buildings have been done. The city originally had agreed to contribute by rebating half of the property taxes collected on the new development for the first five years, up to $1 million. The initial agreement has already been amended three times and a fourth amendment to the terms has been requested by developers. However, Sara Hedges, city attorney, has said she would not recommend the city agree to a fourth amendment “without the financing being resolved.” The financing gap that threatens the project first became public in July when commissioners met as the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency (FPRA) board. The reaction then ranged from suggestions that the project be scrapped to “a glimmer of hope.” “I think it’s time to say goodbye and develop another RFP,” said Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky. “This property is too valuable to be left sitting vacant. I won’t be moving forward on a fourth amendment. We need to bring this back in house and start over. “I’m at wits end at this point. This project doesn’t even remotely look like the original RFP at this point.” Commissioner Michael Broderick cautioned that pulling the plug now could land the city in years of costly litigation because Audubon Development currently owns the property, potentially delaying any development there another 10-12 years. Ware acknowledged in July that his firm–partnering with Audubon–was “surprised” to learn in April that there was a hole in the hotel financing plan. Ware was the only representative from any of the development partners to appear in person at the July FPRA meeting. Commissioner Arnold Gaines said in July he was a “hard no” on the city contributing $15 million to the hotel financing. “I will not put the taxpayers’ money in this,” Gaines said. “If a person who builds hotels can’t find the money, where do you get it? If we say no to the $15 million, can this project be completed?” “That’s our intent,” responded Ware, while unable to provide a guarantee. “It’s gotta come from somebody else,” said Mayor Linda Hudson. “I don’t want the City of Fort Pierce to be in the hotel business.” This is one of several city-backed real estate ventures that has gone sour in recent years. The award of a lease to two, then-city employees for vacant land on Avenue D has resulted in the pending prosecution of former city manager Nicholas Mimms for bid tampering and official misconduct. And the city is on the hook for more than $200,000 in unpaid taxes and rent for the Crabby’s restaurant downtown in a lease agreement it signed with another private interest. Also, the city now looks at $2 million in necessary repairs to the former Means Court building in a lease with Incubate Neighborhood Center, a nonprofit that received substantial funding from a Catholic charity before INC shutdown shortly after opening due to building code violations. The Hometown News sent the same list of questions below to each qualified candidate in the Aug. 18 Republican Primary Election for the District 2 Indian River County Commission seat. The only qualified Democratic candidate in the race also agreed to participate, although he won’t face the winner of the primary until Nov. Question 1 What do you view as the most serious issue facing Indian River County and how would you propose addressing that if elected? Question 2 There will be a referendum this year on raising the Homestead Exemption and potentially cutting ad valorem property tax income significantly to municipalities. If you are elected and that passes, what areas of the county budget would you suggest trimming or cutting out altogether if need-be? Question 3 Do you think the County Commission should address the lack of affordable housing, and if so, in what way? Question 4 There have recently been calls from some citizens to stop the rezoning of agricultural lands for housing and to do more to encourage the return to citrus groves. If elected, how would you respond to such requests? Question 5 If elected, how would you work to improve the quality of life for Indian River County voters? Candidate Bob McPartian 1. The most serious issue is managing growth in a way that protects our quality of life, infrastructure and the Indian River Lagoon. If elected, I will push for better coordination between cities and the county so development is tied to available roads, utilities and environmental capacity. My 15 years on the Sebastian City Council have shown me that early planning and strong interlocal agreements prevent problems before they start. I support tax reform, but I do not support this particular amendment as written. It was developed quickly without a full analysis of its impact, and there is no clear backup plan if it creates significant revenue shortfalls. If it passes, I would protect public safety and core infrastructure first. Then, I would look to reduce non-essential spending, improve efficiency and prioritize programs that deliver clear results for residents rather than across-the-board cuts. Yes, the County Commission should address housing affordability in practical ways. I support streamlining permitting, encouraging a mix of housing types where infrastructure already exists, and working with cities and private partners. Partnering with nonprofits such as Habitat for Humanity to develop housing on existing county-owned property is one concrete step that can help without overextending government resources. Property owners have the right to request zoning changes, and those requests should be evaluated fairly. At the same time, I respect citizens who want to protect agricultural land and encourage citrus. Growth should be directed first to areas already planned for development and served by infrastructure. Any rezoning must be carefully reviewed for impacts on roads, water resources and the Lagoon. I would focus on the basics that matter most to residents: protecting the Indian River Lagoon, maintaining safe roads and reliable infrastructure, supporting public safety, keeping taxes reasonable through disciplined budgeting, and ensuring cities and the county work together. After 15 years of local service, I know steady, practical leadership improves daily life more than flashy promises. Candidate Jennifer Pippin 1, If Amendment 3 is approved by Florida voters, it will provide meaningful property tax relief for homesteaded residents. As a county commissioner, I will work to ensure the county budget reflects that change by prioritizing responsible spending, eliminating waste where possible and protecting essential services without shifting the burden back onto taxpayers through other means. Government must live within its means while providing the core services our residents expect. If the referendum passes, I believe the County Commission has a responsibility to carefully review every line of the budget before asking taxpayers to bear the burden. I would begin by evaluating discretionary spending, including the $3.7 million in funding provided to non-profit organizations and the administrative costs associated with distributing those funds. I would also review the current funding arrangement for school resource officers. Public education is a School District responsibility, and I believe the District should fund the sheriff’s $1.4 million budget currently paid by the county for SROs. Additionally, I would implement a vacancy review process so that when positions become vacant through retirement or resignation, they are evaluated to determine whether the workload can be absorbed more efficiently. I would also review and reduce consulting contracts wherever county staff can perform the work in-house. Finally, I would look for ways to increase revenue from tourism so the burden on local homeowners is reduced. I believe affordable housing is primarily driven by the private sector, not government mandates. The County Commission’s role should be to create an environment where businesses can thrive, which in turn brings better-paying jobs and more opportunities for residents. By reducing unnecessary regulations, streamlining permitting and encouraging responsible development, we can help increase the supply of housing and make it more attainable. I also support measures like Amendment 3, which will allow residents to keep more of their own money and better support their families. I want to keep oranges growing and cows grazing on agricultural land. Once farmland is developed, we can never get it back. I support protecting our agricultural heritage while respecting private property rights. I will work to ensure agricultural land remains agricultural and that development is responsible, planned and supported by the infrastructure needed to protect our quality of life. Improving our quality of life means preserving the things that make this county so special while planning responsibly for the future. When elected, I will work to keep taxes as low as possible through responsible budgeting, support our Sheriff’s Office and first responders, protect our agricultural heritage and ensure growth never outpaces our roads, infrastructure and public safety. I want future generations to enjoy the same safe, beautiful and welcoming Indian River County that my family has been blessed to call home. Candidate Daniel ‘Brooks’ Robinson 1, Our greatest challenge is managing growth responsibly. We need to ensure our roads, utilities, public safety and infrastructure keep pace with growth while protecting the quality of life that makes Indian River County such a great place to live. We don’t have to choose between growth and preservation: We can achieve both through thoughtful planning. The county should begin by reviewing every department, project and expenditure to identify efficiencies and eliminate non-essential spending. My priorities would be protecting public safety, maintaining essential infrastructure and preserving the core services residents rely on every day. I would not commit to cutting specific departments or positions without first conducting a comprehensive review. The county should encourage a range of housing opportunities that meet the needs of our workforce and families while protecting neighborhood character and ensuring infrastructure keeps pace with growth. I believe the private market should lead, with county government focused on responsible planning, efficient permitting and sound infrastructure investment. Agriculture is an important part of Indian River County’s history, economy and identity, and we should do what we can to support our agricultural community. My focus will be on managing growth responsibly, protecting private property rights and ensuring development improves our community. Quality of life is why so many of us choose to live in Indian River County. As commissioner, I will work to keep our community safe, manage growth responsibly, protect our natural resources, strengthen our local economy and be a good steward of taxpayer dollars. I think more land should remain as green space for the local ecology. I would look for ways to improve affordable housing and affordable healthcare for everyone, especially seniors; rental and utility assistance programs; and clean up the Lagoon because a healthy Lagoon makes a healthy IRC. A large law enforcement presence descended on a Fort Pierce neighborhood Tuesday morning as detectives executed a search warrant connected to an alleged fraud scheme that investigators say cost a local business nearly $7 million. Lucie County Sheriff's Office confirmed to CBS12 News that deputies are serving a search warrant as part of the ongoing investigation into the Southern Truss fraud case. Crime scene investigators were seen outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard. Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting Southern Truss Companies. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges, court records show. Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Grasso faces charges of: First-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more Organized fraud of $50,000 or more Conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity (RICO) Money laundering of $100,000 or more Harrs and Mejia each face charges of grand theft, organized fraud and racketeering. Grasso's bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release. Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2019 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions. The amended complaint alleges Grasso alone misappropriated at least $5 million, while Mejia and Harrs allegedly received hundreds of thousands more. The criminal case remains pending. Court records show a magistrate in June declined to pause the related civil case because of the criminal proceedings, instead ordering the defendants to respond to discovery by July 30 and complete depositions by Aug. The sheriff's office has not released details about what investigators are searching for at Grasso's home or whether any additional arrests are expected. CBS12 has a crew at the scene and will update this story as more information becomes available.

A fourth person has been arrested in connection with the death of a 3-month-old child following an investigation, the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said. Jason Gunter, 45, the child’s biological father, was taken into custody by the United States Marshals Service Tuesday morning, at his residence in Mechanicsville, Virginia, on an outstanding warrant obtained by St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office detectives. Gunter has been charged with felony child neglect resulting in great harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the child’s death. He is currently awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County, where he will face the charge. This arrest marks the fourth individual charged as a result of the investigation. Three people were arrested back on July 24 in relation to this case. Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center on back in 2025 , after the 3-month-old was brought to the emergency room by the child’s grandparents. The sheriff’s office said they were notified by medical personnel that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect. The Medical Examiner determined the child’s manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said this investigation remains active as the case moves through the judicial process.

The city of Westlake is experiencing a rapid transformation— thousands of new homes have been approved, major retailers are moving in and families drawn by affordable living and strong community bonds.WPTV reporter Christy Waite spoke with Krystal Lexima who moved her family to Westlake from Wellington in 2018 when the landscape looked very different. "Everything was just dirt and grass. There was just one neighborhood and lots of coyotes," Lexima recalls. "When we came out here there was nothing and that was really scary, but we saw the vision."WATCH: Since Westlake's founding in 2016, the population has exploded, and Mayor J.P. O'Connor says the growth shows no signs of slowing. "We are at about 3,880 homes but there's another 1600 that has been approved that hasn't broken ground yet," O'Connor said.The rapid growth has caught the attention of major retailers. In a significant win for the community, Walmart purchased a 24-acre site where they'll build a massive 188,779-square-foot superstore. Located in Town Center West near Seminole Pratt Whitney Road and 60th Street North, the new Walmart will be a one-stop destination featuring a full grocery store, pharmacy, garden center, automotive center, vision center, convenience store and gas station.The store will sit next to a Lowe's Home Improvement store, which will also serve as a regional headquarters. "Getting a Lowe's is like winning the retail lottery when it comes to a new and thriving city," Mayor O'Connor said.Other businesses currently under construction include Chase Bank, Dollar Tree, Goodwill, Cold Stone Creamery, Westlake Eyecare, Ella's Café, and Mavis Tire & Brakes. John Carter from Minto Communities USA, the developer behind much of Westlake growth, sees these additions as validation of the community's potential. "Bringing in major brands like Walmart and Lowe's is a clear vote of confidence in our community's growth and long-term value," Carter said.All Westlake residents enjoy access to the impressive $23 million Westlake Adventure Park, which features a resort-style lagoon pool with tower slide, adult lap pool and splash pad, concert pavilion and event lawn, BMX pump park and playground, dog park and basketball courts and The Lodge community gathering space. A 3,900-square-foot fieldhouse with event space, coffee bar, and sports fields is also in the works.For O'Connor, the secret to Westlake success is simple: affordability combined with genuine community spirit. "We've got great affordability out here. It's an amazing, utopian place to live where families help each other and just thrive," O'Connor said.From empty lots to a bustling community in less than a decade, Westlake proves that sometimes the best things come to those who can see the vision—even when it's just dirt and grass.

A suspected burglar dressed for happy hour instead of a police lineup is now known across St. Lucie County as the Flamingo Bandit. The nickname comes courtesy of the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office , which is searching for a man photographed wearing a tropical shirt dominated by a giant pink flamingo. Some criminals try to blend in, the agency wrote. This one apparently took fashion advice from a Jimmy Buffett concert. But deputies said the man’s alleged itinerary involved burglary, not boats, beaches or frozen drinks. Investigators said the suspect entered a residence on July 28 and stole a laptop, miscellaneous food and a key to the home. Deputies allege he then returned later that same day and used the stolen key to get inside a second time. Two sharks were spotted along the Atlantic Ocean shore — one that washed up dead and another of fishermen struggling with a hooked one. Both incidents occurred Friday, with video sent to WPBF. Jensen Beach resident and avid beach walker Kathy Green was walking along Normandy Beach on Hutchinson Island in St. Lucie County when she filmed a group of fishermen struggling with a 12-foot shark they had hooked. The fishermen unhooked the deadly beast and released it back into the water. Shark expert and conservationist Jim Abernethy believes it was a great white shark by looking at the video. Also Friday, a hammerhead shark was spotted dead just south of the Jupiter Beach Resort. Christopher Ray, a musician, submitted video to WPBF. Later that day, Fish Wildlife removed the shark. Shark Week 2026 ran from July 26 to Saturday on the Discovery Channel. Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission has ordered Martin County, which also includes Hutchinson Island, to follow rules about people fishing for fish or sharks from the beach or shoreline. Shark fishing requires a state saltwater fishing license to fish within 1,000 feet of the guarded beach boundaries at any time. Under the current county ordinance, shark fishing is prohibited within 1,000 yards of the county's four guarded beaches: Jensen, Stuart, Bathtub and Hobe Sound. On Tuesday, commissioners postponed making a decision and asked attorneys to review the law.

The Florida Department of Environmental Protection has given Fort Pierce until Sept. 15 to review, approve and submit a proposed consent order resolving nearly $16,000 in state fines tied to docks at Little Jim Bait & Tackle.WATCH BELOW:Emails obtained by WPTV from FDEP show the state agency extended the city's deadline by 90 days, meaning city commissioners have not yet formally accepted or rejected the state's enforcement terms. City staff have been negotiating with FDEP to reduce or resolve the thousands of dollars in penalties.The enforcement action follows WPTV's reporting that revealed FDEP alleges the city has been operating docks at Little Jim's on state-owned submerged land without authorization — land the agency says the city never had permission to use.City Commissioner Michael Broderick previously acknowledged the allegation."My information is that accusation is actually true, that there was an extension of the existing docks," Broderick said July 6. Broderick said it remains unclear whether the city or the Little Jim's tenant was responsible for extending the docks without the required permits."Keep in mind that the city of Fort Pierce owns that real estate, so ultimately, in the day, the city of Fort Pierce is the responsible party," Broderick said.The FDEP action is one of several legal and regulatory pressures now surrounding the historic waterfront property. In early July, Fort Pierce city commissioners voted unanimously to reject a settlement offer in a separate lawsuit filed by local resident Kevin Keene, who alleged years of waterfront mismanagement tied to Little Jim's.Under the proposed settlement terms, Keene would have dropped the case if the city halted any new plans for Little Jim until the FDEP permit issues were resolved and allowed a public vote on future waterfront land decisions. The city has filed a motion to dismiss Keene's amended complaint, and Keene said he will continue to pursue litigation."My motivation is only to protect the publicly owned waterfront property and to make sure that major decisions are not being made without enough transparency, caution, and public awareness," Keene said. "This was never about money or personal gain for me."The dispute traces back to WPTV's reporting that the Fort Pierce landmark of nearly 80 years was facing an uncertain future after its lease expired. The city offered the land lease to bidders, drawing an outcry from residents."Our biggest fear is we don't want this to change and be a chain restaurant or a big box store," restaurant co-owner Donna Qvarnstrom said. "It's local and the people love local."After an outpouring of community support, the city kept the restaurant open month to month. Despite five formal proposals submitted to the city — including one from the current operators — the city said none met the criteria and scrapped plans to select a new tenant.Keene argues the handling of Little Jim's is part of a broader pattern of poor waterfront stewardship, pointing to two other controversial city projects: Fisherman's Wharf, where state records show the city promised land it didn't own, and King's Landing, where a developer claims the city promised buildable property that contained 1,500 tons of old power plant concrete. The Fisherman's Wharf situation led to a current multi-million dollar lawsuit filed by that project's developer and threats of a lawsuit from the King's Landing developer.Broderick said the city's management of leased properties needs to change."In my opinion, the handling of city-owned real estate that we subsequently lease out to tenants is — it's not being managed. I will not rest until I get to the bottom of this issue," Broderick said.When asked how the city plans to fix the problem, Broderick said a comprehensive review is needed."This is going to take a top down, bottom up approach to look at the entirety of the portfolio of the city of Fort Pierce and fix this one asset at a time," Broderick said.Broderick also said the city is planning to hire a real estate manager to oversee development decisions and prevent future situations.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A Leon County judge has ordered Florida to rewrite the ballot language for Amendment 3, ruling that the Legislature’s description of its sweeping property-tax proposal is biased, inaccurate and misleading.First reported by Florida Politics, Circuit Judge David Frank granted summary judgment to the challengers Monday night, declared the current title and summary “clearly and conclusively defective” and blocked Secretary of State Cord Byrd from placing that wording on the November ballot.Frank ordered Attorney General James Uthmeier to submit corrected language to the Department of State within 10 days. Read the full ruling.⁠The decision does not remove Amendment 3 itself from the ballot. Frank stressed that the court is not deciding whether the property-tax plan is good policy, only whether voters are receiving a fair and accurate explanation before making that decision.“They fail both prerequisites and must be rewritten,” Frank wrote.Judge calls title a political sloganThree consolidated lawsuits challenged the title “Save Our Homes From Excessive Property Taxes” and a summary promising to benefit taxpayers, protect small businesses, preserve core services and ensure fairness.Frank agreed that the title resembles campaign messaging more than a neutral description.“The title is more akin to a political slogan,” he wrote. “It is not fair or neutral. It advocates a policy position: to stop excessive property taxes.”The judge found the word “save” was designed to provoke an emotional response. He also ruled that invoking “Save Our Homes” could confuse voters because that name is already commonly associated with Florida’s existing 3% cap on annual assessment increases for homesteaded property.Amendment 3 would not change that cap.Frank further found that the promise to save homes from “excessive” taxes could be misleading because the amendment does not guarantee lower overall tax bills. Cities and counties could respond to a smaller tax base by raising millage rates or using special assessments, potentially offsetting some homeowners’ savings.Renters could also face higher costs if landlords pass along increased taxes, Frank wrote.“Simply put, the proposed ballot title does not state the basic legal purpose of the amendment; it endorses it and diverts voters from its actual effect,” the ruling states.Court finds errors throughout summaryThe ruling directs Uthmeier to remove the summary’s opening declaration that the amendment “benefits Florida taxpayers” and four promotional taglines:“Exempting homestead properties from taxation,” “Ensuring funding for core services,” “Protecting small businesses” and “Ensuring fairness for Florida residents.”Frank found several additional problems with the description.The summary says the amendment would exempt the first $250,000 of a homestead’s value when it takes effect in 2027. The proposal would actually set the exemption at $150,000 during 2027 before increasing it to $250,000 in 2028 and adjusting it for inflation beginning in 2029.The court also rejected language promising a “schedule for full elimination” of non-school homestead property taxes. The amendment would instead require lawmakers to establish a procedure through which cities and counties could increase the exemption up to a home’s full assessed value. It would not require local governments to eliminate those taxes.Frank found the promise of “ensuring funding for core services” misleading because the proposal does not guarantee a minimum funding level for police, fire rescue, infrastructure or other services. State economists estimate the measure would substantially reduce the tax revenue available to local governments.The pledge to protect small businesses was also rejected. The amendment would reduce the annual assessment-growth cap from 10% to 5% for all non-homestead property. That includes large commercial properties, rentals and second homes — not specifically small businesses.The judge also ruled that the summary misstates who would face a waiting period before receiving the expanded exemption. The distinction is based on whether someone was a Florida resident by Dec. 31, 2026, and when that person begins claiming a homestead exemption, not simply whether residency was established after Jan. 1, 2027.Finally, Frank found the summary failed to disclose a potentially significant shift in government authority. The proposal would place language in the Constitution allowing the Legislature to control how cities and counties spend property-tax revenue, an alteration to local home-rule powers the judge said voters should be told about.Ruling follows heated hearingThe decision largely adopts arguments made during a July 29 hearing by plaintiffs including the nonprofit Save Our Voters From Misleading Ballot Language, several former mayors, former Republican state Sen. Jeff Brandes and former Democratic U.S. Al Lawson Jr.“This is probably the worst example of a biased ballot question and an inaccurate ballot question that we’ve seen,” plaintiffs’ attorney Jamie Cole told Frank. “This is really just a political campaign flyer.”State attorneys had argued that the title and summary must be considered together and are required to describe only the amendment’s chief purpose—not every possible fiscal or policy consequence.“The summary is supposed to be written for voters, not for lawyers,” state attorney Ben Gibson said during the hearing.Frank ultimately sided with the plaintiffs, rejecting the state’s request for summary judgment.Attorney general gets a roadmapThe ruling provides suggested language for several portions of the replacement summary.Frank said the new wording should clearly state that the non-school homestead exemption would increase to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. It should describe the reduction of the non-homestead assessment cap from 10% to 5%, accurately explain the residency distinction and include the full range of permitted local-government expenditures.The attorney general is not required to use Frank’s examples word for word, but the replacement must correct each deficiency identified in the order.The court will retain jurisdiction over the rewrite. Any challenge to Uthmeier’s replacement language must be filed within 10 days after it is submitted to the Department of State.The order is final for purposes of an appeal, meaning the state can ask a higher court to reverse Frank’s decision. County election officials may begin printing ballots Aug. 27, leaving a compressed timeline for any rewrite, renewed challenge or appeal.What Amendment 3 would doThe Legislature approved Amendment 3 during a June special session called by Gov. Ron DeSantis.For people who establish permanent Florida residency by Dec. 31, the proposal would increase the non-school homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. School district property taxes would remain unaffected.The measure would also reduce the assessment-growth cap for non-homestead property from 10% to 5%, establish a waiting period for newer residents and place constitutional language around how cities and counties spend property-tax revenue.Florida’s Revenue Estimating Conference projected the quantifiable portions would reduce local property-tax collections by nearly $4.93 billion in the 2027-28 fiscal year. The modeled recurring impact is approximately $11.83 billion annually. Read the state fiscal analysis.⁠Amendment 3 requires support from at least 60% of voters to pass in November.

A Fort Myers man was arrested after an apparent road rage incident Saturday night on I-95 in Martin County that caused a family’s vehicle to crash into a barbed wire fence and left them hiding in the woods. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the incident involved a woman traveling in her own vehicle and her brother, his wife, and their young son following in another vehicle while on vacation from North Carolina. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "He tries to run the sister off the road, makes multiple attempts to run her off the road, brake checks her a couple of times. She starts panicking, calling her brother and saying there is something going on, I'm not sure what it is," Budensiek said. He said the brother caught up to the suspect, identified as Michael Spires, who then targeted his vehicle. At one point, Spires performed a pit maneuver, causing the family’s vehicle to spin off the road and crash into a barbed wire fence. Body camera footage shows the family emerging from the woods where they had been hiding after fleeing their vehicle. "The family at that point is extremely alarmed. They think he may be armed; they know he's not thinking clearly, so they jump out of the car, and they flee and they're hiding in the woods," Budensiek said. Spires drove to a nearby gas station and stayed there before speaking with investigators. "I got out of the car, and this blue car ran into me," Spires said. Spires, who is from Fort Myers, was taken into custody and appeared before a judge Monday afternoon. Officials said he had a dog in his vehicle at the time of the incident, which they later learned was stolen from his ex-boyfriend. The dog has since been returned. The sheriff said no one was injured during the incident. "The sister had driven about a few miles further up the road. She came back to the scene to tell her story. They're all safe, but only by the grace of God they are safe because this could have been so much worse," the sheriff said. Detectives said Spires was arrested and charged with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and child abuse. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

Housing affordability is a hot topic at WPTV Let's Hear It community events. At a recent Delray Beach Let's Hear It, we discovered a local solution that's making homeownership possible for low-to-moderate income families."Considering what we know about the economy and how expensive everything is, we'd entirely be homeless," David Obee said.Obee was eager to discuss with WPTV reporter Victor Jorges about what the Delray Beach Community Land Trust means to him and his brother. WATCH: About a decade ago, the brothers were struggling with rising rent when they heard about a community meeting at Pompey Park. That meeting changed their lives—they learned about the Delray Beach Community Land Trust, a nonprofit that helps low-to-moderate income families buy and rent homes at prices they can actually afford.After a year of paperwork, the Obees moved into a 3-bedroom, 2-bathroom house on 14th Avenue. To put that in perspective, they bought their home for around $142,000 in 2009. Today, according to trust executive director Evelyn Dobson, a comparable home would cost at least $450,000. The trust's homes typically cost around $300,000, but grants and other resources can bring that down to about $275,000. The secret to keeping costs low? The Delray Beach Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) usually buys the land and transfers it to the trust. This means homeowners only pay taxes on their house—not the expensive land underneath it.The savings make a huge difference in people's lives, Dobson explains."You can keep your healthcare up, save money for your kids college, go on vacations that you never went on before, you can make improvements to your home," Dobson said.The trust currently manages 146 units total with zero vacancies and five more projects in development. The CRA also offers grants up to $15,000 for exterior home improvements in certain neighborhoods, covering everything from painting and landscaping to driveway repairs and fence installation."We have eight (more) homes coming, hopefully within the next year," Dobson said.To learn more about the Land Trust, visit https://www.delraybeachlandtrust.org/

John Dial John ‘Kaz’ Kazanjian Sarah Heard The Hometown News sent the same list of questions below to each qualified candidate in the August 18 Primary Election for the District 4 Martin County Commission Seat. Question 1: What do you view as the most serious issue facing Martin County and how would you propose addressing that if elected? Question 2: There will be a referendum this year on raising the Homestead exemption and potentially cutting ad valorem property tax income significantly to municipalities. If you are elected and that passes, what areas of the county budget would you suggest trimming or cutting out altogether if need-be? Question 3: Where do you stand on Martin County’s current plan to fund the Brightline train station and potentially relocating that to the county fairgrounds site? Question 4: Do you think the County Commission should address the lack of affordable housing, and if so, in what way? Question 5: On June 23, the County Commission majority voted to approve the Business Development Board’s annual $450,000 funding as part of the Consent Agenda. District 1 Commissioner Eileen Vargas cast the lone opposing vote, insisting the BDB become self-sufficient like the Economic Development Council of Martin County and potentially merge with that entity. If elected, would you support the BDB’s current funding or side with Commissioner Vargas? Question 6: The possibility of data center applications, particularly in the Indiantown area, have been very divisive. Have you studied this issue yourself, and if so, how do you think it should be addressed if you’re elected? Question 7: If elected, how would you work to improve the quality of life for Martin County voters? The most serious issue facing our county right now is over-development, and that problem has only gotten worse with Senate Bill 180, as well as SB102 and the new mandates coming from Tallahassee. These state actions take power away from local voters and leaders and make it harder for Martin County residents to control the kind of growth in their own communities. If I am elected, I will fight to take that authority back. I will go to Tallahassee as often as necessary to represent local control and push to restore the county’s ability to make decisions for itself. Without a repeal or major reform of this law, we will remain trapped in a cycle of over-development no matter what the people of Martin County want. In my view, we should have been more vocal, more organized, and more aggressive in standing up against these state changes before they were passed. We cannot afford to make that mistake again. The consequences for local government budgets are significant, and we must be prepared to act responsibly if it is approved. Like the families and taxpayers we serve, government must learn to live within its means. Over the past several years, citizens have been forced to make tough choices as housing costs, rent, groceries, and electric bills have continued to rise. If this measure passes, I will work to protect essential services first – fire protection, law enforcement, waste management and education – while carefully reviewing non-essential programs and discretionary spending for reductions. We must make sure taxpayer dollars are directed to priorities that truly serve the public. I also believe new development should pay its fair share and not shift additional burdens onto existing taxpayers. In addition, we should explore ways to turn costly county assets – Sailfish Splash, the golf course and the café on the beach – into revenue-producing opportunities. Facilities such as these could potentially be leased to private operators, allowing the county to reduce losses and create income. Every budget should be scrutinized, including the discretionary spending available to the five commissioners. I support a “use it or lose it” policy so that unused funds are returned to the general fund and put toward real needs in the districts. We should closely evaluate every dollar going to 501(c)(3) organizations to ensure there is a measurable return for the community, and we should look for better public-private partnerships where appropriate. I do not support using taxpayer money to fund a private company, especially one that is not U.S.-owned, carries roughly $2 billion in debt and is reportedly losing more than $220 million a year. That said, I would be open to a train station or stop in our county if a private rail company or a qualified buyer emerging from bankruptcy proceedings wanted to invest their own capital here. I would also consider a fair market land-lease for a smaller-scale facility at the fairgrounds or another appropriate location, provided the arrangement protects the public interest. If the company fails or goes out of business, the property should immediately revert to the county, and taxpayers should face zero financial risk. Yes, I do support it, either with non-profits such as Love And Hope In Action or if a developer is seeking to market a project as affordable housing or workforce housing. They should be required to deliver real affordability for the community. That means negotiating firm standards so that a defined percentage of the total units must be reserved at an affordable or workforce price-point. Permits should be made contingent on compliance with those terms. Affordable housing should serve working families, young people, teachers, first responders, and seniors. This is about fairness, accountability, and making sure that growth actually helps the people who live and work here. I support the Business Development Board in its current role. It plays an important part in helping Martin County grow by attracting quality jobs, strengthening our economic base and recruiting the kind of industries that support long-term prosperity. At the same time, if we are forced to make spending cuts, every use of taxpayer dollars must be examined carefully. No public funding should be automatic or off limits. That said, the BDB has a real value to our county. It helps position Martin County to compete for manufacturing opportunities, workforce recruitment, marine industry expansion, aeronautical jobs and other businesses that bring good-paying employment and responsible growth to our community. I am continuing to study this issue and will keep reviewing new information as it becomes available. If elected to the County Commission, I will give this matter my full attention and direct county staff resources toward gathering the facts before taking a position in support of or opposition to it. This is ultimately a decision for the Village of Indiantown, and whatever course they choose, the county should be prepared to assist and support them appropriately. At this time, I do not believe there is enough reliable information for me to make a final judgment. Protecting our natural resources must remain a top priority. I will work to improve water quality in both our fresh and saltwater systems and address the pollution sources that threaten them. I will also work to preserve agricultural lands, defend our development boundaries and review every available option to strengthen our comprehensive plan and restore appropriate limits on urban service expansion. At the same time, I will keep traffic concerns front and center, because growth must never outpace infrastructure. Within the laws and regulations I inherit, I will do everything possible to protect the character of Martin County and make sure our growth policies reflect the interests of current residents and not just future development pressure. Avoid allowing urban development to occur outside the Urban Services Boundary. The legislature is taking that decision-making out of the Board’s hands. Only essential services are allowed to be funded with ad valorem taxes, which means public safety – the Sheriff and Fire Rescue. All other public services are deemed non-essential. Even if funding only public safety, we would not be able to fund public safety by the third year. I am in favor of a train station here. At present the site is downtown. If the majority of residents overwhelmingly favors a fairgrounds location, I would consider it. We do through partnerships with the state and federal agencies, and we partner with Habitat for Humanity. We should continue to evaluate land trusts. I agree that the BDB is far too dependent on government funding. I don’t want to see data centers in unincorporated Martin County. They are not allowed uses on agricultural lands, so a comprehensive plan amendment would have to be approved to change the future land use. I would oppose such an amendment. My priorities have always been to clean up our water, stop over-development and keep our taxes low. Those remain my priorities. Chris Dzadovsky Michael Broderick FORT PIERCE – The Fort Pierce City Commission decided Monday to give King’s Landing plans another look at a special meeting Sept. And while commissioners have agreed to give developers an additional 180 days to attempt to fill a $15 million funding gap, they have said that money won’t come from local taxpayers. Development partner Live Oak Holdings Group LLC, of Jacksonville, will get until early 2027, to see if it can garner the $15 million shortfall from “friends and family” investors who may not demand the 18-22 percent return commanded by typical hotel financiers. But continued work to salvage the mixed-use King’s Landing development that has floundered over the past five years was not universally embraced by city leaders Monday night. Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said he was “not willing to go one step further,” calling for the city to “cut bait and move on” with the downtown waterfront development. Dzadovsky suggested developers already have defaulted on their timelines for financing and getting buildings up. Now, he claimed, those investors want to save the proposed Marriott hotel portion of the project that’s a linchpin for the remaining housing, office, retail and restaurant facets. However, Commissioner Michael Broderick argued that a 180-day extension to find the remaining $15 million capital was “a responsible ask.” suggesting that pulling the plug now could result in five years of costly litigation for the city to reclaim the land currently owned by a private developer, plus a 10-year delay in any development of the former H.D. Paul Bertozzi, Live Oak president and chief executive officer, said Monday he’s already begun contacting “third tier” potential investors. “A hotel should not fail in this market in this location,” said Bertozzi. Broderick said he believes there also may be a “pool of local money that could be interested as well.” Broderick suggested King’s Landing original developers may have known they could fall short of meeting their capital requirements, but Bertozzi said the gap was created as a $50 million hotel project ballooned over time to more than $60 million. Mainsail Lodging and Development, the primary force behind the proposed downtown hotel, has already missed at least three deadlines in contracts with the city, including a requirement to have the hotel’s financing “fully and finally closed” by July 15. The financing gap that threatens the project first became public in July when commissioners met as the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency (FPRA) board. Live Oak officials said they were surprised to first learn a shortfall existed in April. So far, Live Oak has been the only member of the development group that has appeared before the city commission to answer questions. Commissioners said Monday they want “the whole team” to be present Sept. 14 to discuss whether the project has a future. If commissioners decide Sept. 14 to keep the current King’s Landing deal on life support a bit longer, they will still have to act Sept. 15 as the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency to approve a fourth amendment to the original contract. The city has been embroiled in a series of questionable real estate deals involving city-owned land. Fort Pierce is facing state environmental fines for unpermitted docks added at Little Jim Bait and Tackle by the tenant that leases the site from the city. And the city is owed more than $200,000 in delinquent rent and property taxes for land it leased to a private company for Crabby’s restaurant downtown. A lease for vacant land on Avenue D involving two then-city employees resulted in a former city manager facing trial on charges of bid tampering and official misconduct and the city leased the former Means Court building to a non-profit, only to have the building shuttered shortly after it opened due to building code violations that could take $2 million to fix. VERO BEACH — Laughter echoed across Whole Family Pediatrics’ new campus as children proudly carried new backpacks, explored emergency vehicles and enjoyed games during the practice’s Back-to-School Celebration on Aug. The event drew hundreds of families and connected them with school supplies, local resources and the medical team that will care for many of them throughout the school year. The strong turnout reflected the community’s enthusiasm. Families began arriving well before the 10 a.m. start, and even after the celebration got underway, vehicles continued to line 37th Place as parents waited to enter. Inside, Whole Family Pediatrics staff and volunteers distributed backpacks filled with school supplies. Outside, community partners, including Indian River County Fire Rescue, Waste Management, the Boys Girls Clubs, The Buggy Bunch and several other organizations, offered educational resources, interactive activities and healthy refreshments. Organizers planned to distribute 150 backpacks but quickly realized they would need more. “We planned for 150 backpacks,” Director of Compliance and Administration Colette Heid said. “The community response was incredible. We ended up giving away more than 250.” For Vero Beach resident Joselyn Alvarado, the event represented more than receiving school supplies. She said Whole Family Pediatrics’ bilingual staff services help Spanish-speaking families feel welcomed and supported. Marissa Collins, a local nurse who attended with her sons, praised the variety of resources available and the welcoming atmosphere. She said she hopes the celebration becomes an annual tradition. Chief Executive Officer Marie Andress, MBA, CTP, said the practice expanded its traditional back-to-school efforts by creating an event that welcomed families to its new location while strengthening community connections. “We wanted families to meet our staff and connect with local resources,” Andress said. The celebration also highlighted the practice’s year-round support for families, including its diaper pantry, walk-in appointments, same-day sick visits and after-hours access to an on-call nurse. Director of Pediatric Clinical Operations and Director of Quality Tiffany Poisson, PA-C, encouraged parents to establish healthy sleep routines before school begins and seek medical care early when children become ill. Whole Family Pediatrics offers comprehensive pediatric care and family-centered support at its Vero Beach and Fort Pierce locations. Find out more at wholefamilypediatrics.org or call 772-918-9300. A man awaiting a possible retrial in the fatal shooting of his former girlfriend is accused of attacking convicted murderer Otto Lenke inside the St. According to an arrest affidavit, Robert Castro approached Lenke in a jail dorm on July 6 and struck him in the face, knocking off his glasses. Lenke approached an intercom and reported the attack to corrections staff, the affidavit says. A deputy noticed a cut on the upper part of Lenke’s nose, and a nurse treated the injury. A jail sergeant witnessed Castro strike Lenke, according to investigators. Surveillance video also showed Castro approaching Lenke and hitting him in the face, the affidavit says. Lenke later told a detective he had been using a jail-issued tablet to watch a chess game when Castro attacked him. Investigators attempted to interview Castro on July 16. The affidavit says Castro repeatedly stated that he did not understand his Miranda rights and did not want to speak with the detective, ending the interview. Castro, 30, is charged with battery by a person detained in a prison or jail facility, a felony. The new charge was filed July 20. Lenke, a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter, was convicted in May of first-degree murder and first-degree arson in the 2021 death of Richard Benson. Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson three times inside Benson’s Fort Pierce motorcycle shop, poured an accelerant on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. A jury later voted 11-1 to recommend that Lenke be sentenced to death. Castro’s murder conviction reversed Castro was convicted in 2024 of first-degree murder with a firearm in the death of his former girlfriend, Taylor Ann Sato, and sentenced to life in prison. However, the Fourth District Court of Appeal reversed the conviction in February after finding that the trial court failed to properly complete the process for determining whether Castro was competent to stand trial. A psychologist found Castro competent in November 2022. Five days later, his attorneys raised concerns about his condition, and the original judge said Castro had definitely decompensated before ordering another evaluation. The appeals court said the record contained no additional evaluation, report or competency hearing after that order. Nearly two years later, a different judge declared Castro competent based on the original 2022 evaluation. Castro then went to trial and was convicted. The appellate court ruled that a two-year-old evaluation was not sufficient because competency must be assessed close to the time of trial. The case was sent back to the trial court to determine whether Castro’s competency during the 2024 trial can now be reliably evaluated. Castro would receive a new trial if a retrospective evaluation cannot be conducted or if the court determines he was not competent during the original trial. 2022 killing Fort Pierce police accused Castro of killing Sato outside her Timber Ridge Lane home during the early morning hours of July 23, 2022. According to the original arrest affidavit, a man called 911 and said he had shot and killed his girlfriend and was considering killing himself. Officers arrived and found Sato outside the home with multiple gunshot wounds. Investigators reported finding six gunshot wounds and several 9 mm shell casings near her body. Sato’s stepfather told detectives that she and Castro had recently ended a long-term relationship. He said Sato had blocked Castro’s phone number, but Castro continued trying to contact her by sending repeated $1 transactions through Cash App with messages attached. The stepfather also told police Castro had previously threatened to kill Sato. After listening to part of the 911 call, he identified the caller’s voice as Castro’s, according to the affidavit. Castro later surrendered to deputies in St. Investigators said several rounds of 9 mm ammunition were found in his pocket. His police interview ended after an attorney arrived and directed detectives not to question him further.

The victim in a weekend murder-suicide in Port St. Lucie has been identified as a communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. Fifty-year-old Elizabeth Ortega had been employed at PBSO for the last ten years. The shooting happened Saturday night both inside and outside a home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. In a video statement released Monday, police said a man began shooting at the woman inside their home, chased her outside, and continued firing, hitting her multiple times. "One of the neighbors actually located that victim after they observed her lying in the front yard unresponsive," Officer Brittany McNally of the Port St. Lucie Police Department said. On Monday afternoon, PBSO posted about Ortega on social media, saying, in part, "She was a respected and cherished part of our PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room." Police said the shooter was Ortega’s longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Jr. After killing Ortega, Varela went back inside the home and killed himself. McNally said Ortega and Varela had been together for about 30 years, but Ortega had recently ended the relationship. "Although the relationship had ended, it appears the two had agreed to live together until Ralph could find other living arrangements," McNally said. Investigators are working to determine what led to the violence. The couple’s son had left the home just minutes before the shooting and told police everything seemed fine. "There’s no evidence to suggest that there was a disagreement, a disturbance or an argument that occurred directly prior to the shooting," McNally said. The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office has provided therapy dogs to help Ortega’s co-workers cope with the loss. A Treasure Coast man said rising property taxes in Florida pushed him to leave the state and buy a home in Puerto Rico, where he pays nothing in property taxes. WATCH BELOW: 'The price of housing here is much less than Florida,' Jock Tate tells WPTV's Consumer Reporter Matt Sczesny "The property taxes are going up and up and I'm like I just can't afford it," Jock Tate said. Tate now lives in Salinas, Puerto Rico, in a 3-bedroom home he purchased for $95,000. As a disabled veteran, he qualifies for exemptions that eliminate his property tax bill entirely. "The price of housing here is much less than Florida, especially South Florida," Tate said. His move comes as Florida homeowners face rising property tax burdens across the state. According to a Florida Tax Watch study, property taxes rose 146.2% in St. Lucie County between 2014 and 2024. Other Treasure Coast counties saw similar increases — 131.5% in Okeechobee County, 99.4% in Palm Beach County, 90.1% in Indian River County and 90.1% in Martin County. Florida voters will have a chance to weigh in on property taxes this November. A referendum on the ballot would raise the Homestead Exemption, lowering property tax bills for Florida homeowners. Many city and county officials have warned that rolling back property taxes would lead to budget cuts and force local governments to raise other fees and taxes to offset lost revenue.
