The Space Coast Symphony Orchestra will perform Landscapes Legends on Sunday, August 10, at the Community Church of Vero Beach, 1901 23rd Street. The concert features works exploring magic and myth, with guest conductor Patrick Phillips leading the performance. The program opens with Dukas' The Sorcerer's Apprentice, the 11-minute orchestral tone poem famously depicted in Disney's Fantasia. The concert includes the world premiere performance of Kenneth Fuchs' Cloud Slant, a work capturing light, motion and atmosphere. Fuchs won the 2018 GRAMMY Award for Best Classical Compendium for an album recorded with the London Symphony Orchestra for Naxos. Vero Beach music and arts leader Dr. Jacob Craig will perform Edward MacDowell's Piano Concerto No. 2, a deeply romantic and expressive three-movement work composed in 1885. The work holds the distinction of being the first major piano concerto written by an American. Renowned pianist Van Cliburn chose MacDowell's Piano Concerto No. 2 at age 18 for his professional orchestral debut. The concert concludes with Pines of Rome, the 1924 orchestral tone poem by Italian composer Ottorino Respighi. The 22-minute work dramatically depicts four different locations around Rome framed by iconic pine trees. Tickets cost $35 through www.SpaceCoastSymphony.org or at Marine Bank Trust branches, and $40 at the door. Concertgoers aged 18 and under or with a college ID are admitted free. More than 100 women's college basketball players have teamed up to form a union for college athletes as part of their growing push to collectively bargain with their schools, an organizing group announced Friday.The United College Athletes Association said as part of the push, members of the Oregon State women's team filed a petition with state regulators, marking a formal effort to seek collective bargaining rights under state law.RELATED STORY | NCAA transfer portal rules, NIL could change under new bipartisan Senate billThe announcement comes two years after a group of women's basketball players co-signed letters to Southeastern and Big Ten Conference leaders in 2024, requesting a formal collaboration process on issues affecting college athletics.Since those efforts were denied, more than 100 female athletes have signed union authorization cards with the UCAA, agreeing to representation in collective bargaining.The announcement comes a few days after the College Football Players Association revealed that Stanford has become the first football team to organize a player-led chapter — another effort by college athletes to unionize.The UCAA says its mission is to represent and protect athletes through collective bargaining, ensuring that college sports are safe, fair, sustainable and that athletes have a say in decision-making."As interim president of the UCAA, I'm proud to help lead a movement that gives college athletes a real voice in the decisions that shape our lives and careers," University of Maryland basketball player Oluchi Okananwa said in a statement.RELATED STORY | NCAA accuses DraftKings of trademark infringement in March Madness marketingNCAA leaders have long opposed the idea of players becoming employees of their schools, though the idea isn't universally opposed by college leaders. Tennessee athletic director Danny White has been among those who have said collective bargaining is the only real solution to the problems that confront schools that are now paying millions to their players.Attempts to create unions for college athletes at Dartmouth and Southern California stalled in 2024 due to the changing landscape in college sports and the then-incoming Trump administration's new National Labor Relations Board, which wasn't expected to approve the moves.

What the Martin County Sheriff describes as the worst animal hoarding case he has ever seen has grown larger, with 108 animals now rescued. When investigators searched 77-year-old Gail Gustino's home near Hobe Sound on July 20, they found 92 dogs and cats living in triple-digit heat with no ventilation and surrounded by inches of waste. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: Gustino has since been released from jail on bond, with her next court date scheduled for September. The Martin County Sheriff described how Gustino was able to avoid detection. "She walled herself off and made her house where you couldn't just walk up to the front door and see what was going on in there, where code enforcement couldn't just come out there. So while she's got some mental illness component in her life, she's also pretty savvy with law enforcement," the sheriff said. Since the initial rescue, the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says the total number of animals recovered has climbed to 108, with more arriving daily. "Every single day more animals are coming forth from the same case. Apparently Gail had friends that she dropped off animals too and the friends have been bringing the animals to us to surrender them," the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast said. The shelter says it has been overwhelmed by community support since the rescue. "It is so heartwarming to see the community come together. Our hallways are filled with donations. We are using the donations as quickly as they're coming in," the shelter said. Staff says more animals are being medically cleared for adoption every day, but the shelter still needs help. We need fosters," the shelter said. Longtime animal rescuer Tish Ott has been waiting for the chance to bring one of the rescued animals home. "This little girl has been through hell and back, and I just wanted her to finally realize what a real life was," Ott said. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is encouraging people to check its website for the latest adoption listings. A Florida man is behind bars after deputies say he used a PIT maneuver to send a North Carolina family's SUV into a barbed-wire fence during a road rage attack that began on I-95 and, at one point, passed through Stuart. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office , the crash happened around 7:30 p.m. on Saturday near Kanner Highway and I-95. Investigators identified the suspect as 36-year-old Michael Jeffrey Spiers, who is charged with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and child abuse. Deputies say the family had no role in any confrontation before they were targeted. See also: 100-car Florida street takeover sparks 140-mph pursuit ending in 4 arrests According to investigators, Spiers first went after a woman who was driving alone, chasing her through a gas station parking lot before following her onto the highway. The woman frantically called 911 and told dispatchers he repeatedly tried to force her off the road. The woman's brother was following behind her in a separate car with his wife and young son. Authorities say Spiers then turned his attention to the family's vehicle, throwing objects, brake checking and attempting to run it off the roadway. Investigators say witnesses reported Spiers was flailing his arms and making what appeared to be gang signs during the encounters. According to the arrest report, the woman lost Spiers by driving the wrong way up an exit ramp to get back on I-95. Deputies say the suspect continued chasing the family's SUV. Eventually, the suspect intentionally performed a PIT maneuver on the family's car; a tactic typically used by law enforcement to stop fleeing vehicles. The impact of the PIT-maneuver sent the family's SUV spinning off 96th Street near Kanner Highway and crashing into a barbed-wire fence, deputies said. The three family members ran out of the car and into the brush to hide until deputies arrived. Spiers drove to the nearby Sunoco gas station at Kanner Highway and 96th Street where deputies took him into custody. Deputies say Spiers didn't know the victims but believed they were stealing his money. [I] don't know what was in his mind," said Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek. He acted as if he was high on some type of of drug, some kind of a stimulant, or he was having some kind of mental episode. We don't really know." Despite the violent crash, no one was injured, including a child who was inside the family's vehicle. "They did all the things that we would recommend they do. They called 911," said Sheriff Budensiek. "Thankfully, our suspect didn't have a gun; it could have ended so much worse." See also: 1 4-year-old killed in three car collision in PBC leaving two dead and four injured Deputies also found a dog inside Spiers' vehicle. During the investigation, detectives learned the dog had allegedly been stolen in December from someone Spiers use to dated. The dog has since been reunited with its owner, according to the sheriff's office. Spiers was taken into custody and remains jailed on charges of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, child abuse and reckless driving.

A Fort Myers man was arrested after an apparent road rage incident Saturday night on I-95 in Martin County that caused a family’s vehicle to crash into a barbed wire fence and left them hiding in the woods. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the incident involved a woman traveling in her own vehicle and her brother, his wife, and their young son following in another vehicle while on vacation from North Carolina. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "He tries to run the sister off the road, makes multiple attempts to run her off the road, brake checks her a couple of times. She starts panicking, calling her brother and saying there is something going on, I'm not sure what it is," Budensiek said. He said the brother caught up to the suspect, identified as Michael Spires, who then targeted his vehicle. At one point, Spires performed a pit maneuver, causing the family’s vehicle to spin off the road and crash into a barbed wire fence. Body camera footage shows the family emerging from the woods where they had been hiding after fleeing their vehicle. "The family at that point is extremely alarmed. They think he may be armed; they know he's not thinking clearly, so they jump out of the car, and they flee and they're hiding in the woods," Budensiek said. Spires drove to a nearby gas station and stayed there before speaking with investigators. "I got out of the car, and this blue car ran into me," Spires said. Spires, who is from Fort Myers, was taken into custody and appeared before a judge Monday afternoon. Officials said he had a dog in his vehicle at the time of the incident, which they later learned was stolen from his ex-boyfriend. The dog has since been returned. The sheriff said no one was injured during the incident. "The sister had driven about a few miles further up the road. She came back to the scene to tell her story. They're all safe, but only by the grace of God they are safe because this could have been so much worse," the sheriff said. Detectives said Spires was arrested and charged with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and child abuse. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

Lucie Police have identified the victim and suspect in what investigators are calling a murder-suicide in a neighborhood. Officers responded just before 8 p.m. Saturday to a home on SE Oxmoor Terrace after reports of a shooting . Neighbors told CBS12 they heard about four gunshots, followed by another shot a few minutes later. They say they never imagined something like this would happen in their neighborhood. Exclusive cellphone video shared with CBS12 shows Port St. Lucie police surrounding the home with guns drawn, repeatedly ordering Ralph Varela Sr., 50, to come outside. According to police, Varela used an AR-style rifle to shoot his longtime partner, Elizabeth Ortega,50, around 7:30 p.m. Investigators say the couple was in the process of separating. A Treasure Coast man said rising property taxes in Florida pushed him to leave the state and buy a home in Puerto Rico, where he pays nothing in property taxes. Jock Tate now lives in Salinas, Puerto Rico, in a 3-bedroom home he purchased for $95,000. As a disabled veteran, he qualifies for exemptions that eliminate his property tax bill entirely. Tate said the price of housing in Puerto Rico is much less than Florida, especially South Florida. He said property taxes were going up and he could not afford it anymore. His move comes as Florida homeowners face rising property tax burdens across the state. According to a Florida Tax Watch study, property taxes rose 146.2% in St. Lucie County between 2014 and 2024. Other Treasure Coast counties saw similar increases: 131.5% in Okeechobee County, 99.4% in Palm Beach County, 90.1% in Indian River County and 90.1% in Martin County. Florida voters will have a chance to weigh in on property taxes this November. A referendum on the ballot would raise the Homestead Exemption, lowering property tax bills for Florida homeowners. Many city and county officials have warned that rolling back property taxes would lead to budget cuts and force local governments to raise other fees and taxes to offset lost revenue. Boca Raton city staff are proposing two options for a new police headquarters after voters rejected a $175 million bond proposal in March, and the city's new police chief says the project is one of his top priorities.The first option would place a new headquarters on a 16-acre site at Spanish River Boulevard and Broken Sound Boulevard. A petition with nearly 800 signatures is mounting against a proposal that could transform Fort Pierce's Museum Pointe — a public waterfront park along the Indian River Lagoon — into a mega-yacht marina.WATCH BELOW: 'We have been talking for years about better locations for that history center,' Erick Gill tells WPTV's Kate HusseyThe proposal is part of the Port of Fort Pierce's updated 2026 Master Plan. It calls for redeveloping Museum Pointe, which is currently home to a history center, public waterfront access, fishing piers, and green space, into a facility featuring floating docks, a multi-story marina, an event center, a waterfront restaurant, and a clubhouse.Opponents fear the plan could privatize one of the city's most treasured public spaces."Giving public land to private folks," said Terry Howard, a volunteer at the History Center at Museum Pointe Park. For more than 50 years, the museum has preserved artifacts from Florida's Native American tribes, Spanish shipwrecks, and more. The master plan's renderings place the proposed marina clubhouse exactly where the museum stands today."Basically taking away a gem — a public gem that belongs to the people and replacing it with a facility for mega yachts," Howard said. "We're trying to keep this area as it is." St. Lucie County spokesperson Erick Gill said the museum's future is not in jeopardy if the project moves forward."Staff's intent was never to close the museum," Gill said. He added that the master plan is designed to expand economic development, create jobs, and generate county revenue."I think all local governments are looking for a way to generate revenue, so we can continue to lower the taxes for St. Lucie County residents and generate revenue from economic development, and we already have dock space there," Gill said."Anything that's going to be a positive economic driver for the City of Fort Pierce, I'm going to embrace completely," Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick added. Broderick said the city will have the final say on whether the project moves forward, and that commissioners will have to weigh economic benefits against preserving waterfront access.When asked which priority — economic development or waterfront access — would take precedence, Broderick said the answer is not simple."That's the challenging question right there. I believe that we can strike a balance," Broderick said. "We always have to be careful not to eliminate public access to the waterway. Period." Martin County is weighing changes to its local shark fishing ordinance after the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission directed the county to align its rules with state regulations. It's a move that has drawn significant public concern. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission asked the county to bring its ordinance in line with state law, which preempts counties from regulating saltwater fishing. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: "There is a state statute that has essentially preempted the powers from the county to regulate salt water fishing that includes shark fishing. Preemption meaning the state says, 'county you can't control this anymore,'" Assistant County Attorney Melissa Petrick said. State law requires a saltwater fishing license and a special permit for shark fishing. It also allows shark fishing within 1,000 feet of a guarded beach at all hours. Among those opposing the changes is Jessica Veatch, whose then-3-year-old daughter Violet was attacked by a bull shark on Bathtub Beach in Martin County 9 years ago. "I hear a scream that goes Mommy," Veatch said. "I come up out of the water and all I can see is the blood filling the water and I lifted her up out of the water and saw what was left of her leg." Veatch said she believes nearby fishing activity may have lead to the attack.. "We noticed some young men that were spearfishing on the reef," Veatch said. "That is what provoked the attack on my daughter." Veatch said she was alarmed to learn the county may now be forced to eliminate its local shark fishing regulations. "They're currently treating our shoreline like a Pavlov's dog experiment with an apex predator and I don't think that's going to work out in anybody's best interest," Veatch said. Indian River Keeper Jim Moir raised concerns about the potential impact of the changes at the Tuesday commission meeting. "These animals are incredibly important to our ecosystems. The angler offshore are complaining bitterly daily about how many of their caught fish are being depraved by sharks. Attracting more sharks to the coast is not only bad for human safety, but it's bad for angling, its bad for our public awareness, it's bad for the sharks," Moir said. County attorneys suggested the ordinance does not need to be eliminated entirely. "We can rework the ordinance and then instead of eliminating everything we can just reference the illegality of things under state law," Petrick said. County commissioners voted to table the discussion, directing staff to review concerns raised by the community and commissioners and draft new ordinance language. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is challenging the state's Catholic bishops, warning that church-run schools must honor parents' religious vaccine exemptions under state law — or risk losing access to state scholarship funding.In a letter to Catholic school leaders, Uthmeier argues state law requires schools to accept religious vaccine exemptions even if church leaders disagree. More than 525,000 Florida students use state scholarship programs, including roughly 92 percent of Catholic-school students. Daryl Campbell, D-Fort Lauderdale, said.Campbell also pointed to what he called more pressing concerns facing Floridians."We're over here focused on trying to afford things. Palm Beach County health officials have confirmed a locally acquired case of dengue fever, prompting a mosquito-borne illness advisory and warnings from health experts for residents to take mosquito prevention seriously.WATCH BELOW: 'If it happens to bite someone, that someone will likely get the infection,'Unlike most dengue cases seen in South Florida, the patient did not travel outside the area before getting sick."The importance of this announcement is that this is the first case that would happen in someone who has not left Palm Beach County," Dr. Kleper De Almeida, an infectious disease specialist working at several hospitals in Palm Beach County, including Good Samaritan Medical Center, said.Every year, Florida sees what doctors call "imported cases" of dengue, where travelers become infected overseas and return home carrying the virus. But local transmission means mosquitoes in Palm Beach County are now carrying dengue and spreading it to people in the area."What this means is that there are mosquitoes floating around, flying around, carrying the dengue virus," De Almeida said. "If it happens to bite someone, that someone will likely get the infection."Palm Beach County Mosquito Control has already been dispatched in response to the confirmed case. Health experts say the situation will likely not turn into a massive outbreak, but they do expect additional infections."Usually one of these, having one case is a signal that there are mosquitoes flying around with the dengue virus," De Almeida said. "If infected mosquitoes bite an uninfected person, there is a good chance that the person will catch the infection.""We'll probably see a few people, and there would not be a huge number, hopefully," De Almeida said.Dengue symptoms can be intense and often begin with fever and severe pain."The telltale symptom is severe body aches, body and joint aches accompanied by a fever," De Almeida said. The lower back hurts, the joints hurt."Some patients may also develop a rash."There is a rash that comes and goes," De Almeida said.In more severe cases, bleeding complications can develop, including a rash on the skin that does not blanch."There are unfortunately no direct treatment," De Almeida said. "One has to wait it out."Doctors recommend using acetaminophen, like Tylenol, to manage fever and pain instead of medications like ibuprofen or aspirin, which could worsen bleeding complications."If using aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen or other anti-inflammatory medications, it might exacerbate these bleeding complications," De Almeida said.Mosquito experts say one of the best ways to stop the spread starts in your own backyard. Harold Fortes with Mosquito Shield of Palm Beach said standing water is the primary concern."What we're gonna do is spray all the vegetation," he said. "You see these pots right here? So, what mosquitoes does is they lay eggs in there."Fortes said standing water can produce mosquitoes in as little as eight days, with some species breeding in as few as four days."It's rainy season, big time for them to reproduce," he said.Residents are being urged to clean gutters, remove yard debris, and empty trays underneath flower pots. Experts also said bromeliad plants should be rinsed regularly, because they naturally collect water that can allow larvae to grow.De Almeida said dengue is just one of several dangerous illnesses spread by mosquitoes in Florida."There is West Nile that causes a brain infection. There is chikungunya that causes severe joint and muscle pains. We remember Zika that happened a number of years ago," De Almeida said.His message to Palm Beach County residents is simple: avoid mosquito bites whenever possible."We need to be more conscious, more attentive to not being bitten by mosquitoes during the summertime in Florida, because we can be acquiring one of these infections," De Almeida said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. STUART — Martin County residents can help teachers prepare for the new school year by adopting a classroom, funding a project or donating supplies through the Education Foundation of Martin County. As Martin County students prepare to return to school Aug. 10, the Education Foundation of Martin County is inviting residents, civic groups, nonprofits and businesses to help meet classroom needs through three online programs. Adopt-A-Class allows supporters to adopt a specific classroom or school program with a donation of $100 or more. Classrooms and programs may be adopted multiple times, and the foundation hopes to have every classroom adopted at least once during the school year. To adopt a class and make a donation to a classroom or program, visit www.educationfoundationmc.org/p/251/adopt-a-class . Through Fund-A-Project, teachers can post requests for classroom projects designed to support student learning. Donors can select and fund specific educational projects. To view teacher requests, visit www.educationfoundationmc.org/p/285/fund-a-project . Bulletin Board Listings connect community members with nonmonetary classroom needs. Participants may volunteer their time or donate materials, gently used equipment, books, magazines, shoe boxes and other reusable supplies. The aerial view for the P-1 Motor Club being developed on a 626.3-acre property located on the south side of Okeechobee Road near Summerlin Road. Lucie County Commission approved the major final site plan on July 21 with a few modifications to conditions of approval primarily related to the timing of landscape installation. The site plan for the P-1 Motor Club being developed on a 626.3-acre property located on the south side of Okeechobee Road near Summerlin Road. Lucie County Commission approved the major final site plan on July 21 with a few modifications to conditions of approval primarily related to the timing of landscape installation. Lucie County Commission voted unanimously July 21 to approve the final major site plan for the P-1 Motor Club while also agreeing to the developer’s request to modify a few of the 33 staff conditions of approval. Senior Planner Thad Crowe presented the request that evening for the 626.3-acre property located on the south side of Okeechobee Road near Summerlin Road. “This is a final site plan for the P-1 Motor Club on Okeechobee Road, [about] 3.8 miles outside the Urban Service Boundary,” he said. “First, a little history: In 2023, the original comprehensive plan amendment was passed to establish the special district for the P-1 Motor Club. That was followed by a second comprehensive plan amendment in 2025, specifically allowing for public or private provision of potable water. The planned mixed use development was approved in 2025 as well.” Crowe then provided specific details of the plan as he pointed to a map on the overhead screen. “On the right-hand side is one of the tracks,” he said. “On the left-hand side, is the second track, the Treasure Coast Circuit and the P-1 Circuit. A lot of this stuff – the garagemajals, the residences, the R D park – is way into the future. Right now, the applicant is focusing on these two tracks.” Crowe also touched on the applicant’s preliminary landscape plan for the property, which no longer has any native vegetation. “The applicant did have a conceptual landscape plan they submitted with this application,” he continued. “It’s their intent to work with their landscape firm to develop comprehensive landscaping across the whole site, establishing ecosystems such as native oasis with palms and shade. This is a blank slate and an opportunity to establish reforestation and reintroduce native communities to the site.” The senior planner provided his own recommendations on that aspect before reading through the conditions of approval. “We are recommending that the northern and eastern buffer at a minimum should be required in this first phase,” he said. “The landscaping is a work in progress; the applicant has not provided complete details and the Environment Resources Department has been working with us. Their stance on this is that a finalized landscape plan be required prior to development and required landscaping in place prior to the site-development permit. With the recommended conditions, we believe the major site plan is consistent with the adopted P1MC Special District, the PMUD site plan [and] landscape plan.” When no members of the Board had questions, the developer Ari Strauss came to the podium to request relief from a few of those conditions of approval, some actually related to the landscaping. “We have a handful of really minor conditions that we would like to ask the Board to consider modifying,” he said. “We’ve had a number of delays [and] we’re still working through some water agreements. While it’s in discussion, it’s really critical that we demonstrate some progress. We’re anxious to get the first circuit up and running hopefully in several months for our members.” Strauss then enumerated conditions, 6, 7, 27, 31 and 32 for modification. The sixth condition was the only one unrelated to landscaping, but rather required the developer to separate the bicycle or walking lanes from internal roadways. “We intend to build the cross-sections that are included in the PMUD plans, which actually has a seven-foot travel lane on both sides of the road,” he said. “We would adhere to these cross-sections unless we provide an alternate travel path that pulls members or guests away from the travel lanes. In some of our landscape renderings, we show areas where a pedestrian or bike could actually leave the travel lane and then go through unpaved sections.” The seventh condition required him to plant shade trees along the roadways 30 feet apart. “We’re asking if we can change it from shade trees to native trees,” he explained. Instead, we want it to appear more like native plantings.” While Conditions 31 and 32 were related to his desire to preserve native trees along the Summerlin Road right of way, Strauss’ requested relief from number 27 eventually got pushback from county staff. “We would ask for – rather than prior to commencement of development – that we would provide the finalized landscape plan within 12 months of the commencement of development,” he said. “Then within 24 months of commencement, we will complete all the landscaping plans for Okeechobee Road, the entrance, all the completed interior roads and the littoral plantings around the stormwater ponds and lakes. As we get the first track running, we’ll have a lot of work around the site with earth-moving equipment and ponds being dug. It would be difficult to have all of the landscaping done and in place.” District 1 Commissioner James Clasby immediately asked Planning Manager Kori Benton to confirm that his staff had no objections to the applicant’s modifications. “I don’t think we have concerns or conflicts with the provision of time, as long as we have a plan or goal,” Benton replied. Commissioner Clasby then admitting to having met with ERD staff in his office and expressed his support for the modifications. “I don’t mind delaying when they are compliant with their landscaping requirements, only that they eventually do [comply],” he said. “That portion on number 27… seems like a reasonable timeline.” Environmental Regulations Manager Aimee Cooper, however, still wasn’t convinced, asking Strauss to reiterate that timeframe. “Within 12 months of commencement, the applicant shall provide all the way to the landscape typicals plan,” he explained. “Within 24 months of commencement, we will complete the landscaping plans for Okeechobee Road, the entrance, all of the completed interior roads and all of the littoral plantings. If that modification is approved, I believe that eliminates number 28.” His last comment on a separate condition concerned Environmental Planner Brian Ingram, however. “I think ERD’s okay with deferring some of it,” he said. “But by eliminating Condition 28, they would be authorized to use the track without the code-required landscaping.” After back-and-forth clarification questions between commissioners and Strauss, Cooper posed her own question directly to the developer. “I need some details here on what minimum landscaping would be installed for the first track so that we have a better understanding,” she said. “Then for the second track, would it be possible to have a majority of the landscaping installed?” “We could commit to that,” Strauss answered. “For clarification, within 12 months of commencing development, we’ll provide the finalized landscape plan. And where I suggested within 24 months of commencement, we will complete the plans for Okeechobee Road entrance and littoral plantings around the ponds. We could commit to having that done before the second track, the P-1 Circuit, is open, since we believe it will be roughly a year and a half instead of the two years we asked for. If that is amenable to you, we would be amenable to that as well.” After Cooper found that acceptable, the County Commission voted unanimously to approve the major final site with the modifications to the conditions of approval. STUART — Stories of beloved pets and second chances brought readers and animal advocates together as local children’s author Sherry Dunn celebrated the release of her newest book, “The Quiet Bond.” The book signing at the Court House Cultural Center in downtown Stuart was presented in partnership with MartinArts and catered by Riverwalk Café Oyster Bar. Cobie’s Cottage, a local nonprofit that rescues senior dogs and helps find them homes, also participated. Several of the organization’s dogs greeted guests throughout the evening, reinforcing one of the book’s central messages that some of life’s deepest connections are often the quietest. Following a reading, Dunn met with attendees during a book-signing reception. Guests shared stories about pets that had changed their lives. “The goal was never simply to sell books,” Dunn said. “It was to encourage people to cherish the quiet bond they already share with their pets, consider opening their hearts to a senior rescue animal and leave inspired to make a difference.” “The Quiet Bond” is a collection of engaging anecdotes exploring the connection between animals and humans. Through wise and often humorous stories about Dunn’s rescue cat, Jasmine, and quieter reflections, including the meditative experience of watching an aquarium, the book illustrates how animals can bring comfort, improve moods and enrich people’s lives. The evening also showcased the power of community partnerships. The Court House Cultural Center provided an inviting setting. Riverwalk Café Oyster Bar delighted guests with an assortment of hors d’oeuvres including a crowd-favorite baked Brie. Cobie’s Cottage reminded everyone that compassion can change an animal’s life forever. Dunn said she hopes the book will encourage readers to appreciate their pets and consider visiting a local shelter or rescue organization. For information, visit sherrydunn.com or cobiescottage.org . Two senior FIFA officials criticized Gianni Infantino's World Cup sell-off plan Friday with one resigning as a presidential adviser and a second saying staff were deceived by project that must not go ahead.Carlos Cordeiro, who represented the soccer body on the White House Task Force for the World Cup, resigned in protest at the private equity plan."I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup," Cordeiro, a former Goldman Sachs banker, said in a statement resigning as adviser to FIFA President Gianni Infantino that urged other senior FIFA staff to speak out.RELATED STORY | UEFA members threaten FIFA boycott, Concacaf rejects World Cup investor planFIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said in a statement to The Associated Press staff were "deceived" by Infantino's lack of openness planning the private investor scheme and "deserve better than contempt and intimidation.""It is the project of one person," Lamour, a long-time colleague of Infantino at both FIFA and UEFA, wrote. "Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions."Lamour did not resign the post he held since 2024 but said he had a duty to his colleagues."And if that means I lose my job, then so be it" the French official said. "I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."Cordeiro often joined Infantino on working visits to meet U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House in recent years."Let me be clear. I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally," Cordeiro, the former U.S. Soccer Federation president said, calling the $20 billion commercial subsidiary "a bad deal for football.""Football has been central to my life, and after more than 35 years in banking, I understand both the value of this asset and the consequences of giving part of it away" he said. "That is why this proposal should be rejected."RELATED STORY | FIFA's Infantino sets deadline to members in Kushner-backed World Cup planInfantino has proposed spinning off FIFA's commercial businesses — including World Cups and Club World Cups for men and women — into a $20 billion subsidiary with 20% owned by private investors.The "anchor investor," described by FIFA, is a New York-based investment firm created by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner."FIFA already has access to extraordinary financial resources. The organization sits on billions of dollars in reserves and no debt," Cordeiro said, noting FIFA's revenue of $15 billion over the last four years tied to the men's Wold Cup just ended."Against that backdrop, selling a permanent stake in football's most valuable asset to raise $4.2 billion makes little sense. It is mortgaging football's future without any compelling justification," he said.Cordeiro said he shared five years working for FIFA alongside Infantino with "dedicated, principled people who care deeply about the game.""I hope they, too, will speak up," he wrote, "because decisions of this magnitude should be made in the interests of football, not those who stand to profit from it."Infantino has been president of FIFA for more than 10 years and had seemed sure to be reelected unopposed next March. 18 deadline for challengers to come forward.

VERO BEACH – The members of the Vero Beach Planning Zoning Board unanimously recommended July 16 that the City Council change the land use of a seven-acre parcel from residential to commercial so a developer can repurpose the property at 2300 5th Ave. for mixed-use development as part of a northern extension of the Miracle Mile Business District. Planning Development Director Jason Jeffries provided a brief introduction that afternoon for the three related agenda items, of which the last for the rezoning had already been withdrawn. “The applicant, 2300 5th Avenue LLC, has purchased an office building just north of the Miracle Mile Business District,” he said. “Many people locally know this property as the Doctors’ Clinic. Through redevelopment, they’re looking for this site to become integrated into the Miracle Mile area. That required three separate applications: One is the future land use map amendment, the first hearing; then a text amendment to update one of the figures in the map series, which designates the commercial districts; and the rezoning. Most of the presentation is going to occur in the first hearing.” Principal Planner Cheri Fitzgerald then kicked off that presentation. “The request is to change the future land use map from the existing residential medium to the proposed commercial,” she said. “The property is just north of the Miracle Mile commercial district [and] is currently an office/pre-school. To the north is an office complex, and the land use is residential medium; To the south is the Miracle Mile area; to the east is a multifamily residential apartment complex; and to the west is a pre-school/daycare. The amendment is to extend the Miracle Mile commercial district to the north, which would allow mixed-use residential and commercial uses that could better align with more recent development trends.” Fitzgerald based her recommendation of approval on the application’s compliance with city code. “The future land use map amendment is found to be consistent with the standards for review in Section 6525 of the land development regulations,” she explained. “It is compatible with the surrounding area in terms of existing uses and future land-use designations.” Board Member Samantha Irvin was the first to question what the future development might contain. “Do we know yet what type of commercial businesses are going to go there?” she asked. Jeffries tackled that inquiry. “It depends on what’s been submitted to staff,” he replied. That is one of the reasons why our recommendation was not to approve the zoning so that we would get a more specific development plan or some further updates that we’re working on with the B-4 Zoning to ensure it is pedestrian oriented.” Vice-Chairman Thomas “TP” Kennedy then asked about potential traffic impacts but discovered it was probably too early in the process to get clear answers on that concern as well. “Does making it more pedestrian friendly decrease the traffic?” he asked. “Is that what you guys are looking for in the B-4 Zoning?” “Because they say it’s going to be pedestrian oriented, they say there’s more internal capture in the modeling,” Jeffries answered. “Again, this goes back to making sure in the zoning you actually get the pedestrian-oriented development. I think on Indian River Boulevard... some intersection improvements are needed.” Fitzgerald offered her insight as well. “At this level like Jason explained, it’s more theoretical,” she said. “You do the overall analysis and you look at the most practical case with those assumptions, and that’s what the traffic impact analysis did. Once you get a project-specific development, the traffic report will be specified to that site plan.” After more Board member questions related to both traffic and the pedestrian-friendly focus, the applicant’s contracted developer Keith Kyte and contracted Land Planner Rebecca Grohall both came to the podium. “The reason we’re here today is we need the Commercial Land Use Designation to answer those questions,” Kyte said. “We’re aligning it with the city’s 2005 Vision Plan.” Grohall then provided details on the current status of the property and the ideas for repurposing it. “This was originally the Doctors’ Clinics specialized in heathcare,” she said. “A lot of specialty medical practices eventually migrated toward the hospital and opening their own facilities. Today, it’s generally utilized as office and a pre-school and it does face vacancy rates and under-utilization.” Grohall emphasized that the site plan was in limbo until the Commercial Land Use is approved. “The site plan hasn’t even been started because we need to put the foundation in place,” she explained. “Possibly one of those pieces could be a hotel. We’re looking at multifamily units, a true mixed-use development where there’s ground-floor retail and upper floor residential uses. You’ll see the map of how this interfaces with the neighborhood. This is a visualization, and this would be a non-vehicular pedestrian connection that would bring you into the Miracle Mile shopping plaza.” After much further discussion, Vice-Chairman Kennedy wondered why the Parc24 office building currently under construction by Kimley-Horn wasn’t included since it sits just north of the 2300 5th Avenue LLC property. “When I read through this over the past week, I thought for uniformity it might be better for Kimley-Horn to come in too,” he said. “Was there any conversation there with them?” The answer according to Jeffries was cut and dry. “That was staff’s recommendation, but they decided not to become part of this application,” he said. The Planning Zoning Board then voted 4-0 to recommend approval, with Board Member Bethany Fortunato and Chairman Jeb Bittner Absent. They also recommend amending the Miracle Mile Corridor element of the city’s comprehensive plan. Your comment has been submitted. Reported There was a problem reporting this. What the Martin County Sheriff describes as the worst animal hoarding case he has ever seen has grown larger, with 108 animals now rescued.When investigators searched 77-year-old Gail Gustino's home near Hobe Sound on July 20, they found 92 dogs and cats living in triple-digit heat with no ventilation and surrounded by inches of waste.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:Gustino has since been released from jail on bond, with her next court date scheduled for September.The Martin County Sheriff described how Gustino was able to avoid detection."She walled herself off and made her house where you couldn't just walk up to the front door and see what was going on in there, where code enforcement couldn't just come out there. So while she's got some mental illness component in her life, she's also pretty savvy with law enforcement," the sheriff said.Since the initial rescue, the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says the total number of animals recovered has climbed to 108, with more arriving daily."Every single day more animals are coming forth from the same case. Apparently Gail had friends that she dropped off animals too and the friends have been bringing the animals to us to surrender them," the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast said.The shelter says it has been overwhelmed by community support since the rescue."It is so heartwarming to see the community come together. We are using the donations as quickly as they're coming in," the shelter said.Staff says more animals are being medically cleared for adoption every day, but the shelter still needs help."We need resources. Three men from Palm Beach County have been sentenced in federal court for trafficking and sexually exploiting three teenage girls who had run away from foster care, the U.S. Attorney’s Office announced Monday. Antonio Michel, 36, of Delray Beach, was sentenced to 15 years in prison after he pleaded guilty to sex trafficking of a minor; Jaime Figueroa, 36, of Boynton Beach, to 19 years and seven months in prison after he pleaded guilty to production of child sexual abuse material; and Raymond Jean, 46, of Greenacres, to 12 years in prison after he pleaded guilty to sex trafficking of a minor. HSI West Palm Beach and the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office Human Trafficking Task Force investigated the case.“These defendants found missing foster children who needed protection and chose instead to exploit them, supply them with drugs, and sell them for profit,” said U.S. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida.According to court documents, the defendants preyed upon three teenage girls who had run away from foster care. Taking advantage of the victims’ youth, instability, and lack of family support, the defendants transported, harbored, and commercially exploited the minors for financial gain.Michel, often accompanied by Jean, transported the victims to and from hotels, motels, and other locations where commercial sex acts occurred. Michel also rented and paid for multiple hotel and motel rooms used to facilitate the exploitation of the minor victims.Figueroa directed the victims on how much money to charge for commercial sex acts and how to conduct the “dates.” He also regularly supplied crack cocaine to the victims during the course of the trafficking scheme. The victims turned over proceeds from the commercial sex acts to Figueroa. Following Figueroa’s arrest, law enforcement searched his cellphone and discovered that he had produced child sexual abuse material involving one of the victims.“No child should ever be subjected to such cruelty," Special Agent in Charge José R. Figueroa of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Miami said. "These sentences represent an important step toward justice for the victims and demonstrate that HSI and our partners will use every tool available to identify, investigate, and bring child predators to justice.”

By: Samantha Roesler Posted RIVIERA BEACH, Fla. — A 28-year-old West Palm Beach man is dead following a three-vehicle crash on I-95 North in Riviera Beach late Sunday night. The Florida Highway Patrol (FHP) responded to the crash near the 45th Street exit at around 11:20 p.m. A 2015 Cadillac was stopped in the outside center lane when a 2013 BMW traveling behind it was unable to avoid a collision, causing the BMW to hit the rear of the Cadillac. A third vehicle, a Nissan Rogue, was also unable to avoid the collision and struck the rear right portion of the Cadillac. The 28-year-old driver of the Cadillac was transported to St. Mary's Hospital in West Palm Beach, where he was pronounced dead. His identity has not been released. Three other people sustained minor injuries in the crash. Lanes reopened at 3:40 a.m. FHP says this is an on-going investigation.

A federal jury in Fort Pierce convicted a Honduran national, who was illegally in the United States, for his role in a firearms-trafficking operation that purchased firearms in South Florida through straw buyers and smuggled them to Honduras.The jury convicted Luis Matute Figueroa, 33, of Lake Worth, of conspiracy and possession of a firearm by an illegal alien, the U.S. Department of Justice said in a news release Monday.Matute Figueroa overstayed a tourist visa in 2017 and remained in the U.S. without lawful status, the DOJ said. According to investigators, WhatsApp messages recovered during the investigation revealed that Matute Figueroa provided co-conspirators with firearm inventories, pricing information and shipping instructions for weapons destined for Honduras. The messages also contained a photograph and a video of Matute Figueroa in possession of a distinctive gold Colt 1911 pistol."This defendant exploited his unlawful presence in the United States to help traffic American firearms to Honduras," U.S. Reding Quiñones said in the news release. "This verdict reflects our commitment to dismantling international gun-trafficking networks and prosecuting illegal aliens who unlawfully possess and export firearms."According to court records and evidence presented at trial, Matute Figueroa conspired with Gerson Eliu Padilla-Figueroa, Juan Matute Figueroa, Ariel Henriquez-Padilla, and William Mendoza to acquire firearms in the U.S. through straw purchases and illegally export them to Honduras, the DOJ said.Matute Figueroa faces up to five years in federal prison on the conspiracy count and up to 15 years in prison on the firearm possession count. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.The ATF Miami Field Office and Homeland Security Investigations Miami are investigating the case, with assistance from the Broward Sheriff's Office, the Martin County Sheriff's Office, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Attorney Suzanne Huyler is prosecuting the case.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The Florida Department of Environmental Protection has given Fort Pierce until Sept. 15 to review, approve and submit a proposed consent order resolving nearly $16,000 in state fines tied to docks at Little Jim Bait & Tackle.Emails obtained by WPTV from FDEP show the state agency extended the city's deadline by 90 days, meaning city commissioners have not yet formally accepted or rejected the state's enforcement terms. City staff have been negotiating with FDEP to reduce or resolve the thousands of dollars in penalties.The enforcement action follows WPTV's reporting that revealed FDEP alleges the city has been operating docks at Little Jim's on state-owned submerged land without authorization — land the agency says the city never had permission to use.City Commissioner Michael Broderick previously acknowledged the allegation."My information is that accusation is actually true, that there was an extension of the existing docks," Broderick said July 6. Broderick said it remains unclear whether the city or the Little Jim's tenant was responsible for extending the docks without the required permits."Keep in mind that the city of Fort Pierce owns that real estate, so ultimately, in the day, the city of Fort Pierce is the responsible party," Broderick said.The FDEP action is one of several legal and regulatory pressures now surrounding the historic waterfront property. In early July, Fort Pierce city commissioners voted unanimously to reject a settlement offer in a separate lawsuit filed by local resident Kevin Keene, who alleged years of waterfront mismanagement tied to Little Jim's.Under the proposed settlement terms, Keene would have dropped the case if the city halted any new plans for Little Jim until the FDEP permit issues were resolved and allowed a public vote on future waterfront land decisions. The city has filed a motion to dismiss Keene's amended complaint, and Keene said he will continue to pursue litigation."My motivation is only to protect the publicly owned waterfront property and to make sure that major decisions are not being made without enough transparency, caution, and public awareness," Keene said. "This was never about money or personal gain for me."The dispute traces back to WPTV's reporting that the Fort Pierce landmark of nearly 80 years was facing an uncertain future after its lease expired. The city offered the land lease to bidders, drawing an outcry from residents."Our biggest fear is we don't want this to change and be a chain restaurant or a big box store," restaurant co-owner Donna Qvarnstrom said. "It's local and the people love local."After an outpouring of community support, the city kept the restaurant open month to month. Despite five formal proposals submitted to the city — including one from the current operators — the city said none met the criteria and scrapped plans to select a new tenant.Keene argues the handling of Little Jim's is part of a broader pattern of poor waterfront stewardship, pointing to two other controversial city projects: Fisherman's Wharf, where state records show the city promised land it didn't own, and King's Landing, where a developer claims the city promised buildable property that contained 1,500 tons of old power plant concrete. The Fisherman's Wharf situation led to a current multi-million dollar lawsuit filed by that project's developer and threats of a lawsuit from the King's Landing developer.Broderick said the city's management of leased properties needs to change."In my opinion, the handling of city-owned real estate that we subsequently lease out to tenants is — it's not being managed. I will not rest until I get to the bottom of this issue," Broderick said.When asked how the city plans to fix the problem, Broderick said a comprehensive review is needed."This is going to take a top down, bottom up approach to look at the entirety of the portfolio of the city of Fort Pierce and fix this one asset at a time," Broderick said.Broderick also said the city is planning to hire a real estate manager to oversee development decisions and prevent future situations.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A petition with nearly 800 signatures is mounting against a proposal that could transform Fort Pierce's Museum Pointe — a public waterfront park along the Indian River Lagoon — into a mega-yacht marina.WATCH BELOW: 'We have been talking for years about better locations for that history center,' Erick Gill tells WPTV's Kate HusseyThe proposal is part of the Port of Fort Pierce's updated 2026 Master Plan. It calls for redeveloping Museum Pointe, which is currently home to a history center, public waterfront access, fishing piers, and green space, into a facility featuring floating docks, a multi-story marina, an event center, a waterfront restaurant, and a clubhouse.Opponents fear the plan could privatize one of the city's most treasured public spaces."Giving public land to private folks," said Terry Howard, a volunteer at the History Center at Museum Pointe Park. Howard contacted WPTV's Kate Hussey after learning about the master plan. "Development is just rampant in Florida, and at least we can fight for this one particular area and keep it green," Howard said.He said the loss of public waterfront access is a concern — but his biggest worry is the fate of the museum itself."This is the place where this museum should be, right here on this Museum Pointe," said Howard. For more than 50 years, the museum has preserved artifacts from Florida's Native American tribes, Spanish shipwrecks, and more. The master plan's renderings place the proposed marina clubhouse exactly where the museum stands today."Basically taking away a gem — a public gem that belongs to the people and replacing it with a facility for mega yachts," Howard said. "We're trying to keep this area as it is." St. Lucie County spokesperson Erick Gill said the museum's future is not in jeopardy if the project moves forward."Staff's intent was never to close the museum," Gill said. "We have been talking for years about better locations for that history center; it is on a barrier island, in a flood zone, so it may not be the best place to store artifacts."Gill said the museum and its collection would be preserved and relocated if the project proceeds. He added that the master plan is designed to expand economic development, create jobs, and generate county revenue."I think all local governments are looking for a way to generate revenue, so we can continue to lower the taxes for St. Lucie County residents and generate revenue from economic development, and we already have dock space there," Gill said."Anything that's going to be a positive economic driver for the City of Fort Pierce, I'm going to embrace completely," Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick added. Broderick said the city will have the final say on whether the project moves forward, and that commissioners will have to weigh economic benefits against preserving waterfront access.When asked which priority — economic development or waterfront access — would take precedence, Broderick said the answer is not simple."That's the challenging question right there. I believe that we can strike a balance," Broderick said. "We always have to be careful not to eliminate public access to the waterway. Period." For Howard, the stakes go beyond the present."This is a gem that once we develop around it, it'll never be replaced again," Howard said. "The museum has been here since the 1970s. If they want to boat docks for mega yachts, they can do it someplace else." St. Lucie County leaders are scheduled to discuss the proposal and its current status at a 9 a.m. Lucie County Commission Chambers.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. INDIAN RIVER COUNTY – With the six-month Atlantic hurricane season underway, Senior Resource Association (SRA) worked with Florida Power Light Company (FPL) to distribute hurricane preparedness meal kits to seniors in Indian River County. This effort, also in partnership with the Florida Council on Aging, provides vital supplies to vulnerable seniors in the communities the companies serve. Each kit, courtesy of FPL, includes three days of shelf-stable food, water and snacks for seniors who may not be able to leave their homes or receive home-delivered meals immediately after a storm. The kits also include a hurricane preparedness guide with tips and resources. Volunteers from FPL and SRA distributed the kits, helping ensure seniors have the resources they need to stay safe. “FPL has been an incredible partner to our organization, and we’re grateful for their continued commitment to the seniors we serve,” said Senior Resource Association President and CEO Karen Deigl. “Preparing for hurricane season can be stressful, especially for older adults living alone.” “We’re committed to powering strong communities – ensuring our most vulnerable customers have the necessary resources to weather any storm,” said FPL External Affairs Manager Michele Murrell. “By working with Senior Resource Association, seniors in our community are now better prepared for hurricane season.” Since 2016, FPL has worked with local community nonprofits to deliver thousands of hurricane kits to help seniors prepare for storm season. A student receives a back-to-school haircut at Fort Pierce Beauty Academy. A client receives a fresh look at Fort Pierce Beauty Academy. FORT PIERCE — A fresh haircut can help students walk into a new school year with a little more confidence. The Academies of Cosmetology is offering free back-to-school haircuts for school-age children at its three Treasure Coast campuses through Aug. Families do not need appointments or advance registration. Students and parents may walk in, sign in and wait for the next available barbering or cosmetology student, much as they would at a traditional barbershop or salon. Kris Evangelista said the schools have long offered discounted back-to-school haircuts, but began offering them for free only within the past few years. “It’s always been discounts for the kids for back to school, but I believe this is the second or third year we’re doing the free cuts,” Evangelista said. All students at the three campuses are expected to participate, with instructors supervising the work to ensure children receive quality haircuts. Families may request a specific student stylist if they choose. Evangelista said the service is especially meaningful because a haircut can make a difference in how children feel when they return to school. “It’s a fresh year, fresh haircut,” Evangelista said. “It boosts their confidence, their self-esteem.” The promotion has become popular with families, including regular clients who return each year and bring relatives and friends. Evangelista said the academies do not plan to turn anyone away. Michael Prevette owns the Academies of Cosmetology, where Evangelista assists. Evangelista said the academies also plan to continue their community outreach beyond the back-to-school season by hosting free spring and fall festivals. The free back-to-school haircuts are at Beauty and Massage Institute, 1375 U.S. 1, Suite 2, Vero Beach, 772-978-7178; Port St. Lucie Beauty Academy, 10036 South U.S. Lucie, 772-337-4747; and Fort Pierce Beauty Academy, 3028 South U.S. 1, Fort Pierce, 772-464-4885. Martin County is weighing changes to its local shark fishing ordinance after the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission directed the county to align its rules with state regulations. It's a move that has drawn significant public concern. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission asked the county to bring its ordinance in line with state law, which preempts counties from regulating saltwater fishing. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: "There is a state statute that has essentially preempted the powers from the county to regulate salt water fishing that includes shark fishing. Preemption meaning the state says, 'county you can't control this anymore,'" Assistant County Attorney Melissa Petrick said. State law requires a saltwater fishing license and a special permit for shark fishing. It also allows shark fishing within 1,000 feet of a guarded beach at all hours. Among those opposing the changes is Jessica Veatch, whose then-3-year-old daughter Violet was attacked by a bull shark on Bathtub Beach in Martin County 9 years ago. "I hear a scream that goes Mommy," Veatch said. "I come up out of the water and all I can see is the blood filling the water and I lifted her up out of the water and saw what was left of her leg." Veatch said she believes nearby fishing activity may have lead to the attack.. "We noticed some young men that were spearfishing on the reef," Veatch said. "That is what provoked the attack on my daughter." Veatch said she was alarmed to learn the county may now be forced to eliminate its local shark fishing regulations. "They're currently treating our shoreline like a Pavlov's dog experiment with an apex predator and I don't think that's going to work out in anybody's best interest," Veatch said. Indian River Keeper Jim Moir raised concerns about the potential impact of the changes at the Tuesday commission meeting. "These animals are incredibly important to our ecosystems. The angler offshore are complaining bitterly daily about how many of their caught fish are being depraved by sharks. Attracting more sharks to the coast is not only bad for human safety, but it's bad for angling, its bad for our public awareness, it's bad for the sharks," Moir said. County attorneys suggested the ordinance does not need to be eliminated entirely. "We can rework the ordinance and then instead of eliminating everything we can just reference the illegality of things under state law," Petrick said. County commissioners voted to table the discussion, directing staff to review concerns raised by the community and commissioners and draft new ordinance language. An 86-year-old woman died Thursday afternoon following a two-vehicle crash at a Port St. Lucie intersection, police said.Marie Martin was driving a 2006 Hyundai Elantra westbound on SW Lawndale Avenue around 2:30 p.m. when she entered the intersection at SW Savona Boulevard and failed to yield the right-of-way to oncoming traffic, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.A 17-year-old male driving a 2026 Honda HR-V northbound on SW Savona Boulevard struck the driver's side of Martin's vehicle, causing a T-bone collision.Emergency responders had to extricate Martin from her vehicle before transporting her to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with critical injuries. Despite lifesaving efforts by medical staff, Martin later died from her injuries.The teenage driver was not injured in the crash.The Port St. Lucie Police Department's Traffic Homicide Unit is continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding the fatal collision. Additional information will be released as the investigation progresses.

The Florida Department of Health in Palm Beach County has issued a mosquito-borne illness advisory after confirming a case of locally-acquired dengue fever.Dengue fever presents as a flu-like illness with symptoms that can include high fever, severe muscle and joint pain, intense headaches and skin rash in some cases. Symptoms typically appear within 14 days of being bitten by an infected mosquito. While rarely fatal, the illness can be severely uncomfortable and requires supportive medical care as there is no specific cure.Health officials urge residents to eliminate standing water around homes including flower pots, gutters, bird baths, and discarded tires. They also recommend using EPA-approved mosquito repellents, wearing long sleeves and pants when possible, installing or repairing window and door screens, and using air conditioning when available.Palm Beach County Mosquito Control is coordinating with health officials on surveillance and prevention efforts in the affected area. The Department of Health continues statewide monitoring for mosquito-borne illnesses including West Nile virus, Eastern equine encephalitis, and chikungunya.Anyone who develops symptoms should contact their local health department or healthcare provider. For more information on mosquito-borne illness prevention, visit the Florida Department of Health website.

A woman was killed and a man was found dead Saturday evening following what investigators believe was a domestic-related shooting in Port St. Lucie Police Department officers responded around 7:40 p.m. Saturday to the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance.Port St. Lucie police said the suspect in the domestic disturbance Saturday evening has been identified as 50-year-old Ralph Varela Sr. and the victim has been identified as 50-year-old Elizabeth Ortega.The investigation revealed that Varela and Ortega had been involved in a long-term cohabitation domestic relationship and resided together with their adult son, police said. It was learned that Varela and Ortega were in the process of separating.On Saturday at around 7:30 p.m., the adult son left the residence to pick up dinner from a local restaurant, investigators said. Investigators determined there was no known argument or disturbance inside the home prior to his departure. At some point after the adult son left, investigators believe Varela utilized an AR-style .223 caliber rifle and began shooting Ortega inside the residence, detectives said. Ortega fled the home in an attempt to escape, while Varela continued firing. Investigators recovered home surveillance video that captured portions of the incident and the video shows Ortega attempting to flee into the front yard, while Varela continued to fire at her before she collapsed. VERO BEACH — The City Council hashed out its preliminary 2026-27 fiscal year budget July 22, keeping the tentative millage rate at the current 2.9816 mills while approving several fee increases and a $410,000 transfer from the General Fund’s unassigned fund balance to cover salaries for three vacant police officer positions. City Manager Monte Falls launched the discussion and set its parameters. “At the conclusion of the workshops, we have to address the retiree benefits and set a not-to-exceed millage rate,” he said. “We’ll come back later in September and set the final millage rate and adopt the budget. Our audit was submitted on time, and based on that audit, we’re in a very strong financial position. The General Fund has a total fund balance of $54 million, and of that $54 million, 17.7 million is listed as unassigned. The committed fund balance of $35.56 million includes reserves of $5 million for storms. The unfunded pension reserve was $5.3 [million] and the Other Post Employee Benefit reserve of 6.8 million.” While emphasizing that the proposed $36.9 million budget was balanced at the tentative millage rate, Falls also recommended some tweaks to fill previously approved but still vacant police officer positions. “I would like to have a philosophical discussion about the budget, which, as presented, is balanced,” he continued. “It includes additional revenues from fees in the amount of $370,000 and holds three vacancies open in the Police Department. We recommend using $435,160 of the unassigned balance on your sheet of that $5 million to offset the contribution to the OPEB trust. That offset would allow us to fill the Police Department vacancies.” Falls then translated that into terms a city resident with a home assessed at $300,000 could understand. “With a $50,000 Homestead Exemption and a Save Our Homes 3 percent increase, the current millage rate would result in about $25 a year in additional ad valorem tax,” he explained. “What I’d like to zero in on is what would the Council like to do. We brought you the budget balanced with the existing millage and those additional revenues, with the three positions open. We would recommend making that OPEB payment out of the unassigned fund balance that isn’t held out for reserves. That would allow us to then fill those vacancies in the Police Department.” Vice-Mayor Linda Moore was the first to pose a clarification question afterwards. “Is that OPEB a recurring cost?” she asked. “It is a liability we have set aside,” Falls responded. “We have an annual payment on it, but we have had this policy looked at by our outside accounting firm. They concur with us that it is an OPEB liability that can be paid for out of that amount. If you look at the revenue portion of your budget on Page 22, the OPEB trust is that $435,000. So that money would come out of the unfunded reserves to cover that.” Both Moore and Councilmember Taylor Dingle wondered, however, how the city would continue to fund those new positions in next year’s budget. The vice-mayor particularly worried that Amendment 3 on this year’s ballot might severely impact the collection of future ad valorem property taxes needed for that funding. “We are facing the possibility of a $1.3 million hole in the budget,” Moore said. “I feel like it would be irresponsible to fund more staff this year out of money that’s not even technically recurring, and then next year we’re even in a bigger situation. We’re all reading articles in the paper about how this community might have to fire firefighters. I don’t want to fire anybody, so I’m trying to be very, very cautious.” Councilmember John Carroll chimed in with his own clarification question. “How long have these positions been vacant?” he asked. While Vice-Mayor Moore reminded him that they’d been approved since last year, Mayor John Cotugno emphasized the fluid nature of the Vero Beach Police force. “They have been fully staffed at one time,” he explained. “They’ve been down four, they’ve been down two [and] they’re down three now. It’s all over the place.” Mayor Cotugno also pointed that Vero Beach would not suffer the fate of most Florida communities if Amendment 3 passes because the city has a more varied income stream. “We are lucky that we have revenue sources no other municipality has in this county,” he said. “We have a diversified tax base so that we’re not as affected by the property tax referendum if it does pass. We have four enterprise funds; we have an industrial base; and we have residential and commercial.” Even so, Councilmember Aaron Vos worried about tapping the unassigned fund balance to pay for the new officers and hinted at postponing the decision until after November. “I hate raiding our savings piggy bank,” he said. “We have unusual circumstances here [and] a cycle of attrition in our Police Department. They’re in the pipeline, so maybe we could wait until we get Police Chief [David] Currey in here and go through the Police budget. If we move forward with a plan to allocate the funds and – depending on the outcome of the election – we’d back out. We’d have the option to just not hire.” Falls, however, pointed out that the referendum would only affect the 2027/2028 Fiscal Year Budget and not the one currently under review. “If we approve the number of positions, we budget as if we’re going to have those,” he explained. “Throughout the year, we always have some funds that aren’t expanded because we’re not always fully staffed. If we would authorize those positions and then after the election go back, we’d have to have direction from Council as a budget amendment to not hire whatever vacancies you didn’t want to hire.” Because Councilman Vos still feared those new officer salaries would put the city in financial bind, Falls offered another budgetary solution. “There’s a different way we could look at that money that comes out of the unassigned reserves,” he said. “I used the OPEB trust liability because it’s one of the things that the policy says can be used, but it also says it can be used for capital and construction. In this budget, there’s $410,000 of capital in the operating budget below the operating expense line because it’s not an operating expense. If it gave you a better comfort level to say we’ll offset that with some funds from that unassigned, then you’re not paying for a recurring expense.” Vice-Mayor Moore liked that idea, and after much further debate, the City Council approved the addition of that $410,000 to the budget, resulting in a proposed $37,352,589 budget for the 2026/2027 Fiscal Year. Falls told the Hometown News on Sept. 27 that the new police officer salaries would actually only set the city back an extra $300,000. Your comment has been submitted. Martin County commissioners postponed a decision Tuesday on shark fishing rules after the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission directed the county to align its ordinance with state regulations. The county had been reconsidering its rules following complaints that shark fishermen were using drones and remote-controlled boats to carry bait offshore and draw sharks closer to swimming areas. Commissioners asked county attorneys to review the law and return with revised ordinance language. State law preempts counties from regulating saltwater fishing and requires a saltwater fishing license and a special permit for shark fishing. Martin County's current ordinance prohibits shark fishing within 1,000 yards of the county's four guarded beaches: Jensen, Stuart, Bathtub and Hobe Sound. Assistant County Attorney Melissa Petrick told commissioners the state statute means the county can no longer directly control shark fishing regulations. County attorneys said the ordinance may not need to be eliminated entirely. They could rework it to reference activities that are already illegal under state law, including chumming directly from the beach. Residents raised safety and environmental concerns during Tuesday's commission meeting, and commissioners voted to table the discussion while staff reviews those concerns and drafts new language. Volunteers remove litter from Stuart Beach during the 2025 International Coastal Cleanup. For Hometown News STUART — Thousands of pieces of plastic, fishing line and other debris collect along Martin County’s shoreline, but volunteers will have a chance to turn the tide in a single morning. Keep Martin Beautiful will coordinate the 2026 International Coastal Cleanup on Saturday, Sept. 19, bringing residents together to remove litter from local beaches, shorelines and waterways. Last year, volunteers collected nearly 3,000 pieces of microplastic from Martin County’s shoreline during the event. For more than three decades, Keep Martin Beautiful has served as the county’s local coordinator for the worldwide cleanup effort. Each year, more than 1,000 volunteers, including individuals, families, businesses, youth groups and civic organizations, roll up their sleeves to remove litter from the shorelines. In addition to bottles and food packaging, volunteers collect cigarette butts, plastic foam fragments, discarded fishing line and microplastics. The pollutants travel through storm drains and waterways, threatening marine life and damaging coastal habitats. “Our beaches and waterways are at the heart of what makes Martin County such a special place to live,” said Tiffany Kincaid, Keep Martin Beautiful executive director. “The International Coastal Cleanup gives everyone an opportunity to make a real difference. In just one morning, volunteers can create a lasting impact while helping preserve these beautiful places for future generations.” Volunteers are encouraged to register through the Keep Martin Beautiful website and download the free Clean Swell™ app before the event. The app allows participants to record the litter they collect, providing data to Keep Martin Beautiful and the Ocean Conservancy. The information helps scientists identify pollution trends, guide conservation efforts and develop ways to reduce marine debris. Volunteers of all ages are welcome. Whether participating for the first time or returning year after year, every volunteer helps protect Martin County’s coast and becomes part of one of the world’s largest volunteer efforts to keep oceans and waterways healthy. Sponsors include WM, Martin County, Ashley Capital, Hutchinson Shores Resort Spa, Surfing’s Evolution Preservation Foundation, CSA Ocean Sciences, Lucido Associates, Indian Riverkeeper, Ecological Associates, Coastal Waste Recycling, The Guardians of Martin County, Jenkins Landscape, Live With Grace, Ram Real Estate, Solar Electric Power Company, the city of Stuart and the Firefly Group. Keep Martin Beautiful is a nonprofit organization founded in 1994. Its programs include litter prevention, recycling promotion, beautification projects, the Great American Cleanup and Adopt-A-Road and Adopt-A-Street programs.
