(Feature Impact) During back-to-school season, education is naturally at the forefront of most parents’ minds. While a lot of important learning is accomplished in the classroom, there are so many opportunities to continue challenging and developing children’s minds and hearts in family life as well. Learning about history together is a practical way to inspire deep, meaningful conversations about the world, whether from books, documentaries or visits to museums. Now is an opportune time to explore the story of Anne Frank, a Jewish teenager evading Nazi capture during the Holocaust. Families can read her famous diary together then visit “Anne Frank The Exhibition,” presented by the Anne Frank House at the Griffin Museum of Science and Industry. This comprehensive exhibition immerses visitors in the context that shaped Frank’s life, from her early years in Frankfurt through her tragic death and how her father ensured her legacy. The centerpiece is the first full-scale recreation of the Annex where the Frank family and four other Jews hid during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands. The exhibition, recommended for visitors ages 10 and older, is open through early 2027. No matter what piece of history families choose to delve into together, they should take the time to discuss with their kids what they’re thinking and feeling about everything they’re discovering. Then together they can figure out what lessons from the past can be taken into the future. “ Anne Frank ’ s story is a powerful reminder of what happens when fear and hatred are allowed to take root,” said Dr. Chevy Humphrey, Griffin Museum of Science and Industry president and CEO. “ At the same time, it reveals the quiet but enduring strength of curiosity, creativity and resilience, values that sit at the heart of our mission. We hope this exhibition offers meaningful moments of reflection for our guests, particularly young people, and encourages them to think critically about their role in the world they are inheriting.” Learn more about the exhibit and other experiences that bring history and science to life at GriffinMSI.org . Federal prosecutors said a Los Angeles man was sentenced to life in federal prison for selling fentanyl that caused the death of a Treasure Coast man, then continuing to traffic the deadly drug just two days later.U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon imposed the sentence on Alfonso Guerrero, 39, of Los Angeles, after a federal jury convicted him in May 2026 of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute fentanyl resulting in death and distribution of fentanyl resulting in death."A tenth of a gram of fentanyl, about the size of a small pinch of salt, was enough to kill David Eller," U.S. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida said in a statement. "This was not a small drug deal. Guerrero sold the fentanyl that killed his friend and, just two days later, was caught carrying more fentanyl for distribution. Today’s life sentence is the consequence of that deadly conduct and his long record of violence and crime. Together with the DEA and our local law enforcement partners, we will trace fatal doses back to the dealers who sold them and hold those dealers fully accountable."According to court records and evidence presented at trial, the U.S. Attorney's Office said Guerrero sold fentanyl in Indian River County. On May 16, 2023, prosecutors said he exchanged 0.1 gram of fentanyl — commonly known as "a point" — for another controlled substance known as "molly." Officials said the drug transaction was captured on a doorbell camera. Hours later, Eller was found dead inside his Vero Beach home. Investigators recovered drug paraphernalia, including a small piece of burnt aluminum foil that the victim used to receive the fentanyl from Guerrero on the victim's front porch, near his body.Two days later, on May 18, 2023, prosecutors said Guerrero was arrested and found in possession of additional quantities of fentanyl intended for distribution.Officials said Guerrero's extensive criminal history included documented gang membership and prior convictions for attempted robbery with a firearm in California, aggravated assault in Georgia, and cocaine and fentanyl possession offenses in Florida.

The Martin County School District has approved a consolidation of bus routes that officials say will save $255,000 without affecting students or eliminating any driver positions.The school board voted Tuesday unanimously to reduce the number of bus routes by 3, bringing the total from 58 to 55 ahead of the upcoming school year. Lucie Police have identified the victim and suspect in what investigators are calling a murder-suicide in a neighborhood. Officers responded just before 8 p.m. Saturday to a home on SE Oxmoor Terrace after reports of a shooting . Neighbors told CBS12 they heard about four gunshots, followed by another shot a few minutes later. They say they never imagined something like this would happen in their neighborhood. Exclusive cellphone video shared with CBS12 shows Port St. Lucie police surrounding the home with guns drawn, repeatedly ordering Ralph Varela Sr., 50, to come outside. According to police, Varela used an AR-style rifle to shoot his longtime partner, Elizabeth Ortega,50, around 7:30 p.m. Investigators say the couple was in the process of separating. A neighbor who knew the couple confirmed a photo obtained by CBS12 is Ortega and described her as "a sweetheart." "It's really sad," neighbor Heather Callahan said. "Obviously you don't really expect it in a town like this." Callahan said she and her family watched as police flooded the neighborhood after the shooting. "I was just really nervous," she said. "Obviously there's a lot of police, so what is going on?" Investigators say the couple's son had just left to pick up food when the shooting happened. Police say Varela first shot Ortega inside the home. Surveillance video then allegedly shows Ortega running outside in an attempt to escape, but investigators say Varela continued shooting before she collapsed on the front lawn. Ortega was airlifted to a hospital, where she later died. Police used a drone to look inside the home before entering. Investigators say they found Varela dead from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. "I asked the police officers if everything was okay, and they said it wasn't okay, but they had everything contained," Callahan said. Detectives continue to process evidence and are awaiting the medical examiner's report. Investigators also say there was no reported argument or disturbance inside the home in the moments leading up to the shooting.

A suspected burglar dressed for happy hour instead of a police lineup is now known across St. Lucie County as the Flamingo Bandit. The nickname comes courtesy of the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office , which is searching for a man photographed wearing a tropical shirt dominated by a giant pink flamingo. Some criminals try to blend in, the agency wrote. This one apparently took fashion advice from a Jimmy Buffett concert. But deputies said the man’s alleged itinerary involved burglary, not boats, beaches or frozen drinks. Investigators said the suspect entered a residence on July 28 and stole a laptop, miscellaneous food and a key to the home. Deputies allege he then returned later that same day and used the stolen key to get inside a second time. The sheriff’s office shared an image of the flamboyantly dressed suspect, hoping his difficult-to-miss wardrobe will help someone identify him. While we can appreciate a memorable wardrobe, we can’t overlook burglary, the agency wrote. Anyone who recognizes the man or has information about the case is asked to call the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office at 772-462-7300 or email Deputy V. Ancewicz at PatrolTips@stluciesheriff.com . As the sheriff’s office put it, Crime doesn’t get a free pass just because it’s dressed for paradise.

A man awaiting a possible retrial in the fatal shooting of his former girlfriend is accused of attacking convicted murderer Otto Lenke inside the St. According to an arrest affidavit, Robert Castro approached Lenke in a jail dorm on July 6 and struck him in the face, knocking off his glasses. Lenke approached an intercom and reported the attack to corrections staff, the affidavit says. A deputy noticed a cut on the upper part of Lenke’s nose, and a nurse treated the injury. A jail sergeant witnessed Castro strike Lenke, according to investigators. Surveillance video also showed Castro approaching Lenke and hitting him in the face, the affidavit says. Lenke later told a detective he had been using a jail-issued tablet to watch a chess game when Castro attacked him. Investigators attempted to interview Castro on July 16. The affidavit says Castro repeatedly stated that he did not understand his Miranda rights and did not want to speak with the detective, ending the interview. Castro, 30, is charged with battery by a person detained in a prison or jail facility, a felony. The new charge was filed July 20. Lenke, a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter, was convicted in May of first-degree murder and first-degree arson in the 2021 death of Richard Benson. Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson three times inside Benson’s Fort Pierce motorcycle shop, poured an accelerant on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. A jury later voted 11-1 to recommend that Lenke be sentenced to death. Castro’s murder conviction reversed Castro was convicted in 2024 of first-degree murder with a firearm in the death of his former girlfriend, Taylor Ann Sato, and sentenced to life in prison. However, the Fourth District Court of Appeal reversed the conviction in February after finding that the trial court failed to properly complete the process for determining whether Castro was competent to stand trial. A psychologist found Castro competent in November 2022. Five days later, his attorneys raised concerns about his condition, and the original judge said Castro had definitely decompensated before ordering another evaluation. The appeals court said the record contained no additional evaluation, report or competency hearing after that order. Nearly two years later, a different judge declared Castro competent based on the original 2022 evaluation. Castro then went to trial and was convicted. The appellate court ruled that a two-year-old evaluation was not sufficient because competency must be assessed close to the time of trial. The case was sent back to the trial court to determine whether Castro’s competency during the 2024 trial can now be reliably evaluated. Castro would receive a new trial if a retrospective evaluation cannot be conducted or if the court determines he was not competent during the original trial. 2022 killing Fort Pierce police accused Castro of killing Sato outside her Timber Ridge Lane home during the early morning hours of July 23, 2022. According to the original arrest affidavit, a man called 911 and said he had shot and killed his girlfriend and was considering killing himself. Officers arrived and found Sato outside the home with multiple gunshot wounds. Investigators reported finding six gunshot wounds and several 9 mm shell casings near her body. Sato’s stepfather told detectives that she and Castro had recently ended a long-term relationship. He said Sato had blocked Castro’s phone number, but Castro continued trying to contact her by sending repeated $1 transactions through Cash App with messages attached. The stepfather also told police Castro had previously threatened to kill Sato. After listening to part of the 911 call, he identified the caller’s voice as Castro’s, according to the affidavit. Castro later surrendered to deputies in St. Investigators said several rounds of 9 mm ammunition were found in his pocket. His police interview ended after an attorney arrived and directed detectives not to question him further.

A prosecutor says they have dropped charges against Gregory Allen Davis, 49, of Port St. Lucie in an incident June 24 in Port St. Lucie when Davis ordered three juveniles out of their car at gunpoint and told them to get on the ground at the intersection of SW Morelia Lane and SW Acapulco Terrace. Minutes earlier, one of the teens had fired an Orbeez toy gun at the car that Davis and his fiancee were in. An Orbeez toy gun shoots soft water-absorbing beads. According to a prosecutor, the reason they dropped the charges against Davis is because in Florida, citizens have the right to make a citizen's arrest if they see that a felony has been committed in their presence. The felony that Davis saw was the teen firing a gun at his vehicle. "Basically, under Florida law, a citizen has a right to make a citizen's arrest if they observe a felony, occur in their presence. So that's basically what happened here. When someone effects a citizen's arrest, basically, they have the same powers as a police officer would, at least temporarily," said Jason Bruin, Assistant State Attorney, 19th Judicial Circuit. Bruin says if the case had gone to a jury, they would've returned a verdict of not guilty. Davis, in this case, gets out of the vehicle and holds the the people that were in that car at gunpoint. No, we don't recommend that people take the law into their own hands like that. Let the police do their job. Call the police, let the police do their job," Bruin said. Davis was charged with three counts of false imprisonment and three counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Those six charges carry a maximum sentence of 30 years in prison if convicted. "I am very grateful as I am a father of three and everything I do is for my kids. The thought of being away from them is horrifying. I have a daughter that is the same age as the person who did the shooting, and I spend my time teaching my children not to do dumb things like that. Obviously I would never want anyone to ever get hurt. Especially over what they consider to be a prank. I believe behavior like this starts with the parents. It is our job to teach our kids right from wrong and be their parent first and their friend second," Davis said in a text message to CBS12 News, reacting to the fact that the charges against him were dropped. Lucie Police Department on Sunday identified the victim and suspect involved in the domestic-related murder-suicide that occurred the night before at a residence. LUCIE – The Florida Department of Environmental Protection’s Savannas Preserve State Park will conduct a prescribed burn on Monday, August 3rd, weather permitting. The prescribed burn will consist of approximately 100 acres of mesic flatwoods north of Walton Road and west of the Sandhill Crane Park. Prescribed fires are only conducted when weather parameters are suitable. The final decision to burn is made daily, after reviewing the Predicted Fire Weather forecast for that particular day and after obtaining a burn authorization from the Florida Forest Service. Prescribed burning mimics natural fire cycles to restore healthy forests and natural communities, reduce undergrowth that accumulates over time and decreases the potential for wildfire. Burned lands experience an increase in native wildflowers, birds and other wildlife. For more information on Florida s award-winning state parks, visit www.FloridaStateParks.org . Renters in Martin County say keeping up with the cost of living is a challenge, while a local real estate agent said that the market is neither rising nor falling — for now. Renters on the Treasure Coast told WPTV reporter Tyler Hatfield on Friday that the cost of living is putting a strain on their finances, even as a local real estate expert says the rental market has leveled off. Jesse Espinosa, a renter in Martin County, said the price of rent is taking a toll. WATCH BELOW: Treasure Coast renters say costs are straining budgets "I mean, living on your own, you got rent, food. You have pets, I mean, it's almost impossible," Espinosa said. Mike Edel of Martin County said his rent has gone up significantly since he first moved to the area. "It's three times more expensive than it was when I first moved down here," Edel said. Still, Edel said the Treasure Coast offers some relief compared to South Florida. "If you're comparing it to Palm Beach or Miami, it's a discount," Edel said. That relative affordability is part of what drew Hunter Wharton to Martin County after growing up in Palm Beach Gardens. "Affordability and rent prices are a little bit cheaper," Wharton said. Edel, however, said the difference is not dramatic. "It might be a little bit cheaper in the Treasure Coast, but we're only talking a couple hundred bucks," Edel said. Real Estate News Kelley Decowski, a real estate agent in Martin County, said the rental market is currently flat. "We're not seeing rental rates skyrocketing, but they're not really coming down either," Decowski said. Martin County is seeing the highest average rental rates on the Treasure Coast, ranging from $2,300 to $2,500 a month across all unit types. Decowski said those averages reflect a wide range of properties, from luxury and waterfront listings and private homes to apartment complexes. Indian River County has the lowest average rents in the region, ranging from $1,650 to $2,200 a month. Lucie County averages between $2,100 to $2,300 a month. Decowski said more rental inventory is coming to the market, which could push prices down — though inflation remains a wildcard. "We can't necessarily rule out a little bit of price growth with all of the inflationary things that are going on, but I think that we're going to see prices come down because of that inventory hitting the market," Decowski said. For Edel, the bottom line is simple. "Everywhere in Florida is expensive, and that's just the bottom line," Edel said. Despite the costs, Edel said he has accepted the reality of renting in the current market. "You're sort of paying to play," Edel said. The celebration ended with players surprising Manager George with a Gatorade shower after the shutout victory—a moment McIntosh said perfectly reflected the joy and camaraderie the team shared. The Big Brothers Big Sisters Florida specialty license plate raises money to support youth mentoring programs in Palm Beach and Martin counties. MARTIN COUNTY — A daily drive can help put a child on the road to a brighter future through the Big Brothers Big Sisters Florida specialty license plate. Proceeds from the plate support mentoring programs in Martin County and across Florida, including those offered by Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin counties. Available through the Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles, the specialty tag costs $25 annually in addition to the standard vehicle registration fee. The full amount supports youth mentoring. Proceeds go to the Big Brothers Big Sisters Association of Florida and its network of 11 local agencies, including Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties. The funding supports one-to-one mentoring relationships, training and support for volunteer mentors and resources for children in the program. Money from the plates helps recruit and train mentors in Palm Beach and Martin counties, expand access to mentoring services and support workplace readiness programs. Residents can request the Big Brothers Big Sisters specialty plate at a Martin County Tax Collector’s Office. Appointments are available at the main office, 3485 S.E. Willoughby Blvd., Stuart; 11734 S.E. Federal Highway, Hobe Sound; 16550 S.W. Warfield Blvd., Indiantown; and 3001 S.W. Martin Downs Blvd., Palm City. Drivers do not have to wait until their vehicle registration renewal to change their license plate. Because the Palm Beach and Martin County tax collector offices do not offer online specialty plate ordering, residents who prefer to order online may use a neighboring county’s tax collector website that offers the service or a licensed Florida courier tag agency. Tag agencies may charge convenience, service and shipping fees. Customers will need their current license plate number, insurance company and policy number and a copy of a valid Florida driver’s license. New Martin County residents can select the Big Brothers Big Sisters specialty plate when registering a vehicle through the Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles. Drivers seeking a personalized plate can check availability through the department’s Personalized Plate Inquiry tool, complete an Application for Personalized License Plate and submit it at a tax collector’s office. It's a conversation many families avoid because it's uncomfortable, but legal experts say putting off estate planning could leave loved ones facing expensive legal challenges and even put generations of family property at risk.WATCH BELOW: 'They can't sell it. They can't leverage the equity in it,' Tequisha Myles tells WPTV's Vannia JosephThe Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach County is encouraging homeowners to take advantage of a free estate planning and probate assistance program designed to help families protect one of their biggest investments — their home.According to Tequisha Myles with the Legal Aid Society, many families continue paying the mortgage, property taxes and maintaining a home after a loved one dies, but never complete the legal process to transfer ownership."When a homeowner dies without a will, or probate is never completed, the property remains legally in the name of the deceased," Myles said. "People are caring for the property, they're paying the mortgage, they're maybe keeping up with the taxes, but they don't have the title in their name. They can't leverage the equity in it."Without clear ownership, families can face significant financial consequences. Myles said homeowners may not be able to access the equity in the home during emergencies or qualify for disaster assistance after a hurricane."FEMA is not going to do payouts to people that don't have clear title to the property," she said. "You may have been keeping it in the family, but now to really keep it for generational wealth, you've got to actually put it in your name."The Legal Aid Society said its Heirs' Property Project helps eligible Palm Beach County homeowners resolve tangled property titles and complete estate planning documents at no cost.The program, funded through a $1 million grant from the Federal Home Loan Bank of Atlanta and Palm Beach County, includes:A Last Will and TestamentPower of AttorneyDesignation of Health Care SurrogateLiving WillLady Bird DeedProbate and heirs' property assistance, when neededMyles said those services typically cost between $3,000 and $5,000 through a private attorney."We do the drafting, you come in for a signing, it takes an hour and you have peace of mind," Myles said. "It's just a matter of planning, and I think planning helps you prepare for whatever happens."Unlike many legal assistance programs, eligibility is not based on income. Applicants must own a home in Palm Beach County and meet the program requirements.Legal Aid estimates it can still help approximately 150 more families, but applications should be submitted by Sept. 1 so attorneys have enough time to complete the work before grant funding expires at the end of September.Homeowners interested in applying or learning more about the Heirs' Property Project can visit legalaidpbc.org/heirsintake.

Nestled in West Palm Beach's Northwood district, Nine Lives Cafe offers a bright, welcoming space that creates an uplifting atmosphere portraying its positive initiative of finding shelter cats their forever homes.The cafe's origin story begins with a search that came up empty. Co-owner Jada Thornton had fallen in love with the concept while volunteering at a cat cafe in North Carolina. When Thornton and co-owner Razmig Panossian were living in Boston hoping to find a similar experience, they found nothing. Hoping West Palm Beach might offer what Boston lacked, they were disappointed once again – but this time, they took action."We took a leap of faith and decided to open a cat cafe," Thornton explained, embarking on what would become an 18-month journey to bring their vision to life.Creating Nine Lives Cafe wasn't just about opening a business; it was about building something meaningful from the ground up. With Thornton's interior design background and Panossian's construction expertise, they designed and built the entire space themselves."The time did go by fast because we were able to get a lot of support from Furry Friends (Humane), from various other people in the community, mentors." Thornton said. "So it's been a pleasurable process, honestly."The spot features two distinct areas: the main "Cat Heaven" room where visitors can interact with the cats, and a separate coffee area divided by glass. This layout allows even those with cat allergies to enjoy the experience, watching the felines while sipping coffee and enjoying pastries in a cat allergy-safe environment.The $25 entry fee to interact with the cats provides an hour-long "feline therapy session," though most visitors end up staying much longer. "Nobody wants to leave," Thornton said. "They come in here, they stay for hours." The fee supports their nonprofit mission, covering cat care, facility maintenance, and staffing until each cat finds its forever home.Behind the cozy atmosphere lies a serious mission. Palm Beach County faces a staggering euthanasia rate of at least 800 cats monthly, making Nine Lives Cafe's work crucial for local animal welfare. The cafe partners primarily with Furry Friends Animal Rescue, providing a bridge between shelter life and permanent homes."These rescue (cats) are just as lovable and their stories are amazing. They're survivors, so they know how to love," Thornton said, speaking from personal experience with their own rescue cats.The cafe environment offers significant advantages for both cats and potential adopters. Unlike a traditional shelter setting, 'Cat Heaven' provides a home-like environment where felines can roam freely, play, and display their true personalities. This setting helps cats become better socialized while giving visitors a genuine sense of each animal's character."When you're hanging out with the cats, you get to see how they are because they act like it's their home," Panossian explained. "So you get an idea, a good sense of what their personality is like."In true Palm Beach fashion, Nine Lives offers "Paw-lates" – 60-minute mat-based classes that combine classical contemporary flow with feline therapy. The connection isn't coincidental— Joseph Pilates drew inspiration from cats when developing his exercise methodology."It's kind of like a full circle moment for the Pilates world," Thornton explained. The intimate classes, held in dimmed lighting with closed blinds, create a therapeutic environment. The cafe has already facilitated a handful of adoptions– a promising start toward their goal of maintaining 10-12 adoptable cats alongside a few resident cats who provide consistency and companionship.The coffee program at Nine Lives is overseen by David McLennan, the cafe's head of coffee, who brings over 20 years of experience serving coffee everywhere from super yachts to estates to his own coffee shops. McLennan and his wife discovered Nine Lives through Instagram and were immediately drawn to the concept that combined their two passions: cats and coffee."We both love cats and we love coffee, and so this just seemed like a natural thing to reach out to them and see if I could be involved in their coffee program," McLennan explained. The cafe features a specially sourced blend from New York that McLennan describes as "lovely and approachable" with chocolatey, velvety and fruity notes. The menu includes all the classics – hot and iced coffees, mochas, and lattes – along with high-quality matcha. "You can come here as the cafe itself and enjoy the view of the cats."As Nine Lives settles into its role as West Palm Beach's first cat cafe, the team remains focused on their dual mission: providing exceptional experiences for visitors while saving lives. Reservations can be made online at https://ninelivescafe.co/ or visitors can walk in for availability at 2032 North Dixie Highway.Follow Nine Lives Cafe on Instagram @ninelivescafe.com

Federal prosecutors said a Los Angeles man was sentenced to life in federal prison for selling fentanyl that caused the death of a Treasure Coast man, then continuing to traffic the deadly drug just two days later. District Judge Aileen Cannon imposed the sentence on Alfonso Guerrero, 39, of Los Angeles, after a federal jury convicted him in May 2026 of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute fentanyl resulting in death and distribution of fentanyl resulting in death. “A tenth of a gram of fentanyl, about the size of a small pinch of salt, was enough to kill David Eller,” U.S. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida said in a statement. “This was not a small drug deal. Guerrero sold the fentanyl that killed his friend and, just two days later, was caught carrying more fentanyl for distribution. Today’s life sentence is the consequence of that deadly conduct and his long record of violence and crime. Together with the DEA and our local law enforcement partners, we will trace fatal doses back to the dealers who sold them and hold those dealers fully accountable.” According to court records and evidence presented at trial, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said Guerrero sold fentanyl in Indian River County. On May 16, 2023, prosecutors said he exchanged 0.1 gram of fentanyl — commonly known as “a point” — for another controlled substance known as “molly.” Officials said the drug transaction was captured on a doorbell camera. Hours later, Eller was found dead inside his Vero Beach home. Investigators recovered drug paraphernalia, including a small piece of burnt aluminum foil that the victim used to receive the fentanyl from Guerrero on the victim’s front porch, near his body. Two days later, on May 18, 2023, prosecutors said Guerrero was arrested and found in possession of additional quantities of fentanyl intended for distribution. Officials said Guerrero’s extensive criminal history included documented gang membership and prior convictions for attempted robbery with a firearm in California, aggravated assault in Georgia, and cocaine and fentanyl possession offenses in Florida.

West Palm Beach Police Chief Tony Araujo announced Friday the termination of five command-level officers following a nearly two-year administrative investigation into overtime misconduct, marking the latest development in what has rocked the department since 2020.WATCH BELOW: 3 West Palm Beach police captains among those fired in probe"Yesterday, following a thorough, nearly two-year administrative investigation, and after careful review of the findings, I made the difficult decision to terminate five command-level officers," Araujo said during a Friday morning press conference.The firings — which included three captains, a major and an assistant chief — come as the culmination of an investigation that began after a 2020 audit commissioned by the city uncovered nearly $20,000 worth of "double dipping" on timecards and thousands of hours of questionable overtime payments within the police department. The controversy dates back to 2020 when a third-party audit examined the finances of multiple city departments. The audit revealed what officials called "pretty egregious" overtime spending patterns within the police department that had gone undetected for years.The investigation eventually led to the firing of former Police Chief Frank Adderley and placed seven officers on administrative leave related to financial misconduct. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office was brought in to handle the administrative investigation to ensure impartiality.The press conference Friday morning comes after the union pushed back against the terminations, claiming a "different standard" was applied to the fired captains compared to other officers involved in the overtime scheme. The union had previously filed a lawsuit alleging violations of the Police Officers' Bill of Rights, though that lawsuit was subsequently withdrawn."I respect the union. They have their own opinion. They have their own interpretation. I'm going to respectfully disagree," Araujo said. "But again, we're going to leave that to the continued due process that will take place, and I don't begrudge the union for advocating for their membership."WATCH THE FULL PRESS CONFERENCE BELOW:Araujo emphasized that the terminations were part of a broader effort to rebuild trust and accountability within the department. He said the department has strengthened training, reviewed overtime practices, and implemented better supervision of extra duty assignments.The chief acknowledged the department had been on accreditation probation when he arrived, a status that city leadership was unaware of at the time. He said those issues have since been corrected.Araujo indicated the department may need to conduct promotions to fill the vacant leadership positions.The chief stressed that despite the misconduct by some officers, the majority of the department's personnel continue to provide professional service to the community."We have good people at the West Palm Beach Police Department. Be certain of that; we have good leadership," Araujo said. "We can't look at the department as a whole and make a decision of the whole just based on the few."Fraternal Order of Police Union President Adam Myers, who represents the three captains, said a criminal investigation by the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office found no criminality and determined it was an administrative matter."Initially, there was a criminal investigation by the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. They found there was no criminality and basically said it was an administrative issue," Myers said.Myers said the internal affairs report found the city had installed software designed to prevent officers from clocking two simultaneous shifts. Because the command staff members were salaried rather than hourly employees, they used what is called flex time — time earned from working beyond their regular schedule — to offset the extra hours. Myers said the practice was approved and directed by Adderley, who was chief at the time."They would put in vacation hours to take themselves off, so that it would allow the other program to let them pick up their job, and then they go back and take out the time because they aren't hourly employees," Myers said.Investigators found that because the software only checked for scheduling conflicts when a job was selected — and not after leave was removed — the overlapping hours remained. The report said at least four command staff members later admitted to using that process. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, which conducted the internal affairs investigation, called it a vulnerability that undermined the purpose of the system.Myers said the outcome has been difficult for the officers involved."If you follow the direction you're given by your supervision all the way to the top of the agency, and then to be reviewed and found that that's improper because it's a differing opinion is hard," Myers said.Araujo pushed back on that characterization."I'm going to respectfully disagree, but again, we're going to leave that to the continued due process that will take place," Araujo said.Araujo said the department's focus remains on rebuilding trust."Public trust is not something we inherit. It's something we earn," Araujo said.The union will pursue arbitration on behalf of the officers.

An 86-year-old woman died after police said she pulled into the path of an SUV and was struck in a Port St. Lucie intersection Thursday afternoon. The crash happened at about 2:30 p.m. at Southwest Savona Boulevard and Southwest Lawndale Avenue, according to the Port St. Investigators said Marie R. Martin was driving a 2006 Hyundai Elantra west on Lawndale Avenue when she entered the intersection from near a stop sign and failed to yield to a northbound 2026 Honda HR-V. The Honda, driven by a 17-year-old boy, struck the driver’s side of Martin’s car, police said. Body-camera video recorded after the crash shows the Hyundai off the roadway near a cluster of palm trees, with visible damage to its driver’s side and emergency crews working around the vehicle. The Honda also came to rest on the grass nearby, close to vegetation and a roadside sign. Lucie police officers and St. Lucie County Fire District personnel can be seen at the scene, along with fire engines, rescue vehicles and traffic cones blocking part of the intersection. Debris and emergency equipment were scattered across the grass between the two vehicles. See also: Chief: Five West Palm Beach police leaders fired following 'double-dipping' probe Martin had to be extricated from the Hyundai before she was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with critical injuries, police said. A Fort Pierce resort says an abandoned sailboat that washed ashore three weeks ago is damaging property, slamming into other boats, and costing them thousands in business, but state law prevents them from moving it. "This is a danger to people and personal property," said Joe Zebrowski, general manager of Dockside Marina and Resort. The sailboat washed ashore near On The Edge Bar and Grill, and Zabrowski and his team quickly secured it. However, Zabrowski said the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) informed him that the boat cannot be moved. The agency is giving the owners 60 days to claim the vessel, and the resort is also prohibited from moving it. "I did a good deed, but no deed goes unpunished," Zebrowski said. The FWC used a chain to secure the sailboat, but Zebrowski said it hasn’t stopped the vessel from causing problems. "It kept it from floating away but didn’t keep it from whipping back and forth," he said. Zebrowski explained that the sailboat has slammed into a docked boat, destroyed a piling, and forced the restaurant to block off several tables near the vessel, which has significantly impacted their revenue. "These are our prime tables. They probably cost us about 25 percent of our overall business for the past month," Zebrowski said. According to state law, moving a boat that has washed ashore onto private property without proper permission can expose individuals to legal liabilities or even charges of theft. "There needs to be a carveout in however the law takes care of situations like this that takes care of people who are innocent and stop protecting an owner who has abandoned his boat that I don’t think is registered or has insurance," Zebrowski said. The FWC confirmed to WPBF that no one can touch the boat except its owners. WPBF is working to contact the owners of the boat for comment. The FWC is working on providing a more detailed statement. Martin County is weighing changes to its local shark fishing ordinance after the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission directed the county to align its rules with state regulations. It's a move that has drawn significant public concern.The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission asked the county to bring its ordinance in line with state law, which preempts counties from regulating saltwater fishing.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:"There is a state statute that has essentially preempted the powers from the county to regulate salt water fishing that includes shark fishing. Preemption meaning the state says, 'county you can't control this anymore,'" Assistant County Attorney Melissa Petrick said.State law requires a saltwater fishing license and a special permit for shark fishing. It also allows shark fishing within 1,000 feet of a guarded beach at all hours.Among those opposing the changes is Jessica Veatch, whose then-3-year-old daughter Violet was attacked by a bull shark on Bathtub Beach in Martin County 9 years ago."I hear a scream that goes Mommy," Veatch said. "I come up out of the water and all I can see is the blood filling the water and I lifted her up out of the water and saw what was left of her leg."Veatch said she believes nearby fishing activity may have lead to the attack.."We noticed some young men that were spearfishing on the reef," Veatch said. "That is what provoked the attack on my daughter."Veatch said she was alarmed to learn the county may now be forced to eliminate its local shark fishing regulations."They're currently treating our shoreline like a Pavlov's dog experiment with an apex predator and I don't think that's going to work out in anybody's best interest," Veatch said.Indian River Keeper Jim Moir raised concerns about the potential impact of the changes at the Tuesday commission meeting."These animals are incredibly important to our ecosystems. The angler offshore are complaining bitterly daily about how many of their caught fish are being depraved by sharks. Renters in Martin County say keeping up with the cost of living is a challenge, while a local real estate agent said that the market is neither rising nor falling — for now.Renters on the Treasure Coast told WPTV reporter Tyler Hatfield on Friday that the cost of living is putting a strain on their finances, even as a local real estate expert says the rental market has leveled off.Jesse Espinosa, a renter in Martin County, said the price of rent is taking a toll.WATCH BELOW: Treasure Coast renters say costs are straining budgets"I mean, living on your own, you got rent, food. Two sharks were spotted along the Atlantic Ocean shore — one that washed up dead and another of fishermen struggling with a hooked one. Both incidents occurred Friday, with video sent to WPBF. Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission has ordered Martin County to follow rules about people fishing for fish or sharks from the beach or shoreline. A petition with nearly 800 signatures is mounting against a proposal that could transform Fort Pierce's Museum Pointe — a public waterfront park along the Indian River Lagoon — into a mega-yacht marina.WATCH BELOW: 'We have been talking for years about better locations for that history center,' Erick Gill tells WPTV's Kate HusseyThe proposal is part of the Port of Fort Pierce's updated 2026 Master Plan. It calls for redeveloping Museum Pointe, which is currently home to a history center, public waterfront access, fishing piers, and green space, into a facility featuring floating docks, a multi-story marina, an event center, a waterfront restaurant, and a clubhouse.Opponents fear the plan could privatize one of the city's most treasured public spaces."Giving public land to private folks," said Terry Howard, a volunteer at the History Center at Museum Pointe Park. Howard contacted WPTV's Kate Hussey after learning about the master plan. "Development is just rampant in Florida, and at least we can fight for this one particular area and keep it green," Howard said.He said the loss of public waterfront access is a concern — but his biggest worry is the fate of the museum itself."This is the place where this museum should be, right here on this Museum Pointe," said Howard. For more than 50 years, the museum has preserved artifacts from Florida's Native American tribes, Spanish shipwrecks, and more. The master plan's renderings place the proposed marina clubhouse exactly where the museum stands today."Basically taking away a gem — a public gem that belongs to the people and replacing it with a facility for mega yachts," Howard said. "We're trying to keep this area as it is." St. Lucie County spokesperson Erick Gill said the museum's future is not in jeopardy if the project moves forward."Staff's intent was never to close the museum," Gill said. "We have been talking for years about better locations for that history center; it is on a barrier island, in a flood zone, so it may not be the best place to store artifacts."Gill said the museum and its collection would be preserved and relocated if the project proceeds. He added that the master plan is designed to expand economic development, create jobs, and generate county revenue."I think all local governments are looking for a way to generate revenue, so we can continue to lower the taxes for St. Lucie County residents and generate revenue from economic development, and we already have dock space there," Gill said."Anything that's going to be a positive economic driver for the City of Fort Pierce, I'm going to embrace completely," Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick added. Broderick said the city will have the final say on whether the project moves forward, and that commissioners will have to weigh economic benefits against preserving waterfront access.When asked which priority — economic development or waterfront access — would take precedence, Broderick said the answer is not simple."That's the challenging question right there. I believe that we can strike a balance," Broderick said. "We always have to be careful not to eliminate public access to the waterway. Period." For Howard, the stakes go beyond the present."This is a gem that once we develop around it, it'll never be replaced again," Howard said. "The museum has been here since the 1970s. If they want to boat docks for mega yachts, they can do it someplace else." St. Lucie County leaders are scheduled to discuss the proposal and its current status at a 9 a.m. Lucie County Commission Chambers.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. With fewer than three weeks remaining before Florida's primary, the Republican race for governor is producing new ads, dueling polls and increasingly pointed attacks — but little evidence that the contest has tightened at the top.U.S. Byron Donalds remains the clear frontrunner, bolstered by President Donald Trump's early endorsement, superior name recognition and a significant financial advantage over his Republican rivals.This week, a political committee supporting Donalds released a statewide television and digital ad centered on affordability. The spot shows Donalds playing basketball with his sons while promising to cut property taxes, lower insurance rates and reduce housing costs."My boys deserve the same shot I got—but Florida’s pricing out our future," Donalds says.WATCH: Donalds focuses on affordability as Republican rivals scramble for momentumThe ad reflects a campaign increasingly focused on pocketbook issues—and one largely looking past former House Speaker Paul Renner, Lt. Jay Collins and investor James Fishback.University of South Florida political scientist Susan MacManus said the basic shape of the race has changed little. Donalds' three leading challengers remain divided, making it more difficult for any one of them to consolidate the opposition."Name ID, credibility, Trump endorsement—it's made it really hard for the other three candidates to gain any traction, no matter how hard they try," MacManus said.A public Cygnal survey conducted July 12-13 found Donalds leading with 43%, followed by Fishback at 12%, Collins at 11% and Renner at 2%. Another 31% remained undecided. The survey included 500 likely Republican primary voters and had a margin of error of 4.38 percentage points. View the Cygnal poll.Collins' campaign, however, released an internal poll this week showing a significantly closer contest. That survey put Donalds at 46%, Collins at 30%, Fishback at 9.8% and Renner at 5.9%.The Collins campaign argued the results show the race consolidating into a two-candidate contest. Public polling has generally shown Collins much farther behind, with Donalds leading his nearest rivals by roughly 30 points or more.MacManus said Donalds’ support has remained particularly durable among the highly partisan voters most likely to participate in a Republican primary."The three people who are running against Donalds are going to split the vote, which makes Donalds' likelihood of gaining the nomination very, very strong," she said.Fishback is trying to use a courtroom victory to generate momentum after Leon County Circuit Judge David Frank rejected Collins’ attempt to remove him from the ballot.Florida's Constitution requires a candidate for governor to have lived in the state for the seven years preceding the election. Collins pointed to Fishback’s 2020 vote in Washington, D.C., his purchase of a condominium there and tax, mortgage and homestead records as evidence that Fishback had established residency outside Florida.Fishback maintained that he never intended to abandon his Florida residency. Frank ruled that Collins failed to overcome Florida’s legal presumptions favoring continued residency and candidate access to the ballot. Read more about the ruling.Fishback responded by calling on Collins to resign as lieutenant governor.“This was not about election integrity,” Fishback said. "This was about rigging an election."Collins dismissed the demand and criticized the ruling on Thursday."I think that his decision has basically put us in a position where, if you identify as a Floridian, you are a Floridian," Collins said. "I guess we can be trans-Floridian now."Asked whether he would appeal, Collins said his team had not yet made a final decision.Renner is using his closing campaign ads to emphasize his record as House speaker, including the expansion of school-choice programs and conservative legislation passed while he led the chamber.He is casting himself as the most experienced candidate to continue Gov. Ron DeSantis' policies."If you want to have something as close to Ron DeSantis as possible, I am that person by far," Renner said.Renner also escalated his criticism of Dr. Anthony Fauci, alleging the former federal infectious-disease official helped direct taxpayer money to coronavirus research in China that Renner believes led to the pandemic."The one that to me is potentially traitorous is his support in directing taxpayer money…for gain-of-function research," Renner said.Federal audits confirm that National Institutes of Health grants to the nonprofit EcoHealth Alliance included subawards involving the Wuhan Institute of Virology. The Department of Health and Human Services' inspector general found significant failures in NIH and EcoHealth’s oversight of the grants, but its audit did not conclude that the research created SARS-CoV-2 or caused the pandemic. Read the HHS inspector general's findings.The origin of the virus remains unresolved. The World Health Organization said the weight of available scientific evidence favors an animal-to-human spillover, either directly from bats or through another animal. The organization has not ruled out a laboratory incident, saying China has not provided information needed to fully evaluate that possibility. Read the WHO assessment.On the Democratic side, David Jolly is already focusing his attacks on Donalds.Jolly this week promised to halt new AI data-center construction until Florida develops stronger protections for its water supply, electric grid, communities and consumer privacy. His campaign also accused Donalds of being too closely aligned with the industry, pointing to millions of dollars in support it says came from interests connected to data-center development."Byron Donalds wants to hand ‘pristine’ Florida land over to the data center industry that’s funding his campaign," Jolly said. "Florida is not for sale."Donalds has argued Florida should embrace data centers while imposing protections for residents. He recently introduced federal legislation that would require the facilities to secure electricity and water from private sources instead of relying on public utility systems. The proposal is intended to prevent data centers from raising residential utility costs.Vote-by-mail ballots have already been distributed for the Aug. Florida's mandatory early-voting period begins Aug. 8 and continues through Aug. 15, though counties may offer additional days. See Florida's election calendar.

FORT PIERCE — A fresh haircut can help students walk into a new school year with a little more confidence. The Academies of Cosmetology is offering free back-to-school haircuts for school-age children at its three Treasure Coast campuses through Aug. Families do not need appointments or advance registration. Students and parents may walk in, sign in and wait for the next available barbering or cosmetology student, much as they would at a traditional barbershop or salon. Kris Evangelista said the schools have long offered discounted back-to-school haircuts, but began offering them for free only within the past few years. “It’s always been discounts for the kids for back to school, but I believe this is the second or third year we’re doing the free cuts,” Evangelista said. Martin County is weighing changes to its local shark fishing ordinance after the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission directed the county to align its rules with state regulations. It's a move that has drawn significant public concern.The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission asked the county to bring its ordinance in line with state law, which preempts counties from regulating saltwater fishing.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:"There is a state statute that has essentially preempted the powers from the county to regulate salt water fishing that includes shark fishing. Preemption meaning the state says, 'county you can't control this anymore,'" Assistant County Attorney Melissa Petrick said.State law requires a saltwater fishing license and a special permit for shark fishing. It also allows shark fishing within 1,000 feet of a guarded beach at all hours.Among those opposing the changes is Jessica Veatch, whose then-3-year-old daughter Violet was attacked by a bull shark on Bathtub Beach in Martin County 9 years ago."I hear a scream that goes Mommy," Veatch said. "I come up out of the water and all I can see is the blood filling the water and I lifted her up out of the water and saw what was left of her leg."Veatch said she believes nearby fishing activity may have lead to the attack.."We noticed some young men that were spearfishing on the reef," Veatch said. "That is what provoked the attack on my daughter."Veatch said she was alarmed to learn the county may now be forced to eliminate its local shark fishing regulations."They're currently treating our shoreline like a Pavlov's dog experiment with an apex predator and I don't think that's going to work out in anybody's best interest," Veatch said.Indian River Keeper Jim Moir raised concerns about the potential impact of the changes at the Tuesday commission meeting."These animals are incredibly important to our ecosystems. The angler offshore are complaining bitterly daily about how many of their caught fish are being depraved by sharks. Attracting more sharks to the coast is not only bad for human safety, but it's bad for angling, its bad for our public awareness, it's bad for the sharks," Moir said.County attorneys suggested the ordinance does not need to be eliminated entirely."We can rework the ordinance and then instead of eliminating everything we can just reference the illegality of things under state law," Petrick said.County commissioners voted to table the discussion, directing staff to review concerns raised by the community and commissioners and draft new ordinance language.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A joint investigation by the Florida Lottery Division of Security and the United States Postal Service Office of Inspector General (USPS OIG) has led to the arrest of a letter carrier accused of stealing a winning lottery ticket from the mail and fraudulently claiming the prize.USPS letter carrier Lekaysha Lockhart was arrested July 23 after a Florida Lottery player reported that a winning Pick 4 ticket she mailed never reached its intended destination, the Florida Lottery's Office of Communications said in a news release.A Florida Lottery Inspector determined the ticket had been redeemed by Lockhart on June 19 at the Florida Lottery's Miami District Office. Following her arrest, Florida Lottery Special Agents and USPS OIG investigators said Lockhart admitted to stealing the winning lottery ticket and redeeming it.Florida Lottery Secretary Reginald D. Dixon said the case reflects the agency's commitment to player protection."Our players deserve confidence that every Lottery prize is protected through strong security measures and diligent oversight," Dixon said in the news release. "I commend our Division of Security for their outstanding investigative work and thank our partners at the United States Postal Service Office of Inspector General and the Broward County Sheriff's Office for their collaboration in protecting the integrity of Florida Lottery games and bringing this case to a successful resolution."Lockhart was arrested on charges of grand theft, dealing in stolen property, filing a false claim for payment, two counts of unlawful use of a two-way communications device and mail theft. Because the alleged offenses occurred in multiple judicial circuits, the cases will be prosecuted separately, the Florida Lottery Division of Security said.

A petition with nearly 800 signatures is mounting against a proposal that could transform Fort Pierce's Museum Pointe — a public waterfront park along the Indian River Lagoon — into a mega-yacht marina.WATCH BELOW: 'We have been talking for years about better locations for that history center,' Erick Gill tells WPTV's Kate HusseyThe proposal is part of the Port of Fort Pierce's updated 2026 Master Plan. It calls for redeveloping Museum Pointe, which is currently home to a history center, public waterfront access, fishing piers, and green space, into a facility featuring floating docks, a multi-story marina, an event center, a waterfront restaurant, and a clubhouse.Opponents fear the plan could privatize one of the city's most treasured public spaces."Giving public land to private folks," said Terry Howard, a volunteer at the History Center at Museum Pointe Park. Howard contacted WPTV's Kate Hussey after learning about the master plan. "Development is just rampant in Florida, and at least we can fight for this one particular area and keep it green," Howard said.He said the loss of public waterfront access is a concern — but his biggest worry is the fate of the museum itself."This is the place where this museum should be, right here on this Museum Pointe," said Howard. For more than 50 years, the museum has preserved artifacts from Florida's Native American tribes, Spanish shipwrecks, and more. The master plan's renderings place the proposed marina clubhouse exactly where the museum stands today."Basically taking away a gem — a public gem that belongs to the people and replacing it with a facility for mega yachts," Howard said. "We're trying to keep this area as it is." St. Lucie County spokesperson Erick Gill said the museum's future is not in jeopardy if the project moves forward."Staff's intent was never to close the museum," Gill said. "We have been talking for years about better locations for that history center; it is on a barrier island, in a flood zone, so it may not be the best place to store artifacts."Gill said the museum and its collection would be preserved and relocated if the project proceeds. He added that the master plan is designed to expand economic development, create jobs, and generate county revenue."I think all local governments are looking for a way to generate revenue, so we can continue to lower the taxes for St. Lucie County residents and generate revenue from economic development, and we already have dock space there," Gill said."Anything that's going to be a positive economic driver for the City of Fort Pierce, I'm going to embrace completely," Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick added. Broderick said the city will have the final say on whether the project moves forward, and that commissioners will have to weigh economic benefits against preserving waterfront access.When asked which priority — economic development or waterfront access — would take precedence, Broderick said the answer is not simple."That's the challenging question right there. I believe that we can strike a balance," Broderick said. "We always have to be careful not to eliminate public access to the waterway. Period." For Howard, the stakes go beyond the present."This is a gem that once we develop around it, it'll never be replaced again," Howard said. "The museum has been here since the 1970s. If they want to boat docks for mega yachts, they can do it someplace else." St. Lucie County leaders are scheduled to discuss the proposal and its current status at a 9 a.m. Lucie County Commission Chambers.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A prosecutor says they have dropped charges against Gregory Allen Davis, 49, of Port St. Lucie in an incident June 24 in Port St. Lucie when Davis ordered three juveniles out of their car at gunpoint and told them to get on the ground at the intersection of SW Morelia Lane and SW Acapulco Terrace. Minutes earlier, one of the teens had fired an Orbeez toy gun at the car that Davis and his fiancee were in. An Orbeez toy gun shoots soft water-absorbing beads. According to a prosecutor, the reason they dropped the charges against Davis is because in Florida, citizens have the right to make a citizen's arrest if they see that a felony has been committed in their presence. The felony that Davis saw was the teen firing a gun at his vehicle. "Basically, under Florida law, a citizen has a right to make a citizen's arrest if they observe a felony, occur in their presence. So that's basically what happened here. When someone effects a citizen's arrest, basically, they have the same powers as a police officer would, at least temporarily," said Jason Bruin, Assistant State Attorney, 19th Judicial Circuit. Bruin says if the case had gone to a jury, they would've returned a verdict of not guilty. Davis, in this case, gets out of the vehicle and holds the the people that were in that car at gunpoint. No, we don't recommend that people take the law into their own hands like that. Let the police do their job. Call the police, let the police do their job," Bruin said. Davis was charged with three counts of false imprisonment and three counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Those six charges carry a maximum sentence of 30 years in prison if convicted. "I am very grateful as I am a father of three and everything I do is for my kids. The thought of being away from them is horrifying. I have a daughter that is the same age as the person who did the shooting, and I spend my time teaching my children not to do dumb things like that. Obviously I would never want anyone to ever get hurt. Especially over what they consider to be a prank. I believe behavior like this starts with the parents. It is our job to teach our kids right from wrong and be their parent first and their friend second," Davis said in a text message to CBS12 News, reacting to the fact that the charges against him were dropped. A flashing traffic light installed at the intersection of Glades Cut Off Road and Commerce Center Drive more than six months ago is still not fully operational, and neighbors say the confusion it's creating is becoming a safety concern. WATCH BELOW: Flashing traffic light still not operational 6 months after installation The light was installed by the Wylder community in December. When it was first put in, St. Lucie County told WPTV Treasure Coast reporter Tyler Hatfield it still needed to align with the Florida East Coast Railway track signals before it could be fully operational. Brian Packard, who lives near the intersection, said the light has made some difference — but not enough. "They didn't have any reason to slow down. At least now they know there's an intersection," Packard said. Still, Packard said the situation remains dangerous. "It's just not a safe situation," Packard said. Taylor Lorsten reached out to WPTV by email, saying the flashing mode is creating more problems than it's solving. "At first it was (a sigh of) relief, and then it was the confusion," Lorsten said. Lorsten said drivers don't know how to respond to the light. "People are stopping when they shouldn't stop, or go when they shouldn't go," Lorsten said. More than six months after installation, Lorsten said nothing appears to have changed. "We just haven't seen any work being done on that at all," Lorsten said. Lorsten said the flashing light can add major backups and worries that confused, aggressive driving could put her family at risk. "My son, who's a new driver, not knowing what to do when everybody's confused and something really happening bad to him," Lorsten said. WPTV reached out to the Wylder community, FEC Railways and St. Lucie County to find out who is responsible for making the light fully operational, but the answer remains unclear. "It's just not clear whose responsibility it is, and what time frame that would fit into," Packard said. We're still working to hear back from all parties. Martin County commissioners faced a wave of public pushback during Tuesday morning's meeting as residents, local surfers, and marine experts urged local leaders to keep strict limits on beachside shark fishing. The debate centers on potential language changes to local ordinances regarding land-based shark fishing, a practice where anglers deploy lines from the shore using heavy gear, kayaks, or drones to drop bait and chum into deeper waters. Under current Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) rules, shore anglers are required to hold a specialized permit, keep sharks in the water, and use non-offset circle hooks to prevent injury to the animals. However, local ordinances in coastal counties can set stricter safety boundaries near public swimming areas. During public comments, speakers warned that chumming , releasing fish parts and blood into the surf to attract sharks, endangers swimmers, surfers, and families. "I myself have been caught in shark fishing lines, and it is not fun," said local surfer Jay Noyes, speaking in support of beachgoers and surfers. Dottie Lanci, a member of the Hutchinson Island Preservation Initiative, strongly opposed any effort to loosen existing restrictions that ban shark baiting on lifeguard-protected beaches. Lansing called on commissioners to prioritize safety and extend the ban across all county beaches, citing an incident she witnessed outside her home where anglers used drones to drop chum in the water. "The next morning a family of four put up their umbrellas. Two young children were playing in the water there, completely unaware of what took place the day before and that some hungry sharks might still be there," Lanci said. She also noted that other Florida municipalities, such as Miami Beach, passed local bans on land-based shark fishing earlier this year. Safety concerns over shark activity on local beaches are far from theoretical for many residents . In August 2017, a 3-year-old girl named Violet Veatch was bitten on the leg by a suspected bull shark while wading in shallow water at Bathtub Reef Beach in Martin County. The toddler's mother, Jessica Veatch, later pushed for stricter local beach safety regulations , believing the shark was drawn to the crowded swimming area by spearfishermen carrying bloody fish through the water. Jessica Veatch, Violet's mother, says these new regulations would be great, but enforcement of them has been a problem. Enforcement is a big issue. You can put anything down on paper, but if you're not enforcing it, people are going to do what they want to do. We basically have our beaches turning into a cowboy sport, and if you don't like it, then you can go somewhere else. That is basically the mentality that a lot of these fishermen have, said Veatch. Justin Grubich, a marine conservation expert and local surfer who moved to the area from Fort Lauderdale, urged the commission to maintain strong local restrictions. Pointing to recent research presented at statewide conservation forums, Grubich warned that regular baiting near popular beaches conditions wildlife. "There's new scientific evidence or more accumulated scientific evidence that you can create problem sharks like problem bears," Grubich cautioned commissioners, advocating for rules that limit chumming and keep blood out of coastal waters. Commissioners did not take immediate action on the ordinance during the meeting, but requested further review of local public safety boundaries alongside state FWC regulations. County staff confirmed the current ordinance banning chumming is still in place. Current county rules ban fishing on guarded beaches when lifeguards are present. A new ordinance referring residents to FWC for state laws and tightening restrictions on county beaches is currently in the works. There is no timeline for when this new ordinance will come to a vote or exactly what new restrictions will go into place. One of the items discussed was increased drone restrictions on beaches amid concerns that they may be used to bait sharks. Other proposals included extended beach fishing hours and county shark fishing permits.

A Fort Pierce resort says an abandoned sailboat that washed ashore three weeks ago is damaging property, slamming into other boats, and costing them thousands in business, but state law prevents them from moving it. "This is a danger to people and personal property," said Joe Zebrowski, general manager of Dockside Marina and Resort. The sailboat washed ashore near On The Edge Bar and Grill, and Zabrowski and his team quickly secured it. However, Zabrowski said the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) informed him that the boat cannot be moved. The agency is giving the owners 60 days to claim the vessel, and the resort is also prohibited from moving it. "I did a good deed, but no deed goes unpunished," Zebrowski said. The FWC used a chain to secure the sailboat, but Zebrowski said it hasn’t stopped the vessel from causing problems. "It kept it from floating away but didn’t keep it from whipping back and forth," he said. Zebrowski explained that the sailboat has slammed into a docked boat, destroyed a piling, and forced the restaurant to block off several tables near the vessel, which has significantly impacted their revenue. "These are our prime tables. They probably cost us about 25 percent of our overall business for the past month," Zebrowski said. Lucie County Sheriff's Office are investigating the death of a 3-month-old baby in Fort Pierce, which occurred in August of last year, and say further charges could be pending. Additional details about the case reveal the environment in which the infant was living. "I can tell you the facts of this case. Doesn't even paint a picture clear to what we saw at the hospital," Detective Corporal Jennifer Diaz said. Investigators identified the three caregivers as the baby's mother, Nicole Maxwell, the baby's grandfather, Robert Maxwell, and his girlfriend, Vikki Koon. According to authorities, none of the caregivers could explain how the baby died. However, findings from the medical examiner determined the cause of death. "There were a lack of food and a lack of fluid intake. So therefore, the baby potentially was not properly being fed and due to the child's age, was unable to care for themselves," Diaz said. The baby and Nicole Maxwell’s 9-year-old son, who has autism, lived in the mobile home with their grandfather and his girlfriend. Nicole Maxwell lived with her boyfriend in Vero Beach but would visit occasionally. Authorities noted that the family has a history of involvement with the Department of Children and Families. Maxwell's other children are currently in foster care. Court records revealed Facebook messages between Nicole Maxwell and her father, Robert Maxwell, raising concerns about the infant's health. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates One message on Aug. 12 mentioned that "the infant was out of food." Another message on Aug. 19 showed Nicole asking if the infant was okay. 20, Robert Maxwell stated, "the infant had died." The autopsy found the infant was emaciated and had a sunken abdomen. Nicole Maxwell was questioned by investigators. "I did interview the mother, and there were a lack of emotion and a lack of empathy towards the death of the child," Diaz said. Tasha Wright, who identified herself as Nicole Maxwell’s boyfriend’s mother, expressed disbelief over Maxwell’s arrest. This is not the girl who's been living in my house for three months," Wright said. All three caregivers remain in custody as the investigation continues. Martin County commissioners faced a wave of public pushback during Tuesday morning's meeting as residents, local surfers, and marine experts urged local leaders to keep strict limits on beachside shark fishing. The debate centers on potential language changes to local ordinances regarding land-based shark fishing, a practice where anglers deploy lines from the shore using heavy gear, kayaks, or drones to drop bait and chum into deeper waters. Under current Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) rules, shore anglers are required to hold a specialized permit, keep sharks in the water, and use non-offset circle hooks to prevent injury to the animals. However, local ordinances in coastal counties can set stricter safety boundaries near public swimming areas. During public comments, speakers warned that chumming , releasing fish parts and blood into the surf to attract sharks, endangers swimmers, surfers, and families. "I myself have been caught in shark fishing lines, and it is not fun," said local surfer Jay Noyes, speaking in support of beachgoers and surfers. Dottie Lanci, a member of the Hutchinson Island Preservation Initiative, strongly opposed any effort to loosen existing restrictions that ban shark baiting on lifeguard-protected beaches. Lansing called on commissioners to prioritize safety and extend the ban across all county beaches, citing an incident she witnessed outside her home where anglers used drones to drop chum in the water. "The next morning a family of four put up their umbrellas. Two young children were playing in the water there, completely unaware of what took place the day before and that some hungry sharks might still be there," Lanci said. She also noted that other Florida municipalities, such as Miami Beach, passed local bans on land-based shark fishing earlier this year. Safety concerns over shark activity on local beaches are far from theoretical for many residents . In August 2017, a 3-year-old girl named Violet Veatch was bitten on the leg by a suspected bull shark while wading in shallow water at Bathtub Reef Beach in Martin County. The toddler's mother, Jessica Veatch, later pushed for stricter local beach safety regulations , believing the shark was drawn to the crowded swimming area by spearfishermen carrying bloody fish through the water. Jessica Veatch, Violet's mother, says these new regulations would be great, but enforcement of them has been a problem. Enforcement is a big issue. You can put anything down on paper, but if you're not enforcing it, people are going to do what they want to do. We basically have our beaches turning into a cowboy sport, and if you don't like it, then you can go somewhere else. That is basically the mentality that a lot of these fishermen have, said Veatch. Justin Grubich, a marine conservation expert and local surfer who moved to the area from Fort Lauderdale, urged the commission to maintain strong local restrictions. Pointing to recent research presented at statewide conservation forums, Grubich warned that regular baiting near popular beaches conditions wildlife. "There's new scientific evidence or more accumulated scientific evidence that you can create problem sharks like problem bears," Grubich cautioned commissioners, advocating for rules that limit chumming and keep blood out of coastal waters. Commissioners did not take immediate action on the ordinance during the meeting, but requested further review of local public safety boundaries alongside state FWC regulations. County staff confirmed the current ordinance banning chumming is still in place. Current county rules ban fishing on guarded beaches when lifeguards are present. A new ordinance referring residents to FWC for state laws and tightening restrictions on county beaches is currently in the works. There is no timeline for when this new ordinance will come to a vote or exactly what new restrictions will go into place. One of the items discussed was increased drone restrictions on beaches amid concerns that they may be used to bait sharks. Other proposals included extended beach fishing hours and county shark fishing permits.
