Federal prosecutors said a Los Angeles man was sentenced to life in federal prison for selling fentanyl that caused the death of a Treasure Coast man, then continuing to traffic the deadly drug just two days later. District Judge Aileen Cannon imposed the sentence on Alfonso Guerrero, 39, of Los Angeles, after a federal jury convicted him in May 2026 of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute fentanyl resulting in death and distribution of fentanyl resulting in death. “A tenth of a gram of fentanyl, about the size of a small pinch of salt, was enough to kill David Eller,” U.S. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida said in a statement. “This was not a small drug deal. Guerrero sold the fentanyl that killed his friend and, just two days later, was caught carrying more fentanyl for distribution. Today’s life sentence is the consequence of that deadly conduct and his long record of violence and crime. Together with the DEA and our local law enforcement partners, we will trace fatal doses back to the dealers who sold them and hold those dealers fully accountable.” According to court records and evidence presented at trial, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said Guerrero sold fentanyl in Indian River County. On May 16, 2023, prosecutors said he exchanged 0.1 gram of fentanyl — commonly known as “a point” — for another controlled substance known as “molly.” Officials said the drug transaction was captured on a doorbell camera. Hours later, Eller was found dead inside his Vero Beach home. Investigators recovered drug paraphernalia, including a small piece of burnt aluminum foil that the victim used to receive the fentanyl from Guerrero on the victim’s front porch, near his body. Two days later, on May 18, 2023, prosecutors said Guerrero was arrested and found in possession of additional quantities of fentanyl intended for distribution. Officials said Guerrero’s extensive criminal history included documented gang membership and prior convictions for attempted robbery with a firearm in California, aggravated assault in Georgia, and cocaine and fentanyl possession offenses in Florida.

Newly released 911 calls capture desperate attempts to save two men after gunfire erupted outside a Port St. Lucie home , leaving one caller pleading for help as a wounded man faded in front of her. Multiple callers contacted dispatchers shortly before 3:30 a.m. July 19 after hearing repeated gunshots near Southeast Rivergreen Circle. The calls show residents trying to direct officers toward the shooting while remaining inside their homes as police rushed to the neighborhood. Please, please, the caller told a dispatcher shortly after 3:28 a.m. When asked whether anyone had been hit, she answered, Yes. The caller repeatedly urged one of the wounded men to remain conscious. Breathe, baby, please, she said. Officers responding to Southeast Rivergreen Circle found 24-year-old Carl Loubeau and 22-year-old Juliun Stokes suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. Both were taken to hospitals, where they later died. The calls show how quickly the shooting unfolded. The first caller apparently mistook the gunfire for fireworks and asked police to check the area near the dog park because the noise had awakened his young daughter. Within seconds, other residents began reporting gunshots, screaming and people lying outside. One neighbor said about eight shots woke him but told the dispatcher he was too frightened to look outside. No, I don’t even want to look, he said. Another caller estimated hearing 10 shots, followed by a brief pause and another burst. It got quiet for less than a minute, and then a couple more rounds went off, the caller said. A resident watching through a home security camera reported seeing someone lying in a driveway. I’m looking through my camera because I didn’t want to go outside, the caller said. I woke up from the gunshots and the screaming, and I just see someone laying in the driveway. Man who returned fire calls 911 The most significant call appears to have come from 20-year-old Dwayne Walker, whom investigators identified as the man who returned fire after Loubeau allegedly shot Stokes . Somebody shot my cousin, and I shot back, Walker told a dispatcher. Walker pleaded for police and paramedics to hurry, saying his cousin was not responding. See also: PBSO seeks more victims after barber arrested in alleged trafficking of 17-year-old He shot my cousin, sir, Walker said as officers arrived. Walker also repeatedly told officers that the guns had been dropped and said he did not want any trouble. The guns are dropped, he said. I haven’t done anything at all, sir. Later in the call, Walker described what he said happened before the shooting. We were just coming to a house, and her boyfriend shot my cousin, Walker said. Because my cousin said, Hey,’ to him, and he laughed, and he said, Do I know you?’ And he shot my cousin. Police initially said an argument over a house key had escalated into a shootout between the two victims. Investigators later revised that account, saying jealousy involving a woman apparently triggered the violence and that Stokes did not fire a weapon. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk, Stokes and several friends had gone bowling with Loubeau’s girlfriend earlier that night. When the group returned to the home and realized they were locked out, the woman called Loubeau and asked him to bring a spare key. Police believe Loubeau became jealous when he arrived and saw his girlfriend with Stokes and Walker. Investigators said Loubeau approached Stokes as he stood beside the open driver’s door of a Ford Mustang and opened fire. Police believe Loubeau may have mistaken Stokes for Walker, who authorities said had some type of relationship with Loubeau’s girlfriend. Walker, who was near the rear of the Mustang, drew a lawfully carried handgun and returned fire, striking Loubeau, police said. Investigators determined Walker acted in self-defense and said he will not face criminal charges. Police said Loubeau fired eight rounds from a 9 mm handgun and one round from a .380-caliber weapon. Walker fired eight rounds from a .40-caliber handgun, according to the department’s preliminary findings. See also: PBSO seeks more victims after barber arrested in alleged trafficking of 17-year-old Stokes was armed, but investigators said there was no evidence that he fired his weapon. The 911 recordings also capture the chaotic arrival of officers, who can be heard ordering people to the ground and demanding that they keep their hands visible while callers continued begging for medical aid. He needs an ambulance, someone shouted as police secured the scene. No arrests have been made. Detectives are continuing to review forensic evidence, phone records, toxicology findings and autopsy reports before formally closing the investigation. Anyone with additional information is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000 .

A man awaiting a possible retrial in the fatal shooting of his former girlfriend is accused of attacking convicted murderer Otto Lenke inside the St. According to an arrest affidavit, Robert Castro approached Lenke in a jail dorm on July 6 and struck him in the face, knocking off his glasses. Lenke approached an intercom and reported the attack to corrections staff, the affidavit says. A deputy noticed a cut on the upper part of Lenke’s nose, and a nurse treated the injury. A jail sergeant witnessed Castro strike Lenke, according to investigators. Surveillance video also showed Castro approaching Lenke and hitting him in the face, the affidavit says. Lenke later told a detective he had been using a jail-issued tablet to watch a chess game when Castro attacked him. Investigators attempted to interview Castro on July 16. The affidavit says Castro repeatedly stated that he did not understand his Miranda rights and did not want to speak with the detective, ending the interview. Castro, 30, is charged with battery by a person detained in a prison or jail facility, a felony. The new charge was filed July 20. Lenke, a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter, was convicted in May of first-degree murder and first-degree arson in the 2021 death of Richard Benson. Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson three times inside Benson’s Fort Pierce motorcycle shop, poured an accelerant on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. A jury later voted 11-1 to recommend that Lenke be sentenced to death. Castro’s murder conviction reversed Castro was convicted in 2024 of first-degree murder with a firearm in the death of his former girlfriend, Taylor Ann Sato, and sentenced to life in prison. However, the Fourth District Court of Appeal reversed the conviction in February after finding that the trial court failed to properly complete the process for determining whether Castro was competent to stand trial. A psychologist found Castro competent in November 2022. Five days later, his attorneys raised concerns about his condition, and the original judge said Castro had definitely decompensated before ordering another evaluation. The appeals court said the record contained no additional evaluation, report or competency hearing after that order. Nearly two years later, a different judge declared Castro competent based on the original 2022 evaluation. Castro then went to trial and was convicted. The appellate court ruled that a two-year-old evaluation was not sufficient because competency must be assessed close to the time of trial. The case was sent back to the trial court to determine whether Castro’s competency during the 2024 trial can now be reliably evaluated. Castro would receive a new trial if a retrospective evaluation cannot be conducted or if the court determines he was not competent during the original trial. 2022 killing Fort Pierce police accused Castro of killing Sato outside her Timber Ridge Lane home during the early morning hours of July 23, 2022. According to the original arrest affidavit, a man called 911 and said he had shot and killed his girlfriend and was considering killing himself. Officers arrived and found Sato outside the home with multiple gunshot wounds. Investigators reported finding six gunshot wounds and several 9 mm shell casings near her body. Sato’s stepfather told detectives that she and Castro had recently ended a long-term relationship. He said Sato had blocked Castro’s phone number, but Castro continued trying to contact her by sending repeated $1 transactions through Cash App with messages attached. The stepfather also told police Castro had previously threatened to kill Sato. After listening to part of the 911 call, he identified the caller’s voice as Castro’s, according to the affidavit. Castro later surrendered to deputies in St. Investigators said several rounds of 9 mm ammunition were found in his pocket. His police interview ended after an attorney arrived and directed detectives not to question him further.

The Martin County School District has approved a consolidation of bus routes that officials say will save $255,000 without affecting students or eliminating any driver positions. The school board voted Tuesday unanimously to reduce the number of bus routes by 3, bringing the total from 58 to 55 ahead of the upcoming school year. District officials say all bus stops will remain the same and students will not be impacted by the change. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: "Right now, we have 55 routes and roughly 56 drivers. So we have all of our routes covered," Superintendent Michael Maine said. The $255,000 in savings reflects a reduced transportation budget and will not be redirected to a specific expense, according to the school district. Parents have mixed reactions. Marino Reyes and Tiffany Gugumuck expressed support for the financial decision. "I think that's a great thing. A quarter million dollars that's a lot of money just for that one situation there. So many other needs that we can put the money towards," Reyes and Gugumuck said. Parent Ken Winstanley wondered what the change means for the budget. "Where's the money gonna go to?" Winstanley said. Michael Skinner, the President of the local AFSCME labor union chapter, voiced concerns during public comment on behalf of the bus drivers. "As what my feedback from the bus drivers were is that their routes or their buses are always full and cutting routes are not actually a good idea," Skinner said. Transportation Director Ruth Spires pushed back on that concern, noting that the buses hold a maximum of 77 passengers and are not operating at capacity. Spires also confirmed that no drivers were let go as part of the consolidation. "We were already challenged with a shortage last year. So the routes that were merged—consolidated—yes, the drivers were already covering. So no one was cut at all," Spires said. Drivers will be paid for any additional hours they work as a result of the consolidation, Spires explained. The district said it is confident it will maintain the same level of service with fewer buses on the road. Lucie Police Department is investigating after an 86-year-old woman died in a two-vehicle crash. Officers responded at approximately 2:30 p.m. Thursday at the intersection of Southwest Savona Boulevard and Southwest Lawndale Avenue, east of Interstate 95. The preliminary investigation indicates that a 2026 Honda HR-V, driven by a 17-year-old boy, was traveling northbound on Southwest Savona Boulevard approaching the intersection with SW Lawndale Avenue. Newly released 911 calls capture desperate attempts to save two men after gunfire erupted outside a Port St. Lucie home , leaving one caller pleading for help as a wounded man faded in front of her. Multiple callers contacted dispatchers shortly before 3:30 a.m. July 19 after hearing repeated gunshots near Southeast Rivergreen Circle. The calls show residents trying to direct officers toward the shooting while remaining inside their homes as police rushed to the neighborhood. Please, please, the caller told a dispatcher shortly after 3:28 a.m. When asked whether anyone had been hit, she answered, Yes. The caller repeatedly urged one of the wounded men to remain conscious. Breathe, baby, please, she said. Officers responding to Southeast Rivergreen Circle found 24-year-old Carl Loubeau and 22-year-old Juliun Stokes suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. Both were taken to hospitals, where they later died. The calls show how quickly the shooting unfolded. The first caller apparently mistook the gunfire for fireworks and asked police to check the area near the dog park because the noise had awakened his young daughter. Within seconds, other residents began reporting gunshots, screaming and people lying outside. One neighbor said about eight shots woke him but told the dispatcher he was too frightened to look outside. No, I don’t even want to look, he said. Another caller estimated hearing 10 shots, followed by a brief pause and another burst. It got quiet for less than a minute, and then a couple more rounds went off, the caller said. A resident watching through a home security camera reported seeing someone lying in a driveway. I’m looking through my camera because I didn’t want to go outside, the caller said. I woke up from the gunshots and the screaming, and I just see someone laying in the driveway. Man who returned fire calls 911 The most significant call appears to have come from 20-year-old Dwayne Walker, whom investigators identified as the man who returned fire after Loubeau allegedly shot Stokes . Somebody shot my cousin, and I shot back, Walker told a dispatcher. Walker pleaded for police and paramedics to hurry, saying his cousin was not responding. See also: PBSO seeks more victims after barber arrested in alleged trafficking of 17-year-old He shot my cousin, sir, Walker said as officers arrived. Walker also repeatedly told officers that the guns had been dropped and said he did not want any trouble. The guns are dropped, he said. I haven’t done anything at all, sir. Later in the call, Walker described what he said happened before the shooting. We were just coming to a house, and her boyfriend shot my cousin, Walker said. Because my cousin said, Hey,’ to him, and he laughed, and he said, Do I know you?’ And he shot my cousin. Police initially said an argument over a house key had escalated into a shootout between the two victims. Investigators later revised that account, saying jealousy involving a woman apparently triggered the violence and that Stokes did not fire a weapon. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk, Stokes and several friends had gone bowling with Loubeau’s girlfriend earlier that night. When the group returned to the home and realized they were locked out, the woman called Loubeau and asked him to bring a spare key. Police believe Loubeau became jealous when he arrived and saw his girlfriend with Stokes and Walker. Investigators said Loubeau approached Stokes as he stood beside the open driver’s door of a Ford Mustang and opened fire. Police believe Loubeau may have mistaken Stokes for Walker, who authorities said had some type of relationship with Loubeau’s girlfriend. Walker, who was near the rear of the Mustang, drew a lawfully carried handgun and returned fire, striking Loubeau, police said. Investigators determined Walker acted in self-defense and said he will not face criminal charges. Police said Loubeau fired eight rounds from a 9 mm handgun and one round from a .380-caliber weapon. Walker fired eight rounds from a .40-caliber handgun, according to the department’s preliminary findings. See also: PBSO seeks more victims after barber arrested in alleged trafficking of 17-year-old Stokes was armed, but investigators said there was no evidence that he fired his weapon. The 911 recordings also capture the chaotic arrival of officers, who can be heard ordering people to the ground and demanding that they keep their hands visible while callers continued begging for medical aid. He needs an ambulance, someone shouted as police secured the scene. No arrests have been made. Detectives are continuing to review forensic evidence, phone records, toxicology findings and autopsy reports before formally closing the investigation. Anyone with additional information is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000 .

The King's Landing development project in downtown Fort Pierce is advancing, with construction milestones bringing excitement to the community and local business owners. Brooke Harris, Team Lead of the Beachfront Brooke Team powered by Keller Williams Realty, shared updates on the progress. "They're almost done with Villa's 9 and 10, and then the foundation has already been in for 7 and 8," Harris said. She added that two residences have been sold and are nearing completion. The project features ten luxury villas, condos, retail spaces, restaurants, a parking garage, and a hotel. "We'll have the Marriott Hotel, which they have signed an agreement with, so that's great," Harris said. Officials emphasized the project's location in the waterfront district near the city marina and historic downtown. "It's waterfront, and it's connecting downtown to Edgartown, so it gives you that walkability factor to go down to shopping, restaurants, retail, and also, if you have a boat, you can store it right here at the marina," Harris said. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Michelle Chaffee Cavalcanti, executive director of Main Street Fort Pierce, highlighted the significance of the development for the city. It's got the potential to have a lot of impact on our businesses, bringing in visitors, having our locals have somewhere for our families to stay when they come. But also, just being a destination where people can come walk, shop, live, and play," Chaffee Cavalcanti said. Business owners are optimistic about the benefits of having more residents in the downtown area, especially with most amenities within walking distance. "Well, it makes a huge impact because if you can just walk everywhere, it means that you can not only just walk to a restaurant, but you can walk into another business afterwards and shop and get information," Chaffee Cavalcanti said. She added, "It becomes an experience and not just a singular destination." Officials said the estimated completion date is November 2029. Federal prosecutors said a Los Angeles man was sentenced to life in federal prison for selling fentanyl that caused the death of a Treasure Coast man, then continuing to traffic the deadly drug just two days later.U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon imposed the sentence on Alfonso Guerrero, 39, of Los Angeles, after a federal jury convicted him in May 2026 of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute fentanyl resulting in death and distribution of fentanyl resulting in death."A tenth of a gram of fentanyl, about the size of a small pinch of salt, was enough to kill David Eller," U.S. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida said in a statement. "This was not a small drug deal. Guerrero sold the fentanyl that killed his friend and, just two days later, was caught carrying more fentanyl for distribution. Today’s life sentence is the consequence of that deadly conduct and his long record of violence and crime. Together with the DEA and our local law enforcement partners, we will trace fatal doses back to the dealers who sold them and hold those dealers fully accountable."According to court records and evidence presented at trial, the U.S. Attorney's Office said Guerrero sold fentanyl in Indian River County. On May 16, 2023, prosecutors said he exchanged 0.1 gram of fentanyl — commonly known as "a point" — for another controlled substance known as "molly." Officials said the drug transaction was captured on a doorbell camera. Hours later, Eller was found dead inside his Vero Beach home. Investigators recovered drug paraphernalia, including a small piece of burnt aluminum foil that the victim used to receive the fentanyl from Guerrero on the victim's front porch, near his body.Two days later, on May 18, 2023, prosecutors said Guerrero was arrested and found in possession of additional quantities of fentanyl intended for distribution.Officials said Guerrero's extensive criminal history included documented gang membership and prior convictions for attempted robbery with a firearm in California, aggravated assault in Georgia, and cocaine and fentanyl possession offenses in Florida.

A man awaiting a possible retrial in the fatal shooting of his former girlfriend is accused of attacking convicted murderer Otto Lenke inside the St. According to an arrest affidavit, Robert Castro approached Lenke in a jail dorm on July 6 and struck him in the face, knocking off his glasses. Lenke approached an intercom and reported the attack to corrections staff, the affidavit says. A deputy noticed a cut on the upper part of Lenke’s nose, and a nurse treated the injury. A jail sergeant witnessed Castro strike Lenke, according to investigators. Surveillance video also showed Castro approaching Lenke and hitting him in the face, the affidavit says. Lenke later told a detective he had been using a jail-issued tablet to watch a chess game when Castro attacked him. Investigators attempted to interview Castro on July 16. The affidavit says Castro repeatedly stated that he did not understand his Miranda rights and did not want to speak with the detective, ending the interview. Castro, 30, is charged with battery by a person detained in a prison or jail facility, a felony. The new charge was filed July 20. Lenke, a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter, was convicted in May of first-degree murder and first-degree arson in the 2021 death of Richard Benson. Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson three times inside Benson’s Fort Pierce motorcycle shop, poured an accelerant on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. A jury later voted 11-1 to recommend that Lenke be sentenced to death. Castro’s murder conviction reversed Castro was convicted in 2024 of first-degree murder with a firearm in the death of his former girlfriend, Taylor Ann Sato, and sentenced to life in prison. However, the Fourth District Court of Appeal reversed the conviction in February after finding that the trial court failed to properly complete the process for determining whether Castro was competent to stand trial. A psychologist found Castro competent in November 2022. Five days later, his attorneys raised concerns about his condition, and the original judge said Castro had definitely decompensated before ordering another evaluation. The appeals court said the record contained no additional evaluation, report or competency hearing after that order. Nearly two years later, a different judge declared Castro competent based on the original 2022 evaluation. Castro then went to trial and was convicted. The appellate court ruled that a two-year-old evaluation was not sufficient because competency must be assessed close to the time of trial. The case was sent back to the trial court to determine whether Castro’s competency during the 2024 trial can now be reliably evaluated. Castro would receive a new trial if a retrospective evaluation cannot be conducted or if the court determines he was not competent during the original trial. 2022 killing Fort Pierce police accused Castro of killing Sato outside her Timber Ridge Lane home during the early morning hours of July 23, 2022. According to the original arrest affidavit, a man called 911 and said he had shot and killed his girlfriend and was considering killing himself. Officers arrived and found Sato outside the home with multiple gunshot wounds. Investigators reported finding six gunshot wounds and several 9 mm shell casings near her body. Sato’s stepfather told detectives that she and Castro had recently ended a long-term relationship. He said Sato had blocked Castro’s phone number, but Castro continued trying to contact her by sending repeated $1 transactions through Cash App with messages attached. The stepfather also told police Castro had previously threatened to kill Sato. After listening to part of the 911 call, he identified the caller’s voice as Castro’s, according to the affidavit. Castro later surrendered to deputies in St. Investigators said several rounds of 9 mm ammunition were found in his pocket. His police interview ended after an attorney arrived and directed detectives not to question him further.

A Fort Pierce pizza shop known for giving back is creating an even bigger space to inspire young readers. Big Apple Pizza owner Scott Van Duzer is expanding the restaurant’s free book program by transforming its outdoor patio into a dedicated reading room where children can pick up a book any time they visit. For years, Van Duzer has kept shelves of free books inside the restaurant, inviting children to take one home at no cost. He said seeing kids light up when they discover a new book has been one of the most rewarding parts of the program. “The books are there so when the kids come in the store they’re easily available,” Van Duzer said. “They’ll come in and they’re excited they can take whatever they want home.” As more children have stopped by to pick up books, the collection has continued to grow. Van Duzer said the restaurant has simply run out of space inside, prompting the decision to turn the outdoor patio into a permanent reading room. “We have so many books and we are trying to keep ahead of the game that we have turned our porch into what’s going to be the reading room,” Van Duzer said. “So now anytime a child stops by they can get a book free of charge no questions asked.” The goal, he said, is to make books easy to access and help encourage a lifelong love of reading. Whether a family comes in for pizza or simply stops by for a book, every child is welcome to take one home. For Van Duzer, giving back has always been part of the restaurant’s mission. He said that commitment comes from the example his mother set while he was growing up. “I didn’t have a lot,” Van Duzer said. “My mom was pretty instrumental in my life so she just said if you can give back, give back. We live that every day.” Construction on the new reading room is underway and is expected to be completed later this fall. Until then, children can continue picking up free books inside Big Apple Pizza, where the message remains the same: every child is welcome to take a book home, no questions asked. Big Apple Pizza is located at 2311 S 35th St, Fort Pierce FL 34981.

Lucie County sheriff's deputy was fired after an Internal Affairs investigation found she created a social media post that mocked Sheriff Richard Del Toro's "Standards of Performance." According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Internal Affairs report, on Oct. 10, 2025, Sheriff Richard Del Toro was made aware of a Facebook post on Deputy Tina Speicker's personal social media account featuring an image titled "Standards of Power." The report says the image closely resembled Del Toro's "Standards of Performance," which was introduced after he was sworn into office. The Standards of Performance outlined eight performance expectations for employees, agency divisions and the Sheriff's Office's core values. See also: PSL police seek missing 14-year-old girl last seen Tuesday night The report says Speicker's Facebook post mirrored the "Standards of Performance" but replaced the original language with phrases depicting domination, manipulation and exploitation. Investigators alleged the post was intended to disparage the Sheriff's Office and Sheriff Del Toro and violated agency rules and regulations. According to the Internal Affairs report, Speicker's "Standards of Power" graphic stated: Top-down domination. Keep everyone beneath you guessing who's next to take the blame. Set confusion for others to follow. The less they know, the more control you have. Display a ruthless work ethic with a focus on self-preservation. Take credit for wins, redirect the failures. Demonstrate selective respect. Favor those who serve your goals; silence those who don't. Being unfair-strategically. Tip the scales to your advantage. Remain obsessive and paranoid. Control every detail, question every motive. Be committed to manipulation and influence. Knowledge is leverage trade it like currency. You own what you exploit and sign off to survive. The Internal Affairs investigator identified several similarities between the "Standards of Power" graphic and Del Toro's "Standards of Performance," including that both contained eight principles, used similar wording and sentence structure, began each bullet point with the same first word and featured a similar two-tone outline. Investigators concluded the graphic was intended to parody the Sheriff's official standards. During the investigation, the Sheriff's Office interviewed Sheriff Del Toro, agency supervisors, other deputies and Speicker. The IA report states Speicker acknowledged posting the graphic to her Facebook page but said it was intended as commentary on Congress and the federal government shutdown. The report also found Speicker gave inconsistent statements during multiple interviews, leading investigators to sustain allegations of criticism of orders or policies, conduct unbecoming, violating the code of ethics for public officers and employees, and false testimony. As a result of the investigation, Speicker was terminated on June 12, 2026. The investigation concluded that Speicker violated Sheriff's Office policies regarding criticism of orders or policies, conduct unbecoming, the code of ethics for public officers and employees, and false testimony.

Lucie police officer resigned while under investigation after walking away from a vehicle containing a man who had shot and killed himself, only to return minutes later as backup. According to an internal affairs report, 23-year-old Officer Mathew Brown resigned on April 17, 2026, facing sustained findings for neglect of duty and inefficiency. Surveillance video from the Treasure Coast Church of God Worship Center showed Brown pulling behind a dark blue Porsche at 1:47 a.m. Brown shined his lights on the car, ran a license plate check, and walked up to the passenger side. However, after looking through the window, Brown turned right around and drove off without calling dispatch or checking on the person inside. At 2:02 a.m., a second officer stopped to check on the suspicious car and found a man dead inside from a gunshot wound, with a handgun sitting on his lap. Paramedics confirmed he was dead, and investigators ruled the death a suicide. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk recounts his first reaction to the investigation. Very frustrated and just seeking for some understanding because I can't fathom how a police officer would respond to a situation the way he did, said Niemczyk. As he was sent back to the scene as backup, Brown told the responding officer he had driven by earlier but "didn't see anyone in it." Related: Sergeant demoted, officer suspended after Boynton Beach traffic stop investigation Body camera footage captured Brown telling the officer to "go blue," muting both of their cameras for 32 seconds. When a supervisor later pointed out fresh tire tracks in the muddy grass right next to the Porsche, Brown stayed silent, failing to admit they were from his patrol SUV. Investigators concluded Brown failed to do a basic welfare check, offer help, or properly report what he saw. Brown submitted his resignation on April 2 while under investigation, which Niemczyk accepted. Internal Affairs formally sustained the violations on June 24th, marking his file as "resigned under investigation." Two other responding officers were cleared of any wrongdoing. He opted to resign and, you know, prior to the investigation being completed. So, we never had the opportunity to interview him on the record and get his explanation for his behavior. So, it's kind of unsolved in my mind, said Niemczyk. The chief says the public shouldn't expect this out of law enforcement, noting that Brown was the exception, not the expectation. This is not normal common behavior by a police officer. They have a right to expect police officers to provide all due care for human life and dignity. And that did not happen in this case. We're very disappointed, Niemczyk said.

A prosecutor says they have dropped charges against Gregory Allen Davis, 49, of Port St. Lucie in an incident June 24 in Port St. Lucie when Davis ordered three juveniles out of their car at gunpoint and told them to get on the ground at the intersection of SW Morelia Lane and SW Acapulco Terrace. Minutes earlier, one of the teens had fired an Orbeez toy gun at the car that Davis and his fiancee were in. An Orbeez toy gun shoots soft water-absorbing beads. According to a prosecutor, the reason they dropped the charges against Davis is because in Florida, citizens have the right to make a citizen's arrest if they see that a felony has been committed in their presence. The felony that Davis saw was the teen firing a gun at his vehicle. "Basically, under Florida law, a citizen has a right to make a citizen's arrest if they observe a felony, occur in their presence. So that's basically what happened here. When someone effects a citizen's arrest, basically, they have the same powers as a police officer would, at least temporarily," said Jason Bruin, Assistant State Attorney, 19th Judicial Circuit. Bruin says if the case had gone to a jury, they would've returned a verdict of not guilty. Davis, in this case, gets out of the vehicle and holds the the people that were in that car at gunpoint. No, we don't recommend that people take the law into their own hands like that. Let the police do their job. Call the police, let the police do their job," Bruin said. Davis was charged with three counts of false imprisonment and three counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Those six charges carry a maximum sentence of 30 years in prison if convicted. "I am very grateful as I am a father of three and everything I do is for my kids. The thought of being away from them is horrifying. Martin County commissioners faced a wave of public pushback during Tuesday morning's meeting as residents, local surfers, and marine experts urged local leaders to keep strict limits on beachside shark fishing. The debate centers on potential language changes to local ordinances regarding land-based shark fishing, a practice where anglers deploy lines from the shore using heavy gear, kayaks, or drones to drop bait and chum into deeper waters. Under current Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) rules, shore anglers are required to hold a specialized permit, keep sharks in the water, and use non-offset circle hooks to prevent injury to the animals. However, local ordinances in coastal counties can set stricter safety boundaries near public swimming areas. During public comments, speakers warned that chumming , releasing fish parts and blood into the surf to attract sharks, endangers swimmers, surfers, and families. "I myself have been caught in shark fishing lines, and it is not fun," said local surfer Jay Noyes, speaking in support of beachgoers and surfers. Dottie Lanci, a member of the Hutchinson Island Preservation Initiative, strongly opposed any effort to loosen existing restrictions that ban shark baiting on lifeguard-protected beaches. Lansing called on commissioners to prioritize safety and extend the ban across all county beaches, citing an incident she witnessed outside her home where anglers used drones to drop chum in the water. "The next morning a family of four put up their umbrellas. Two young children were playing in the water there, completely unaware of what took place the day before and that some hungry sharks might still be there," Lanci said. She also noted that other Florida municipalities, such as Miami Beach, passed local bans on land-based shark fishing earlier this year. Safety concerns over shark activity on local beaches are far from theoretical for many residents . In August 2017, a 3-year-old girl named Violet Veatch was bitten on the leg by a suspected bull shark while wading in shallow water at Bathtub Reef Beach in Martin County. The toddler's mother, Jessica Veatch, later pushed for stricter local beach safety regulations , believing the shark was drawn to the crowded swimming area by spearfishermen carrying bloody fish through the water. Jessica Veatch, Violet's mother, says these new regulations would be great, but enforcement of them has been a problem. Enforcement is a big issue. You can put anything down on paper, but if you're not enforcing it, people are going to do what they want to do. We basically have our beaches turning into a cowboy sport, and if you don't like it, then you can go somewhere else. That is basically the mentality that a lot of these fishermen have, said Veatch. Justin Grubich, a marine conservation expert and local surfer who moved to the area from Fort Lauderdale, urged the commission to maintain strong local restrictions. Pointing to recent research presented at statewide conservation forums, Grubich warned that regular baiting near popular beaches conditions wildlife. "There's new scientific evidence or more accumulated scientific evidence that you can create problem sharks like problem bears," Grubich cautioned commissioners, advocating for rules that limit chumming and keep blood out of coastal waters. Commissioners did not take immediate action on the ordinance during the meeting, but requested further review of local public safety boundaries alongside state FWC regulations. County staff confirmed the current ordinance banning chumming is still in place. Current county rules ban fishing on guarded beaches when lifeguards are present. A new ordinance referring residents to FWC for state laws and tightening restrictions on county beaches is currently in the works. There is no timeline for when this new ordinance will come to a vote or exactly what new restrictions will go into place. One of the items discussed was increased drone restrictions on beaches amid concerns that they may be used to bait sharks. Other proposals included extended beach fishing hours and county shark fishing permits.

West Palm Beach Police Chief Tony Araujo announced Friday the termination of five command-level officers following a nearly two-year administrative investigation into overtime misconduct, marking the latest development in what has rocked the department since 2020.WATCH WPTV'S MOST RECENT REPORT:"Yesterday, following a thorough, nearly two-year administrative investigation, and after careful review of the findings, I made the difficult decision to terminate five command-level officers," Araujo said during a Friday morning press conference.The firings come as the culmination of an investigation that began after a 2020 audit commissioned by the city uncovered nearly $20,000 worth of "double dipping" on timecards and thousands of hours of questionable overtime payments within the police department.WATCH THE FULL PRESS CONFERENCE BELOW:The controversy dates back to 2020 when a third-party audit examined the finances of multiple city departments. The audit revealed what officials called "pretty egregious" overtime spending patterns within the police department that had gone undetected for years.The investigation eventually led to the firing of former Police Chief Frank Adderley and placed seven officers on administrative leave related to financial misconduct. P1 Motor Club is under construction on 650 acres off Okeechobee Road in St. Lucie County, replacing fairways with racing circuits and preparing to welcome its first drivers this fall. The private racetrack resort community features 10 miles of racing circuits designed for street cars, race cars and go-karts. Chris DuPlessis, Director of Fun for P1 Motor Club, compared the concept to a high-end golf resort, except with a racetrack instead of a golf course. The first track under construction is the 3-mile Treasure Coast Track, set to open in October. Over the next six months, crews will continue work on additional circuits, including the flagship 4.5-mile P1 International Circuit. DuPlessis said the club is designed for drivers of all ages and skill levels, with kids as young as 8 years old driving go-karts all the way up to grandparents still driving their cars on track, making it a family club. Membership comes with a $192,000 initiation fee and $12,000 in yearly dues. The club already has 260 members. Construction on a clubhouse and homes for up to 125 residents is scheduled to begin in 2027. The development will also include condos and customizable garages with living spaces situated directly along the tracks. Despite the scale of the project, developers say they want to preserve the character of the region by planting trees, creating lakes, and incorporating natural landscaping throughout the property. DuPlessis said it will feel like the racetrack has been there for 100 years, comparing the scope of work to building a city. P1 Motor Club is expected to be fully completed by 2028. A Fort Pierce pizza shop known for giving back is creating an even bigger space to inspire young readers. Big Apple Pizza owner Scott Van Duzer is expanding the restaurant’s free book program by transforming its outdoor patio into a dedicated reading room where children can pick up a book any time they visit. For years, Van Duzer has kept shelves of free books inside the restaurant, inviting children to take one home at no cost. He said seeing kids light up when they discover a new book has been one of the most rewarding parts of the program. “The books are there so when the kids come in the store they’re easily available,” Van Duzer said. “They’ll come in and they’re excited they can take whatever they want home.” As more children have stopped by to pick up books, the collection has continued to grow. Van Duzer said the restaurant has simply run out of space inside, prompting the decision to turn the outdoor patio into a permanent reading room. “We have so many books and we are trying to keep ahead of the game that we have turned our porch into what’s going to be the reading room,” Van Duzer said. “So now anytime a child stops by they can get a book free of charge no questions asked.” The goal, he said, is to make books easy to access and help encourage a lifelong love of reading. Whether a family comes in for pizza or simply stops by for a book, every child is welcome to take one home. For Van Duzer, giving back has always been part of the restaurant’s mission. He said that commitment comes from the example his mother set while he was growing up. “I didn’t have a lot,” Van Duzer said. “My mom was pretty instrumental in my life so she just said if you can give back, give back. We live that every day.” Construction on the new reading room is underway and is expected to be completed later this fall. Until then, children can continue picking up free books inside Big Apple Pizza, where the message remains the same: every child is welcome to take a book home, no questions asked. Big Apple Pizza is located at 2311 S 35th St, Fort Pierce FL 34981.

Lucie police officer resigned while under investigation after walking away from a vehicle containing a man who had shot and killed himself, only to return minutes later as backup. According to an internal affairs report, 23-year-old Officer Mathew Brown resigned on April 17, 2026, facing sustained findings for neglect of duty and inefficiency. Surveillance video from the Treasure Coast Church of God Worship Center showed Brown pulling behind a dark blue Porsche at 1:47 a.m. Brown shined his lights on the car, ran a license plate check, and walked up to the passenger side. However, after looking through the window, Brown turned right around and drove off without calling dispatch or checking on the person inside. At 2:02 a.m., a second officer stopped to check on the suspicious car and found a man dead inside from a gunshot wound, with a handgun sitting on his lap. Paramedics confirmed he was dead, and investigators ruled the death a suicide. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk recounts his first reaction to the investigation. Very frustrated and just seeking for some understanding because I can't fathom how a police officer would respond to a situation the way he did, said Niemczyk. As he was sent back to the scene as backup, Brown told the responding officer he had driven by earlier but "didn't see anyone in it." Related: Sergeant demoted, officer suspended after Boynton Beach traffic stop investigation Body camera footage captured Brown telling the officer to "go blue," muting both of their cameras for 32 seconds. When a supervisor later pointed out fresh tire tracks in the muddy grass right next to the Porsche, Brown stayed silent, failing to admit they were from his patrol SUV. Investigators concluded Brown failed to do a basic welfare check, offer help, or properly report what he saw. Brown submitted his resignation on April 2 while under investigation, which Niemczyk accepted. Internal Affairs formally sustained the violations on June 24th, marking his file as "resigned under investigation." Two other responding officers were cleared of any wrongdoing. He opted to resign and, you know, prior to the investigation being completed. So, we never had the opportunity to interview him on the record and get his explanation for his behavior. So, it's kind of unsolved in my mind, said Niemczyk. The chief says the public shouldn't expect this out of law enforcement, noting that Brown was the exception, not the expectation. This is not normal common behavior by a police officer. They have a right to expect police officers to provide all due care for human life and dignity. And that did not happen in this case. We're very disappointed, Niemczyk said.

A Fort Pierce resort says an abandoned sailboat that washed ashore three weeks ago is damaging property, slamming into other boats, and costing them thousands in business, but state law prevents them from moving it. "This is a danger to people and personal property," said Joe Zebrowski, general manager of Dockside Marina and Resort. The sailboat washed ashore near On The Edge Bar and Grill, and Zabrowski and his team quickly secured it. However, Zabrowski said the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) informed him that the boat cannot be moved. The agency is giving the owners 60 days to claim the vessel, and the resort is also prohibited from moving it. "I did a good deed, but no deed goes unpunished," Zebrowski said. The FWC used a chain to secure the sailboat, but Zebrowski said it hasn’t stopped the vessel from causing problems. "It kept it from floating away but didn’t keep it from whipping back and forth," he said. Zebrowski explained that the sailboat has slammed into a docked boat, destroyed a piling, and forced the restaurant to block off several tables near the vessel, which has significantly impacted their revenue. "These are our prime tables. They probably cost us about 25 percent of our overall business for the past month," Zebrowski said. According to state law, moving a boat that has washed ashore onto private property without proper permission can expose individuals to legal liabilities or even charges of theft. "There needs to be a carveout in however the law takes care of situations like this that takes care of people who are innocent and stop protecting an owner who has abandoned his boat that I don’t think is registered or has insurance," Zebrowski said. The FWC confirmed to WPBF that no one can touch the boat except its owners. WPBF is working to contact the owners of the boat for comment. The FWC is working on providing a more detailed statement. Martin County’s fire chief is warning that a proposed expansion of Florida’s homestead exemption could significantly reduce funding for Fire Rescue, potentially leading to station closures, firefighter layoffs and longer emergency response times. The measure, which will go before Florida voters in November, could lower property tax bills for homeowners. However, local governments have warned that it could also reduce revenue used to pay for public services. During Tuesday’s Martin County Commission meeting, Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli presented a planning exercise outlining how his department could respond to the projected revenue loss. This is real," Cianciulli said. Martin County Fire Rescue projects its annual budget would decline by $9.5 million in the first year. By the second year, the annual loss would reach $16.5 million, a 22% reduction from the department’s current budget. Under the scenario, Fire Rescue could close Station 18 on Britt Road, Station 33 in Hobe Sound, and Station 23 on Kanner Highway. Cianciulli added the department could be forced to lay off as many as 116 firefighters by the second year. That is equivalent to one of the department’s three shifts. The chief also warned that the funding loss could force Martin County to eliminate specialized teams responsible for hazardous materials incidents, technical rescues and dive operations. The department could then have to request assistance from neighboring agencies in Palm Beach or St. Lucie counties, potentially increasing response times. In an interview after the meeting, Cianciulli pointed to the deadly Camp Mystic flooding in Texas as an example of the delays that can occur when a community must rely on outside resources. "They had to call for outside assets, a 14-hour response to start mitigating that scene," Cianciulli said. "We’re in a position in the county, if we have any incident here, we are able to do an immediate mitigation. We’re not wasting any second." Your neighborhood: Local coverage from WPBF 25 News During public comment, one resident and a commissioner questioned whether reducing employee salaries could help address the potential shortfall. Cianciulli responded, saying Martin County already has difficulty recruiting trained firefighter-paramedics because departments farther south offer better compensation. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. "When we did our last class that we had, we had roughly 22 open positions; I only had about three paramedics that actually graduated that class," Cianciulli said. "The rest were firefighter EMTs. It’s because the compensation package for a firefighter medic that is already trained is much higher down south." Cianciulli advised residents to learn as much as possible about the proposal and its potential effects before casting their ballots in November.

It calls for redeveloping Museum Pointe, which is currently home to a history center, public waterfront access, fishing piers, and green space, into a facility featuring floating docks, a multi-story marina, an event center, a waterfront restaurant, and a clubhouse.Opponents fear the plan could privatize one of the city's most treasured public spaces."Giving public land to private folks," said Terry Howard, a volunteer at the History Center at Museum Pointe Park. Gabby Rothman, MPA Florida voters will soon make an important decision about property taxes. Amendment 3 would substantially increase the homestead exemption from non-school property taxes and require the Legislature to establish a schedule for eventually eliminating those taxes on qualifying homesteaded property. The amendment needs approval from at least 60 percent of voters to pass. Local government officials are warning that the loss of property tax revenue could lead to hiring freezes, reduced services, higher fees, and employee layoffs. Those concerns should be taken seriously. State economists have projected that the amendment could reduce local government property tax revenue across Florida by nearly $5 billion during its first fiscal year of implementation, with the impact increasing substantially in later years. But before government leaders begin frightening employees and residents with immediate predictions of layoffs, they should answer a fundamental question: Are we making full use of the people, skills, and opportunities already available in our community? I ask that question because I have personally watched an innovative government workforce solution succeed. For many years, I worked with Diamond Litty, the elected Public Defender for Florida’s 19th Judicial Circuit. Diamond did not believe that every staffing challenge automatically required another permanent government position with a salary, insurance, retirement benefits, and continuing costs. She looked for opportunities. One of the best examples was the Investigator Intern Program she created. The program gave participants structured training and practical experience while providing meaningful investigative assistance to the Public Defender’s Office. These were not volunteers simply answering telephones or stuffing envelopes. Participants learned how to interview clients and witnesses, review case information, assist with investigations, and understand the real responsibilities of the criminal justice system. The office received additional workforce capacity. Participants received extensive training and experience that could open the door to a new career. I watched Diamond create that program. I watched it grow and earn recognition far beyond our circuit. More importantly, I learned from it. Diamond demonstrated that innovation in government does not always begin with additional tax revenue. Sometimes it begins with a leader who recognizes two separate needs and finds a responsible way to connect them. That lesson stayed with me throughout my own public service career. Years later, while earning my Master of Public Administration degree, I began researching whether a similar philosophy could address two different challenges. Local governments have workforce needs. At the same time, many senior homeowners living on limited incomes struggle to keep up with property taxes and the increasing costs of remaining in their homes. My research “Is a ‘Work Off’ Program a Property Tax Solution for Florida Fixed Income Seniors?” examined programs in three states that allowed qualifying senior homeowners to perform approved public service in exchange for a limited property tax benefit. I developed a proposed model that would allow an eligible senior to contribute documented and supervised service to a participating government agency. The value of that service, up to an annual limit of $1,500, could then be applied toward a portion of the homeowner’s property tax obligation. Eligibility would be based on financial need. Work assignments would be clearly defined. Hours would be recorded and verified. Participants would be supervised and would not make legal decisions, determine taxes, handle public money, or perform work beyond their training and authority. A senior with experience in accounting might assist with an appropriate records project. A retired teacher might help prepare public education materials. Someone with administrative experience might assist with customer navigation, appointment scheduling, telephone support, outreach, or document organization. Let me be clear: the proposal was not intended to replace essential employees. It was designed to recognize that retirement does not erase a person’s knowledge, experience, or desire to contribute. This research also became personal to me during my campaign for St. Lucie County Tax Collector. I thought about the senior homeowner who might eventually stand at the counter and say, “I have lived in my home for decades, but I can no longer afford this tax bill.” The Tax Collector does not determine property values, establish tax rates, or create exemptions. The office must collect the amount placed on the tax roll and follow Florida law when taxes become delinquent. Without an authorized alternative, the Tax Collector may have little more to offer than an explanation of the law and the consequences of nonpayment. I believed we could at least study whether a better option was possible. A Tax Collector could not create this program independently. It would require legislative authority, legal review, funding, and cooperation among the taxing authorities, Property Appraiser, Tax Collector, senior service organizations, risk management professionals, and participating government agencies. Questions involving liability, confidentiality, insurance, workers’ compensation, public records, and the possible displacement of employees would have to be resolved. Those are legitimate concerns. They are also the kind of questions serious public administrators should be willing to examine rather than using them as reasons to reject innovation. No volunteer or service exchange program could absorb the entire financial impact of Amendment 3. It would be dishonest to suggest otherwise. Some government positions require professional training, legal authority, institutional knowledge, and permanent public accountability. Volunteers cannot simply replace essential employees. But it is equally unreasonable to act as though government has only two choices: collect the same amount of money or begin laying off employees. Other questions should be asked first. Can vacancies remain open? Can processes be simplified? Can technology reduce repetitive work? Can colleges provide supervised interns? Can retirees contribute their professional skills? Can government partner with community organizations? Can administrative layers be reduced before frontline positions are threatened? Perhaps the amendment will pass. Either way, the debate has exposed a larger problem. Too often, government waits for a financial crisis before discussing efficiency and innovation. That work should already be happening. I watched Diamond Litty identify an opportunity that others might have overlooked. She connected people seeking experience with an office that needed help, then built a structured program that benefited both. That same philosophy inspired my own thesis research defense. Look at the people already around us. Respect the value of their experience. Establish appropriate safeguards. Before government tells residents which services must disappear or tells employees which jobs may be lost, in my professional opinion, leaders should first demonstrate that they have explored every responsible opportunity available. "They'll come in and they're excited they can take whatever they want home."As more children have stopped by to pick up books, the collection has continued to grow. Van Duzer said the restaurant has simply run out of space inside, prompting the decision to turn the outdoor patio into a permanent reading room."We have so many books and we are trying to keep ahead of the game that we have turned our porch into what's going to be the reading room," Van Duzer said. "So now anytime a child stops by they can get a book free of charge no questions asked."The goal, he said, is to make books easy to access and help encourage a lifelong love of reading. Whether a family comes in for pizza or simply stops by for a book, every child is welcome to take one home.For Van Duzer, giving back has always been part of the restaurant's mission. He said that commitment comes from the example his mother set while he was growing up."I didn't have a lot," Van Duzer said. "My mom was pretty instrumental in my life so she just said if you can give back, give back. We live that every day."Construction on the new reading room is underway and is expected to be completed later this fall. Until then, children can continue picking up free books inside Big Apple Pizza, where the message remains the same: every child is welcome to take a book home, no questions asked.Big Apple Pizza is located at 2311 S 35th St, Fort Pierce FL 34981.

A groundbreaking ceremony marked the start of construction on a new K-8 school in Fort Pierce that will combine three St. Lucie County schools into one state-of-the-art facility.The new school will be built on land behind Dan McCarty Middle School and is expected to welcome between 1,500 and 1,800 students when it opens. It will consolidate Dan McCarty Middle, St. Lucie Elementary and Lawnwood Elementary into a single campus.WATCH BELOW: New $70M K-8 school breaks ground in Fort PierceSuperintendent Jon Prince said the project is moving forward as planned."On time, on budget, on schedule," Prince said.Prince said the new facility will feature state-of-the-art technology and serve the north part of St. Lucie County."It's going to be very popular in the community. That's for sure," Prince said.The decision to consolidate comes as the existing schools show their age. All three were built several decades ago."These schools were built in the 50s and 60s, and you know, a lot of these schools have been retrofitted, but they're still not quite as efficient as (they) can be," Prince said.Dan McCarty Middle Principal Latricia Stubbs-James said the wear and tear is visible inside the building."Some of the things that we have in there are antiquated," Stubbs-James said.She is glad students in the northern part of the county will now receive the investment they need."Being able to actually know that our schools in the north part of the county are also getting the attention that they deserve and they need would be great," Stubbs-James said.She also said the K-8 model offers unique benefits for younger students."Kindergarten students can see what it looks like to be an eighth grader at a new K-8. What does it look like to be a fifth grader?" Stubbs-James said.The district is funding the $70 million project in part by selling the properties where the three older schools currently stand, offsetting the cost of maintaining aging buildings. Prince said the K-8 model is already proven across the district, which operates 11 other K-8 schools."Attendance is better, test scores are better and also grades are better in the K-8s," Prince said.The new Fort Pierce K-8 school is expected to be completed in August 2028.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Martin County commissioners faced a wave of public pushback during Tuesday morning's meeting as residents, local surfers, and marine experts urged local leaders to keep strict limits on beachside shark fishing. The debate centers on potential language changes to local ordinances regarding land-based shark fishing, a practice where anglers deploy lines from the shore using heavy gear, kayaks, or drones to drop bait and chum into deeper waters. Under current Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) rules, shore anglers are required to hold a specialized permit, keep sharks in the water, and use non-offset circle hooks to prevent injury to the animals. However, local ordinances in coastal counties can set stricter safety boundaries near public swimming areas. During public comments, speakers warned that chumming , releasing fish parts and blood into the surf to attract sharks, endangers swimmers, surfers, and families. "I myself have been caught in shark fishing lines, and it is not fun," said local surfer Jay Noyes, speaking in support of beachgoers and surfers. Dottie Lanci, a member of the Hutchinson Island Preservation Initiative, strongly opposed any effort to loosen existing restrictions that ban shark baiting on lifeguard-protected beaches. Lansing called on commissioners to prioritize safety and extend the ban across all county beaches, citing an incident she witnessed outside her home where anglers used drones to drop chum in the water. "The next morning a family of four put up their umbrellas. Two young children were playing in the water there, completely unaware of what took place the day before and that some hungry sharks might still be there," Lanci said. She also noted that other Florida municipalities, such as Miami Beach, passed local bans on land-based shark fishing earlier this year. Safety concerns over shark activity on local beaches are far from theoretical for many residents . In August 2017, a 3-year-old girl named Violet Veatch was bitten on the leg by a suspected bull shark while wading in shallow water at Bathtub Reef Beach in Martin County. The toddler's mother, Jessica Veatch, later pushed for stricter local beach safety regulations , believing the shark was drawn to the crowded swimming area by spearfishermen carrying bloody fish through the water. Justin Grubich, a marine conservation expert and local surfer who moved to the area from Fort Lauderdale, urged the commission to maintain strong local restrictions. Pointing to recent research presented at statewide conservation forums, Grubich warned that regular baiting near popular beaches conditions wildlife. "There's new scientific evidence or more accumulated scientific evidence that you can create problem sharks like problem bears," Grubich cautioned commissioners, advocating for rules that limit chumming and keep blood out of coastal waters. Commissioners did not take immediate action on the ordinance during the meeting, but requested further review of local public safety boundaries alongside state FWC regulations.

Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast, with every county in the region seeing an increase in median home sale prices. This news comes after price drops from 2023 to 2025.Martin County, median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000 St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000WATCH BELOW: Treasure Coast single-family home prices on the riseKelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand."The good news for buyers is that we're not seeing huge jumps in prices," Decowski said.But Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now."Because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down. They are probably going to continue to increase," Decowski said.Decowski said inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers."That means that buyers need to be realistic with their offers. They need to come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes. Sellers need to price their homes realistically, and they need to present a well-maintained product," Decowski said.For some Martin County homeowners, the rising prices are reshaping long-term plans. Cara Collins, who bought her home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell."I think this is going to be our family home as long as the market's still as high as it is," Collins said.Collins said current prices are higher than she would hope for, and that the market has changed what would be possible for her family today."I wouldn't be able to be a stay-at-home mom and be able to afford a home for my kids if we would be buying now," Collins said.It's a different story with condos and townhomes. Prices have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and only increased by less than a percent in Indian River County.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. hero.headline: Indian River County Sheriff's Office searches for missing 24-year-old man last seen Tuesday afternoon
hero.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office is attempting to locate Kaden Joseph Simon, a 24-year-old man who was last seen leaving his residence around 2:30 p.m. on Tuesday. Simon was wearing black pants, a black shirt and flip-flop sandals when he left. His direction of travel was unknown.

Simon has brown hair and brown eyes, stands at 5-foot-7, and weighs 160 pounds. The sheriff's office announced the search for Simon on Tuesday.

Anyone with information regarding his whereabouts is asked to contact Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-8477. The sheriff's office did not release additional information about the circumstances surrounding his disappearance.

The Indian River County Sheriff's Office is located in Indian River County, which includes Vero Beach, Sebastian, and Fellsmere.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office employee killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
hero.teaser: Elizabeth Ortega, 50, a communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, was killed Saturday night in Port St. Lucie by her longtime boyfriend, who then killed himself.
hero.body:
Elizabeth Ortega had been employed at the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office for the last ten years. The shooting happened Saturday night both inside and outside a home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. Officer Brittany McNally of the Port St. Lucie Police Department said a man began shooting at the woman inside their home, chased her outside and continued firing, hitting her multiple times. 'One of the neighbors actually located that victim after they observed her lying in the front yard unresponsive,' McNally said.

Police said the shooter was Ortega's longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Sr. After killing Ortega, Varela went back inside the home and killed himself. McNally said Ortega and Varela had been together for about 30 years, but Ortega had recently ended the relationship. 'Although the relationship had ended, it appears the two had agreed to live together until Ralph could find other living arrangements,' McNally said. The couple's son had left the home just minutes before the shooting and told police everything seemed fine.

The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said Ortega began her emergency communications career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001. In February 2016, the Greenacres Police Department and its communications unit merged with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. 'She was a respected and cherished part of our PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room,' the sheriff's office said in a statement.
hero.article_text: The victim in a weekend murder-suicide in Port St. Lucie has been identified as a communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. Fifty-year-old Elizabeth Ortega had been employed at PBSO for the last ten years. The shooting happened Saturday night both inside and outside a home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. In a video statement released Monday, police said a man began shooting at the woman inside their home, chased her outside, and continued firing, hitting her multiple times. "One of the neighbors actually located that victim after they observed her lying in the front yard unresponsive," Officer Brittany McNally of the Port St. Lucie Police Department said. On Monday afternoon, PBSO posted about Ortega on social media, saying, in part, "She was a respected and cherished part of our PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room." Police said the shooter was Ortega’s longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Jr. After killing Ortega, Varela went back inside the home and killed himself. McNally said Ortega and Varela had been together for about 30 years, but Ortega had recently ended the relationship. "Although the relationship had ended, it appears the two had agreed to live together until Ralph could find other living arrangements," McNally said. Investigators are working to determine what led to the violence. The couple’s son had left the home just minutes before the shooting and told police everything seemed fine. "There’s no evidence to suggest that there was a disagreement, a disturbance or an argument that occurred directly prior to the shooting," McNally said. The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office has provided therapy dogs to help Ortega’s co-workers cope with the loss.
