cards.headline: U.S. Marshals arrest baby's father in Fort Pierce malnutrition death case
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced Tuesday that the biological father of a 3-month-old who died from severe dehydration and malnutrition has been arrested by the United States Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. Jason Gunter, 45, faces felony child neglect causing great harm and awaits extradition to St. Lucie County. The investigation began Aug. 20, 2025, when Robert Maxwell and his girlfriend Vikki Koon brought 3-month-old Robert Gunter to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce. Medical staff immediately observed signs the infant had been dead for some time, including rigor mortis, fixed pupils and skin discoloration. He was pronounced dead at 11:35 a.m. after resuscitation efforts failed.

According to a 37-page arrest affidavit, text messages recovered during the investigation showed family members repeatedly warning both parents that something was wrong with the child. Messages sent to Nicole Maxwell, the child's mother, stated, 'The baby's got nothing to eat. I don't know what to give him.' Other messages urged Gunter to come to Florida because something was wrong with the infant. A separate text message recovered from Gunter's phone stated, 'The baby is starving.' Investigators allege Gunter did not return to Florida, seek immediate intervention or contact emergency services despite those warnings.

An autopsy revealed Robert Gunter weighed 11 pounds, 12 ounces at a pediatric appointment July 24, 2025. Less than a month later, at the time of his death, he weighed only 9 pounds, 3.5 ounces, placing him below the first percentile for children his age. The Medical Examiner's Office found evidence of severe dehydration and malnutrition, including poor skin elasticity, loss of body fat, sunken features, elevated sodium levels, organ damage and an absence of food contents in the stomach and upper intestinal tract. The manner of death was classified as homicide.

Three others were previously charged in the case. Nicole Maxwell, 27, Robert Maxwell and Vikki Koon, 38, each face charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Each was held on a $1.5 million bond. When investigators executed a search warrant at the mobile home on Silverstream Circle where the baby had been staying, they documented what they described as an extreme environmental hazard filled with clutter, moldy food, exposed electrical wiring, live rodents and widespread cockroach infestations. Two other children connected to the home were placed in a safe environment with assistance from the Florida Department of Children and Families.
cards.article_text: A fourth person has been arrested in connection with the death of a 3-month-old baby who allegedly died from severe dehydration and malnutrition. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced Tuesday that the child's biological father, 45-year-old Jason Gunter, was taken into custody by the United States Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. Detectives had obtained an arrest warrant for Gunter in connection with the ongoing investigation into the child's death. He has been charged with felony child neglect causing great harm and is awaiting extradition to St. The arrest comes after three others were previously charged in the case: the child's mother, 27-year-old Nicole Maxwell; the child's grandfather, Robert Maxwell; and Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, 38-year-old Vikki Koon. See also: Body found in ocean off Boca Raton coast, investigation underway All three were charged with aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Each was held on a $1.5 million bond. Investigation Began After Baby Was Brought to Hospital The investigation began on Aug. 20, 2025, when Koon and Robert Maxwell brought 3-month-old Robert Gunter to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce. Medical staff immediately observed signs that the infant had been dead for some time, including rigor mortis, fixed pupils and skin discoloration. He was pronounced dead at 11:35 a.m. after resuscitation efforts failed. Detectives assigned to the case conducted interviews with family members at the hospital before serving search warrants and beginning what would become a months-long investigation. Caregivers Allegedly Noticed Warning Signs According to a 37-page arrest affidavit, the infant had been primarily living with Koon and Robert Maxwell after Gunter moved to Virginia. During interviews, detectives learned caregivers had noticed numerous warning signs in the days leading up to the child's death. Investigators say Koon admitted the baby was often fed only a few times a day and claimed he sometimes drank as little as two bottles daily. She told detectives she noticed the child was becoming increasingly thin, pale and lethargic. She also described frequent vomiting, excessive sleeping and a decrease in wet diapers. Despite those concerns, detectives say no one sought emergency medical treatment. Text messages obtained during the investigation showed family members repeatedly warning both parents that something was wrong. 12, 2025, messages sent to Nicole Maxwell stated, "The baby's got nothing to eat. I don't know what to give him." Days later, additional messages warned that the baby was sick, covered in marks and sleeping constantly. Other messages urged Gunter to come to Florida because something was wrong with the infant. According to detectives, neither parent took action that resulted in immediate medical care for the child. Search Warrant Revealed Conditions Inside Home When investigators executed a search warrant at the mobile home on Silverstream Circle where the baby had been staying, they documented what they described as an "extreme environmental hazard." The affidavit details a residence filled with clutter, moldy food, exposed electrical wiring, live rodents and widespread cockroach infestations. Detectives reported finding baby bottles containing curdled milk and observed insects crawling in and around a collapsed playpen. Vomit-like substances were also found on a couch and nearby flooring. Crime scene investigators noted the home appeared extremely dirty and poorly maintained, with evidence suggesting the playpen was not actively being used by the infant despite statements from caregivers. Autopsy Findings Led to Homicide Ruling An autopsy later revealed the extent of the infant's condition. According to the Medical Examiner's Office, Robert Gunter weighed 11 pounds, 12 ounces at a pediatric appointment on July 24, 2025. Less than a month later, at the time of his death, he weighed only 9 pounds, 3.5 ounces, placing him below the first percentile for children his age. The autopsy found evidence of severe dehydration and malnutrition, including poor skin elasticity, loss of body fat, sunken features, elevated sodium levels, organ damage and an absence of food contents in the stomach and upper intestinal tract. Examiners also documented numerous lesions and insect bites across the infant's body. The Medical Examiner ultimately determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition and classified the manner of death as homicide, writing that the infant was dependent on caregivers for nutrition and hydration and that the failure to provide those necessities directly caused his death. Father's Role Under Scrutiny Investigators say Gunter was aware of concerns about the child's condition. The criminal complaint states that messages sent to Gunter warned that the baby had marks on his body, was sleeping excessively and appeared ill. Detectives also recovered messages discussing food shortages and concerns the infant was not being properly cared for. Despite those warnings, investigators allege Gunter did not return to Florida, seek immediate intervention or contact emergency services. A separate text message recovered from his phone stated: "The baby is starving." Detectives included that message among evidence supporting criminal charges. Sheriff's officials said the investigation remains active as the case moves through the court system. Meanwhile, two other children connected to the home were placed in a safe environment with assistance from the Florida Department of Children and Families.

hero.headline: Deputies execute search warrant at Fort Pierce home in $7 million Southern Truss fraud investigation
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies descended on a Fort Pierce neighborhood Tuesday morning to execute a search warrant at the home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard. The warrant is part of an ongoing investigation into an alleged fraud scheme that investigators say cost Southern Truss Companies nearly $7 million. Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting the business.

Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Neighbor Greg Longhway said he watched deputies storm the house Tuesday morning. "Oh, they came ripping in, and the SWAT gear and everything with the guns pulled and hollering. Come out that search warrant. Come out with your hands up," he said. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to charges of first-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more, organized fraud of $50,000 or more, conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity, and money laundering of $100,000 or more. Her bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges.

The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility, according to the criminal complaint. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, investigators say server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records. A forensic audit later recovered a secret shadow ledger on her computer, according to the complaint, tracking where the missing money had actually gone.

Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2018 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions.

Neighbors on Sunset Boulevard told CBS12 News they had long been suspicious of Grasso's lifestyle. They got 4 or 5 brand new trucks. They got food delivery every day, four different food deliveries. I mean, we always wondered what was going on over there," neighbor Greg Longhway said. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release. They don't talk to anybody, which is fine; we don't care," Longhway said. "We figured something was up over there, though." The amended complaint alleges Grasso alone misappropriated at least $5 million, while Mejia and Harrs allegedly received hundreds of thousands more. The criminal case remains pending. Court records show a magistrate in June declined to pause the related civil case because of the criminal proceedings, instead ordering the defendants to respond to discovery by July 30 and complete depositions by Aug. Neighbors say they saw someone arrested by a SWAT team this morning. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has not confirmed any additional arrests or what investigators were searching for on Tuesday.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office makes fourth arrest in death of 3-month-old child
cards.teaser: Jason Gunter, 45, the child's biological father, was arrested Tuesday by U.S. Marshals at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia, and charged with felony child neglect causing great bodily harm.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced Tuesday that Jason Gunter, 45, the biological father of a 3-month-old child who died, was taken into custody by the United States Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. The arrest was made on an outstanding warrant obtained by St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives. Gunter is charged with felony child neglect causing great bodily harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the infant's death.

Gunter is awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County, where he will face the charge. The arrest marks the fourth made as part of the sheriff's office's investigation into the child's death. The investigation remains active as the case moves through the judicial process.

hero.headline: Tradition Lakes K-8 prepares to open in St. Lucie County with 1,600 students expected
hero.teaser: The new campus will open Aug. 10, offering much-needed classroom space for one of the county's fastest-growing communities.
hero.body:
Tradition Lakes K-8 in St. Lucie County is set to open its doors on Aug. 10, offering much-needed classroom space for one of the county's fastest-growing communities. Principal Latanya Greene said the school's motto, 'Traditions begin here,' reflects the focus on building a foundation of achievements and accomplishments. 'Throughout this process, we have talked a lot about traditions and accomplishments and the achievements that we want to build and grow at this school. Hence, our motto for the school year is that tradition leads K through eight. Traditions begin here,' Greene said.

The new campus comes at a critical time for the Tradition area, where population growth has led to overcrowding at nearby schools. District leaders expect as many as 1,600 students on opening day, with many families benefiting from the school's convenient location. 'We are busting at the seams in the south and the west. And this school is so conveniently located to families that we're going to have a tremendous number of students that are walking or even other parents dropping the kids off in a golf cart,' said John R. Prince, superintendent of St. Lucie County Public Schools.

Greene said success will be measured not only by academics but also by the sense of community created during the school's inaugural year. 'The academics component is going to be there, but it is going to be walking through this inaugural year and looking back on all the traditions that we have created as a team, as a family, and the strength of our culture, and how we just grow throughout the first year will be beyond the definition of success for us,' Greene said.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office employee killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
cards.teaser: Elizabeth Ortega, 50, a communications officer with 10 years at PBSO, was killed by her longtime boyfriend Saturday night at their home on Southeast Oxmoor Terrace.
cards.body:
Elizabeth Ortega, a 50-year-old communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, was killed in a murder-suicide Saturday night at her home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace in Port St. Lucie. Ortega had been employed at PBSO for the last ten years. Port St. Lucie police said a man began shooting at the woman inside their home, chased her outside, and continued firing, hitting her multiple times. 'One of the neighbors actually located that victim after they observed her lying in the front yard unresponsive,' Officer Brittany McNally of the Port St. Lucie Police Department said.

Police said the shooter was Ortega's longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Jr. After killing Ortega, Varela went back inside the home and killed himself. McNally said Ortega and Varela had been together for about 30 years, but Ortega had recently ended the relationship. 'Although the relationship had ended, it appears the two had agreed to live together until Ralph could find other living arrangements,' McNally said. The couple's son had left the home just minutes before the shooting and told police everything seemed fine. 'There's no evidence to suggest that there was a disagreement, a disturbance or an argument that occurred directly prior to the shooting,' McNally said.

On Monday afternoon, PBSO posted about Ortega on social media, saying, in part, 'She was a respected and cherished part of our PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room.' The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office has provided therapy dogs to help Ortega's co-workers cope with the loss. Ortega began her emergency communications career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001. In February 2016, the Greenacres Police Department and its communications unit merged with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office.

hero.headline: Florida man used police maneuver to run North Carolina family off road near Stuart
hero.body:
A Florida man used a PIT maneuver to send a North Carolina family's SUV into a barbed-wire fence during a road rage attack that began on I-95 and passed through Stuart on Saturday evening. Michael Jeffrey Spiers, 36, is charged with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and child abuse after the crash near Kanner Highway and I-95 around 7:30 p.m.

Spiers first chased a woman driving alone through a gas station parking lot before following her onto the highway, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The woman called 911 and told dispatchers he repeatedly tried to force her off the road. She lost Spiers by driving the wrong way up an exit ramp to get back on I-95. The woman's brother was following behind her in a separate car with his wife and young son.

Spiers then turned his attention to the family's vehicle, throwing objects, brake checking and attempting to run it off the roadway. Witnesses reported Spiers was flailing his arms and making what appeared to be gang signs during the encounters. Spiers intentionally performed a PIT maneuver on the family's SUV, a tactic typically used by law enforcement to stop fleeing vehicles. The impact sent the family's SUV spinning off 96th Street near Kanner Highway and crashing into a barbed-wire fence.

The three family members ran out of the car and into the brush to hide until deputies arrived. Deputies arrested Spiers at the nearby Sunoco gas station at Kanner Highway and 96th Street. Sheriff John Budensiek said Spiers did not know the victims but believed they were stealing his money. Deputies found a dog inside Spiers' vehicle that had allegedly been stolen in December from someone Spiers used to date. The dog has been reunited with its owner. Spiers remains jailed on charges of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, child abuse and reckless driving.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County cities push for more trees and shade as extreme heat bakes neighborhoods
hero.body:
Palm Beach County Parks and Recreation says the number one need they hear from people, aside from beach access, is shade. Community Greening, a South Florida nonprofit, says adequate tree canopy coverage is around the 30 to 40 percent range and virtually every city in Palm Beach County is at least in the 20 percent range and most are lower. The nonprofit has helped plant and give away nearly 30,000 trees across Palm Beach, Broward and parts of Martin County over the past decade.

Neighborhoods that have adequate tree canopy coverage are on average 7 to 10 degrees cooler than the neighborhoods right next to them that don't have that adequate tree canopy coverage, including at nighttime once the sun is out of the way, according to Josh Weiner, director of communications and engagement for Community Greening. Palm Beach County Parks and Recreation recently partnered with Community Greening to plant 1,000 trees at Dyer Park in West Palm Beach. The county has also started installing additional shade structures, including new coverings over bleachers at Sandalfoot Cove Park in Boca Raton.

The Resilient Glades Tree Campaign aimed to revitalize tree canopy coverage in South Bay, Belle Glade, Pahokee and Canal Point by planting 2,000 trees at county parks and hosting eight giveaway events. The project was expected to receive roughly $1 million before funding was cut by the Environmental Protection Agency. Community Greening next tree giveaway is scheduled for September at Halpatiokee Regional Park in Martin County. The nonprofit is also partnering with the city of Boca Raton to plant 100 native shade trees along El Rio Trail in September.

hero.teaser: U.S. Marshals arrested the biological father of a 3-month-old child in Virginia on a felony child neglect charge. He is the fourth person charged in connection with the infant's death.
hero.body:
Jason Gunter, 45, the biological father of a 3-month-old child who died, was taken into custody Tuesday by the U.S. Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. The arrest was made on an outstanding warrant obtained by St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives. Gunter is charged with felony child neglect causing great bodily harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the infant's death and is awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County.

The arrest marks the fourth made as part of the sheriff's office investigation into the child's death. The investigation began when the baby's grandparents brought the child to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. Medical personnel told deputies the child had been pronounced dead and showed signs of injuries consistent with possible neglect. St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said the investigation remains active as the case moves through the judicial process.

A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Longhway said the family largely kept to themselves. They've never said a word to anybody. They've been there for a year and a half, two years. They don't talk to anybody, which is fine; we don't care," Longhway said. "We figured something was up over there, though." The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility, according to the criminal complaint. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, investigators say server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records. A forensic audit later recovered a secret "shadow ledger" on her computer, according to the complaint, tracking where the missing money had actually gone. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2018 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions. The amended complaint alleges Grasso alone misappropriated at least $5 million, while Mejia and Harrs allegedly received hundreds of thousands more. The criminal case remains pending. Court records show a magistrate in June declined to pause the related civil case because of the criminal proceedings, instead ordering the defendants to respond to discovery by July 30 and complete depositions by Aug. Neighbors say they saw someone arrested by a SWAT team this morning. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has not confirmed any additional arrests or what investigators were searching for on Tuesday.

Jackson refused several lawful commands to exit the vehicle and actively resisted the officers' attempts to detain her.

Howard was taken into custody without incident. Both suspects were transported to the St. Lucie County Jail and charged with possession of cocaine and possession of drug paraphernalia. Jackson was also charged with resisting an officer without violence and tampering with physical evidence.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County schools open Aug. 10 with new Tradition Lakes K-8 campus and AI courses
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Public Schools will open for students on Aug. 10 with enrollment expected to hold steady at 42,505 students, though the district is adding new facilities and programs. Tradition Lakes K-8 will welcome students in western St. Lucie County as the district's newest campus, serving the Tradition area where population growth has been expanding. Superintendent Jon Prince said enrollment is projected to remain flat this year after the district lost 150 students last year instead of gaining the 350 projected by the state, costing around $14 million in state and federal funding.

The district's tentative budget is $1.07 billion, nearly $60 million less than last year's final budget. Prince said the district made significant cuts, most at the district level rather than directly impacting schools, and no staff were laid off but were instead moved to other positions. Despite the budget reduction, the district is adding two new artificial intelligence courses at Legacy High School this year.

Over the past seven years, enrollment in St. Lucie County Public Schools has increased by 7 percent, but Prince attributes this year's plateau to more families choosing homeschooling or private schools. Families are already preparing for the first day. Parent Jovani Taylor said he has been purchasing school supplies, books and clothing for his daughter Jayla, who will be starting fourth grade. Another parent, Julia Lopez, said her daughter will be starting VPK and noted the district's growth, saying she sees schools like almost every corner.

Prince said the district expects as many as 1,600 students at Tradition Lakes K-8 on opening day, with many families benefiting from the school's convenient location in an area of very expansive growth. Principal Latanya Greene said the school's motto is 'Traditions begin here,' reflecting the focus on building a foundation of achievements and accomplishments. Greene said success will be measured not only by academics but also by the sense of community created during the school's inaugural year.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office employee killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
cards.teaser: Elizabeth Ortega, 50, a communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office for 10 years, was killed Saturday night by her longtime boyfriend at their Port St. Lucie home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace.
cards.body:
Elizabeth Ortega, 50, a communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, was killed Saturday night in a murder-suicide at her Port St. Lucie home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. Ortega had been employed at PBSO for the last ten years. Police said her longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Jr., began shooting at her inside their home, chased her outside, and continued firing, hitting her multiple times. One of the neighbors located Ortega lying in the front yard unresponsive, according to Port St. Lucie Police Department Officer Brittany McNally.

McNally said Ortega and Varela had been together for about 30 years, but Ortega had recently ended the relationship. Although the relationship had ended, it appears the two had agreed to live together until Varela could find other living arrangements. The couple's son had left the home just minutes before the shooting and told police everything seemed fine. McNally said there is no evidence to suggest that there was a disagreement, disturbance or argument that occurred directly prior to the shooting.

Ortega began her emergency communications career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001. In February 2016, the Greenacres Police Department and its communications unit merged with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said in a statement that Ortega was a respected and cherished part of the PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office has provided therapy dogs to help Ortega's co-workers cope with the loss.
cards.article_text: The victim in a weekend murder-suicide in Port St. Lucie has been identified as a communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. Fifty-year-old Elizabeth Ortega had been employed at PBSO for the last ten years. The shooting happened Saturday night both inside and outside a home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. In a video statement released Monday, police said a man began shooting at the woman inside their home, chased her outside, and continued firing, hitting her multiple times. "One of the neighbors actually located that victim after they observed her lying in the front yard unresponsive," Officer Brittany McNally of the Port St. Lucie Police Department said. On Monday afternoon, PBSO posted about Ortega on social media, saying, in part, "She was a respected and cherished part of our PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room." Police said the shooter was Ortega’s longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Jr. After killing Ortega, Varela went back inside the home and killed himself. McNally said Ortega and Varela had been together for about 30 years, but Ortega had recently ended the relationship. "Although the relationship had ended, it appears the two had agreed to live together until Ralph could find other living arrangements," McNally said. Investigators are working to determine what led to the violence. The couple’s son had left the home just minutes before the shooting and told police everything seemed fine. "There’s no evidence to suggest that there was a disagreement, a disturbance or an argument that occurred directly prior to the shooting," McNally said. The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office has provided therapy dogs to help Ortega’s co-workers cope with the loss. cards.body:

Crews have worked throughout the summer to prepare the campus for its first group of students. Principal Latanya Greene said the school's motto, 'Traditions begin here,' reflects the focus on building a foundation of achievements and accomplishments.

The new campus comes at a critical time for the Tradition area, where population growth has led to overcrowding at nearby schools. District leaders expect as many as 1,600 students on opening day, with many families benefiting from the school's convenient location. Superintendent John R. Prince said the district is busting at the seams in the south and the west, and this school is so conveniently located to families that a tremendous number of students will be walking or even having parents drop the kids off in a golf cart. Greene said success will be measured not only by academics but also by the sense of community created during the school's inaugural year, looking back on all the traditions created as a team and as a family and the strength of the school's culture.

Principal Latanya Greene said the school’s motto, "Traditions begin here," reflects the focus on building a foundation of achievements and accomplishments. "It's about being in an environment that you can grow and continue with great levels. But bigger than that, you begin to set the tone of creating those strong academics that move with you from year to year to year. You develop friendships," Greene said. hero.headline: Martin County REACH Center launches workforce training programs in aviation, healthcare, and manufacturing
hero.body:
Martin County's REACH Center has opened its doors and begun offering workforce training programs designed to prepare residents for jobs in high-demand industries. The roughly $4.5 million facility completed construction earlier this year and is now hosting courses ranging from medical administrative assistant certification to technical aviation training for Daher Aerospace.

Evelyn Lopez was among the first 10 students to complete a medical administrative assistant cohort this summer. She passed the certification exam and is now exploring job opportunities. The program included mock interviews with professionals to prepare students for the hiring process. Lopez said her parents were proud of her achievement because it opened more career opportunities.

George Stokus, assistant county administrator, said the center serves students uncertain about college, those without financial means to pursue higher education immediately, and adults seeking career changes or skill improvements. The facility aims to create a local pipeline for jobs in aviation, marine, medicine, manufacturing, and environmental studies.

Ted Astolfi, CEO and president of the Economic Council of Martin County, said the center's mission focuses on creating upward economic mobility for the community. The center aims to help residents grow into better jobs rather than remain at a single economic level. Additional programs are planned to expand the range of training opportunities available to Martin County residents.

cards.headline: Florida man used PIT maneuver to run North Carolina family off road near Stuart during I-95 road rage attack
cards.teaser: Michael Jeffrey Spiers faces aggravated battery and child abuse charges after deputies say he chased a family on I-95 and intentionally spun their SUV into a barbed-wire fence near Kanner Highway.
cards.body:
A 36-year-old Florida man is in custody after deputies say he used a PIT maneuver to send a North Carolina family's SUV into a barbed-wire fence during a road rage attack that began on I-95 and passed through Stuart. Michael Jeffrey Spiers faces charges of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, child abuse, and reckless driving following the Saturday evening incident near Kanner Highway and I-95. The Martin County Sheriff's Office said the family had no role in any confrontation before they were targeted.

Deputies said Spiers first chased a woman driving alone through a gas station parking lot before following her onto the highway, repeatedly trying to force her off the road. The woman's brother was following behind her in a separate car with his wife and young son. Spiers then turned his attention to the family's vehicle, throwing objects, brake checking, and attempting to run it off the roadway. Witnesses reported Spiers was flailing his arms and making what appeared to be gang signs during the encounters. The woman escaped by driving the wrong way up an exit ramp to get back on I-95.

Spiers performed an intentional PIT maneuver on the family's SUV, sending it spinning off 96th Street near Kanner Highway and into a barbed-wire fence. cards.teaser: Sheriff's deputies recorded a visibly shaken family emerging from the bushes near Kanner Highway after a driver chased them for miles and forced them off the road Saturday.
cards.body:
Body camera footage shows a North Carolina family walking out of the bushes near Kanner Highway, just west of I-95 in Martin County, after being chased off the road over the weekend. The couple, visiting Florida with their young son, appeared visibly shaken as they recounted the incident to a sheriff's deputy. The family said the suspect chased the man's sister for miles, prompting the wife to call 911. The wife told the dispatcher the driver was chasing the sister with his lasers on while she had a baby in her car.

The man explained that he and his wife tried to intervene but the driver then focused on them instead. The family pulled over, hoping the driver would move ahead, but he got out of his vehicle and came back. The man's sister managed to escape, but the driver continued to follow the couple and eventually forced them off the road. The man told the deputy the driver performed an evasive maneuver that sent their car off the road in what he described as a pit maneuver.

Deputies identified the driver as Michael Spiers and arrested him at a nearby gas station. Sheriff John Budensiek said the family did not know what was coming next and were extremely grateful they were not injured. Budensiek said the suspect did not have a gun and the situation could have ended much worse.

hero.headline: Florida Sheriffs Association warns homestead exemption ballot measure could lengthen law enforcement response times
hero.teaser: The statewide association says a November ballot measure to increase the homestead exemption and lower tax bills for homeowners could create longer law enforcement response times.
hero.body:
The Florida Sheriffs Association has entered the tax reform debate, raising concerns about a November ballot measure that would increase the homestead exemption and lower tax bills for homeowners. The association states it has significant concerns with the referendum, warning it could potentially create longer law enforcement response times. Former Martin County Sheriff William Snyder said the association's position carries weight, noting that Florida sheriffs are always moderate in their responses and tend to be very supportive of the governor, making their opposition to the governor in this case a clear signal.

Snyder said he understands the frustration driving the push for tax relief but warned the savings may come with hidden costs. He explained that instead of paying for services out of their left pocket, taxpayers will pay for it out of their right pocket, as sheriffs' offices and fire departments would look to other taxes and fees to make up the difference. Snyder served as Martin County sheriff for 12 years and managed the department's budgets throughout that time.

Snyder said his department looked at every single nickel and could shave a little off the edges, but when 80 percent of the budget is personnel services, unless deputies or firefighters are let go, there is not much that can be done with the budget. The debate over cutting taxes and its impact on public safety is central to the amendment question facing voters in November. County and city leaders are grappling with how they would manage significant cuts in revenue as homeowners look to Tallahassee for relief from high tax bills.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County schools open Aug. 10 with flat enrollment at 42,505 students
hero.teaser: St. Lucie County Public Schools will open Aug. 10 with enrollment expected to remain flat at 42,505 students, despite the district opening a new school to accommodate growth in western St. Lucie County.
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Public Schools will open for students on Aug. 10 with enrollment expected to remain flat at 42,505 students, despite seven years of growth that increased enrollment by 7 percent. Superintendent Jon Prince attributes this year's plateau to more families choosing homeschooling or private schools. Last year, the state projected an increase of 350 students, but the district instead lost 150, costing it around $14 million in state and federal funding.

The district opened Tradition Lakes K-8, its newest school, to serve students in western St. Lucie County where the Tradition area is experiencing expansive growth. This year's tentative district budget is $1.07 billion, nearly $60 million less than last year's final budget. Prince said the district made significant cuts, mostly at the district level rather than at schools, and no staff were laid off but instead moved to other positions.

Despite budget reductions, the district is adding new programs. Two new courses focused on artificial intelligence will be available to students this year at Legacy High School. Prince said the district needs to provide avenues for students interested in AI-related careers based on future legislation.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County detectives execute search warrant at Fort Pierce home in $7 million Southern Truss fraud case
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives executed a search warrant Tuesday morning at a Fort Pierce home connected to an alleged fraud scheme that cost Southern Truss Companies nearly $7 million. Crime scene investigators were seen outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard. Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting the local truss manufacturing business.

Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Grasso faces charges of first-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more, organized fraud of $50,000 or more, conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity and money laundering of $100,000 or more. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges. Her bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges.

Neighbor Greg Longhway said he watched deputies storm the house Tuesday morning. Deputies came in with SWAT gear and guns pulled, hollering about the search warrant and ordering people to come out with their hands up, he said. Longhway said he and other neighbors had long been suspicious of the lifestyle at the Grasso residence, noting they had four or five brand new trucks and received four different food deliveries every day. The family largely kept to themselves and never spoke to neighbors during the year and a half to two years they lived there, he said.

The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records, according to the criminal complaint. A forensic audit later recovered a secret shadow ledger on her computer tracking where the missing money had actually gone. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail.

Lucie County Sheriff's Office confirmed to CBS12 News that deputies are serving a search warrant as part of the ongoing investigation into the Southern Truss fraud case. Crime scene investigators were seen outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard. Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting Southern Truss Companies. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges, court records show. Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Neighbors on Sunset Boulevard told CBS12 News they had long been suspicious of Grasso's lifestyle. They got 4 or 5 brand new trucks. They got food delivery every day, four different food deliveries. I mean, we always wondered what was going on over there," neighbor Greg Longhway said. Grasso faces charges of: First-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more Organized fraud of $50,000 or more Conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity (RICO) Money laundering of $100,000 or more Harrs and Mejia each face charges of grand theft, organized fraud and racketeering. Grasso's bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges. Longhway said he watched deputies storm the house Tuesday morning. "Oh, they came ripping in, and the SWAT gear and everything with the guns pulled and hollering. Come out that search warrant. Come out with your hands up," he said. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release. Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Longhway said the family largely kept to themselves. They've never said a word to anybody. They've been there for a year and a half, two years. They don't talk to anybody, which is fine; we don't care," Longhway said. "We figured something was up over there, though." The alleged scheme started to unravel after a tornado damaged the Southern Truss facility, according to the criminal complaint. With the plant largely shut down, the company's owner noticed operating costs staying suspiciously high, including fuel charges for a company jet that wasn't flying. When he confronted Grasso and told her outside forensic accountants were being brought in, investigators say server logs show she began logging into the company's financial system overnight to alter records. A forensic audit later recovered a secret "shadow ledger" on her computer, according to the complaint, tracking where the missing money had actually gone. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2018 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions. The amended complaint alleges Grasso alone misappropriated at least $5 million, while Mejia and Harrs allegedly received hundreds of thousands more. The criminal case remains pending. Court records show a magistrate in June declined to pause the related civil case because of the criminal proceedings, instead ordering the defendants to respond to discovery by July 30 and complete depositions by Aug. Neighbors say they saw someone arrested by a SWAT team this morning. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has not confirmed any additional arrests or what investigators were searching for on Tuesday.

cards.headline: Fourth arrest made in death of 3-month-old child in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: Jason Gunter, the biological father of a 3-month-old child who died from dehydration and malnutrition, was arrested Tuesday in Virginia and awaits extradition to St. Lucie County.
cards.body:
Jason Gunter, 45, the biological father of a 3-month-old child, was taken into custody Tuesday morning by the United States Marshals Service at his residence in Mechanicsville, Virginia, on an outstanding warrant obtained by St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives. Gunter has been charged with felony child neglect resulting in great harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the child's death. He is currently awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County, where he will face the charge.

This arrest marks the fourth individual charged as a result of the investigation. Three people were arrested July 24 in relation to this case. Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center in 2025 after the 3-month-old was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents. The sheriff's office said they were notified by medical personnel that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect. The Medical Examiner determined the child's manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition.

cards.headline: Two accused of drug possession in Fort Pierce after officers find them parked in empty field
cards.teaser: Leslie Howard, 70, and Rakeya Jackson, 28, were arrested July 31 after Fort Pierce police found them in a vehicle parked in an empty field on North 10th Street with drug paraphernalia in plain view.
cards.body:
Leslie Howard, 70, and Rakeya Jackson, 28, were arrested after Fort Pierce Police Department officers responded to a call before 5 a.m. on July 31 regarding a suspicious vehicle parked in an empty field on North 10th Street. When officers arrived, they found Howard and Jackson and observed drug paraphernalia in plain view, according to the Fort Pierce Police Department.

The department says Jackson refused several lawful commands to exit the vehicle and actively resisted the officers' attempts to detain her. Howard was taken into custody without incident. Both suspects were transported to the St. Lucie County Jail and charged with possession of cocaine and possession of drug paraphernalia. Jackson was also charged with resisting an officer without violence and tampering with physical evidence.

cards.headline: Treasure Coast homeowners say door-to-door solar sales left them with decades of debt and malfunctioning systems
cards.teaser: Several Treasure Coast homeowners told WPTV they were sold solar systems through door-to-door sales with the expectation of significantly reduced electric bills, but were left with financial obligations ranging from $40,000 to $60,000 lasting as long as 25 years.
cards.body:
Several Treasure Coast homeowners said door-to-door solar pitches left them with decades of debt, malfunctioning systems and power bills that never disappeared. What began with a knock at the door ended for homeowners with financial obligations ranging from $40,000 to $60,000 and lasting as long as 25 years. The homeowners told WPTV they were sold on the expectation that solar panels would significantly reduce or eliminate their electric bills. Instead, some said they were left with malfunctioning systems, continued utility costs and solar companies that later dissolved or filed for bankruptcy.

Documents Ana Perez shared with WPTV show she leased a roughly $40,000 solar system in November 2021. She said her monthly Florida Power & Light bill initially dropped from about $100 to approximately $30. That changed in the spring of 2026, when her bill climbed up to $131. When Perez called FPL, they told her the system had been down since the end of February. By July, bills reviewed by WPTV showed Perez was paying nearly $300 a month, about $150 to FPL and another $150 for the solar lease. That was roughly three times what she said she had paid before installing the panels. When Perez tried to have the system repaired under its 10-year warranty, she learned the installer had gone out of business. cards.article_text: Florida homeowners say door-to-door solar pitches left them with decades of debt, malfunctioning systems and power bills that never disappeared. WATCH WPTV'S REPORT BELOW: Now, a WPTV investigation found some salespeople may not have held licenses required under state law — and some contracts were missing a key consumer disclosure.What began with a knock at the door ended, for several Treasure Coast homeowners, with financial obligations ranging from $40,000 to $60,000 and lasting as long as 25 years.The homeowners told WPTV they were sold on the expectation that solar panels would significantly reduce or eliminate their electric bills.Instead, some said they were left with malfunctioning systems, continued utility costs and solar companies that later dissolved or filed for bankruptcy.“What a waste of money,” homeowner Paula Wass said.“We got taken,” added her husband, David McCauley.WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey reviewed the experiences of Wass and McCauley, Mike and Judy Schopp, Jane Bibee and Ana Perez as part of an ongoing investigation into Florida’s residential solar industry.Since WPTV’s first report, Marty Jacobson, an investigator with the Florida attorney general’s Seniors vs. Crime program, said additional homeowners have filed complaints against solar companies after seeing the investigation.Documents Perez shared with WPTV show she leased a roughly $40,000 solar system in November 2021. She said her monthly Florida Power & Light bill initially dropped from about $100 to approximately $30.That changed in the spring of 2026, when her bill climbed up to $131. “When I called FPL, they told me my system had been down since the end of February,” Perez said.By July, bills reviewed by WPTV showed Perez was paying nearly $300 a month — about $150 to FPL and another $150 for the solar lease. That was roughly three times what she said she had paid before installing the panels.When Perez tried to have the system repaired under its 10-year warranty, she learned the installer had gone out of business."So no phone that you called you got through," said Perez. "We've had systems that were just complete removals," said Justin Hoysradt, president of solar installation company Vinyasan Corp. Hoysradt said he has received a growing number of calls from homeowners facing similar problems, prompting him to launch a separate company, Fix My Solar, to repair or replace systems for homeowners whose original installers are no longer operating.“The calls were coming in so frequently,” Hoysradt said, "and the reality was, a lot of the competitors on the list weren't actually licensed solar contractors." Florida law requires solar installation companies to hold active contractor licenses. The statute also states that "even the attempted sale of contracting services" "constitutes contracting" and "requires the corresponding license." WPTV searched state licensing records for each installation company identified by the homeowners. Nearly all appeared to hold active contractor licenses.But when WPTV searched for four individual salespeople listed in the contracts, only one appeared in the state’s contractor licensing database.WATCH PREVIOUS REPORT: Florida seniors say solar companies left them in debt and in the darkHoysradt said a person or company selling solar contracting services without the proper construction industry license could be operating as an unlicensed contractor.Jacobson also told WPTV that people selling solar installation contracts door-to-door are required to be properly licensed.“It is more frequent than anyone would like to admit," said Hoysradt, "and there are penalties for that." The salesperson listed in the Schopps’ contract was cited in 2023 for solicitation.According to a notice to appear reviewed by WPTV, an officer wrote that the salesperson admitted 'he knew he was wrong for soliciting solar without a permit' and 'knew it was past the city’s permitted solicitation hours.' Court records show he later pleaded no contest, received six months of probation, was fined nearly $350 and was ordered to complete community service.“I answered the door, and then he was telling me, ‘We’re not like all these other solar companies. This is going to be for you, the people,’” Mike Schopp recalled. Lucie County court records show the salesperson listed on Bibee’s third-party-financed solar lease also pleaded no contest to an unlicensed solicitation misdemeanor in 2023 and was fined nearly $350.Bibee signed her solar lease two years after that case.WPTV attempted to contact every salesperson listed in the contracts by phone, email and social media. None responded.Several telephone numbers were disconnected, and some emails bounced back."There are types of enforcement that are starting to pop up," said Hoysradt, "but the harm that can be caused is significant." The contracts reviewed by WPTV contained language disclaiming guarantees about savings, electric bill reductions or system output.The agreements stated that if the panels failed to produce enough electricity, the homeowner would remain responsible for paying the difference to the utility company.WATCH BELOW: Families say solar panel promises left them trapped in costly 25-year loans“Everybody’s supposed to read the agreement, but a lot of the agreements are 20 pages long, and a lot of them are signed on an iPad,” Hoysradt said.Some homeowners said the written terms did not match the expectations created during the sales pitches.“You feel like a sap, and you feel like, ‘I should have known better,’” Wass said. Of the four sets of contract documents reviewed by WPTV, only the agreements involving Bibee and Perez included the required disclosure.The documents reviewed for Wass, McCauley and the Schopps did not include it."If you do not have this disclosure in your agreement, there are substantial penalties to the contracting organizations that did not give it to you," said Hoysradt. Florida law says a seller who willfully violates the disclosure requirements may face a penalty of up to the total cost of the solar system.The law also says a homeowner may be able to file a lawsuit seeking certain finance charges, fees and attorney’s fees.However, the statute does not explicitly state whether an entire solar contract becomes unenforceable when the required disclosure is missing."And I would love to hear directly from our regulators that that statute does govern the sale of solar energy," said Hoysradt. WPTV repeatedly asked the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation whether missing disclosures could affect the enforceability of a contract and whether the individual salespeople identified in the investigation were required to hold contractor licenses.WPTV first contacted the agency in June, followed up several times and sent an additional request July 27. The agency acknowledged the inquiry but had not provided substantive answers as of publication.Records obtained from the Florida attorney general’s office show nearly 750 consumer complaints have been filed against just three solar companies featured in WPTV’s investigation.That total does not include complaints involving other solar businesses that WPTV has not yet examined.The complaints vary in nature and are not limited to allegations involving unlicensed solar sales or missing disclosure forms.Jacobson said homeowners experiencing similar problems should preserve their contracts, financing documents, sales materials, utility bills and communications with the companies involved. They may also file complaints with Seniors vs. Crime or the Florida attorney general’s office.WPTV has connected the featured homeowners with consumer assistance resources.Bibee said Fix My Solar helped her better understand her options for attempting to cancel her contract.Perez said a contractor was ultimately able to repair her system and get the panels producing power again.Still, Perez said the experience left her regretting the agreement.“I never should have gotten it,” she said, “because it’s owning me.”This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

hero.headline: Detectives execute search warrant at Fort Pierce home in $7 million Southern Truss fraud investigation
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office executed a search warrant Tuesday morning at a Fort Pierce home connected to an alleged fraud scheme that investigators say cost Southern Truss Companies nearly $7 million. Crime scene investigators gathered evidence outside the home of Laura Beth Grasso in the Indian River Estates neighborhood near Sunset Boulevard.

Grasso was arrested July 16 along with Sheri Lynn Harrs and Tina Marie Mejia following what the sheriff's office described as a years-long scheme targeting the company. Grasso has pleaded not guilty to the charges. Investigators allege Grasso worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller and used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses.

Grasso faces charges of first-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more, organized fraud of $50,000 or more, conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity (RICO), and money laundering of $100,000 or more. Her bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release.

Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. Southern Truss also filed a civil lawsuit against the three women, alleging they carried out a coordinated scheme between 2019 and 2025 to divert company funds through unauthorized payroll payments, wire transfers and other transactions.

Investigators allege Grasso, who worked as the company's bookkeeper and comptroller, used her administrative access to bypass financial controls and funnel millions of dollars out of the business. Detectives say the money was spent on luxury vehicles, vacations, designer goods, jewelry and other personal expenses. Grasso faces charges of: First-degree grand theft of $100,000 or more Organized fraud of $50,000 or more Conducting an enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity (RICO) Money laundering of $100,000 or more Harrs and Mejia each face charges of grand theft, organized fraud and racketeering. Grasso's bond was set at a combined $1.15 million across the four charges. Prosecutors have asked a judge to hold a hearing on the legitimacy and source of any bail premium or collateral before allowing Grasso to be released from the St. Lucie County Jail, arguing in a court filing that a defendant should not be able to use money obtained through criminal activity to secure her release. Tuesday's search follows an earlier warrant served on a vehicle connected to Grasso. A judge signed that warrant July 24, authorizing detectives to search a blue 2025 Chevrolet Tahoe registered to Grasso that had been towed to the sheriff's office evidence compound the day after her arrest. According to an inventory filed with the court, deputies found roughly $8,500 in cash, a jewelry organizer with jewelry, a Louis Vuitton purse and wallet, and a loaded Smith & Wesson M&P .40 Shield pistol in the glove box. The amended complaint alleges Grasso alone misappropriated at least $5 million, while Mejia and Harrs allegedly received hundreds of thousands more. The criminal case remains pending. Court records show a magistrate in June declined to pause the related civil case because of the criminal proceedings, instead ordering the defendants to respond to discovery by July 30 and complete depositions by Aug. The sheriff's office has not released details about what investigators are searching for at Grasso's home or whether any additional arrests are expected. CBS12 has a crew at the scene and will update this story as more information becomes available.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's communications officer killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
cards.teaser: Elizabeth Ortega, a communications officer with nearly 25 years of emergency communications experience, was shot and killed Saturday night at her Port St. Lucie home by her longtime partner.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office identified the victim Monday as Elizabeth Ortega, a communications officer who served in emergency communications for nearly 25 years. Ortega began her emergency communications career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001 and joined the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office Emergency Communications Division following the agencies' merger in February 2016. Port St. Lucie police responded around 7:40 p.m. Saturday to the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance.

Investigators identified the suspect as 50-year-old Ralph Varela Sr. and confirmed Ortega was also 50 years old. Police said the two had been in a long-term domestic relationship, lived together with their adult son and were in the process of separating. Police believe Varela used an AR-style .223-caliber rifle to shoot Ortega inside the home. Investigators said Ortega attempted to flee the residence, but Varela continued firing as she ran into the front yard. Home surveillance video captured portions of the shooting, according to detectives.

Responding officers found Ortega suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. She was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she later died. Police said Varela returned inside the home after the shooting, where officers later found him dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. PBSO said Ortega's son, Ralph Varela Jr., is a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue.

Investigators said Ortega attempted to flee the residence, but Varela continued firing as she ran into the front yard. Home surveillance video captured portions of the shooting, according to detectives."One of the neighbors actually located that victim, after they observed her lying in the front yard unresponsive suffering from gunshot wounds," Holly told WPTV.Responding officers found Ortega suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. hero.headline: Road rage attack ends with driver using police tactic to crash family's SUV into fence near Stuart
hero.body:
A Florida man faces aggravated battery and child abuse charges after deputies say he used a PIT maneuver to send a North Carolina family's SUV into a barbed-wire fence during a road rage attack that began on Interstate 95 and passed through Stuart. The Martin County Sheriff's Office arrested 36-year-old Michael Jeffrey Spiers following the crash around 7:30 p.m. Saturday near Kanner Highway and Interstate 95. Deputies say the family had no role in any confrontation before they were targeted.

According to investigators, Spiers first chased a woman driving alone through a gas station parking lot before following her onto the highway. The woman frantically called 911 and told dispatchers he repeatedly tried to force her off the road. The woman's brother was following behind her in a separate car with his wife and young son. Authorities say Spiers then turned his attention to the family's vehicle, throwing objects, brake checking and attempting to run it off the roadway. Witnesses reported Spiers was flailing his arms and making what appeared to be gang signs during the encounters. The woman lost Spiers by driving the wrong way up an exit ramp to get back on Interstate 95. Deputies say the suspect continued chasing the family's SUV.

The suspect intentionally performed a PIT maneuver on the family's car, a tactic typically used by law enforcement to stop fleeing vehicles. The impact sent the family's SUV spinning off 96th Street near Kanner Highway and crashing into a barbed-wire fence. The three family members ran out of the car and into the brush to hide until deputies arrived. Spiers drove to the nearby Sunoco gas station at Kanner Highway and 96th Street where deputies took him into custody. Deputies say Spiers didn't know the victims but believed they were stealing his money. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said Spiers acted as if he was high on some type of drug, some kind of a stimulant, or he was having some kind of mental episode. No one was injured, including a child who was inside the family's vehicle.

Sheriff Budensiek said the family did all the things the sheriff's office would recommend by calling 911. Thankfully, our suspect didn't have a gun; it could have ended so much worse, Budensiek said. Deputies also found a dog inside Spiers' vehicle. During the investigation, detectives learned the dog had allegedly been stolen in December from someone Spiers used to date. The dog has since been reunited with its owner. Spiers remains jailed on charges of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, child abuse and reckless driving.

hero.headline: Fourth arrest made in St. Lucie County infant death investigation
hero.body:
A fourth person has been arrested in connection with the death of a 3-month-old child in St. Lucie County. Jason Gunter, 45, the child's biological father, was taken into custody Tuesday morning by the United States Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Virginia. The arrest was made on an outstanding warrant obtained by St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives. Gunter is charged with felony child neglect causing great harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the infant's death.

The investigation began in 2025 when deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center after the 3-month-old was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents. Medical personnel notified the sheriff's office that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect. The Medical Examiner determined the child's manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition.

Gunter is currently awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County, where he will face the charge. This arrest marks the fourth individual charged as a result of the investigation. Three people were arrested on July 24 in relation to this case. The child's mother, 27-year-old Nicole Maxwell, the child's grandfather Robert Maxwell, and Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, 38-year-old Vikki Koon, were each charged with aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Each was held on a $1.5 million bond.

The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said the investigation remains active as the case moves through the judicial process. hero.headline: Fourth arrest made in St. Lucie County infant death case as father taken into custody in Virginia
hero.body:
A 3-month-old child died in St. Lucie County in 2025 from dehydration and malnutrition, and the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced Tuesday that the child's biological father has been arrested as the fourth person charged in the case. Jason Gunter, 45, was taken into custody by the United States Marshals Service Tuesday morning at his residence in Mechanicsville, Virginia, on an outstanding warrant obtained by St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives. Gunter has been charged with felony child neglect resulting in great harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the child's death and is awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County.

Three people were arrested on July 24 in the case. Nicole Maxwell, 27, the child's mother, Robert Maxwell, 61, the child's grandfather, and Vikki Koon, 38, Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, were all charged with aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Each was held on $1.5 million bond. Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center in 2025 after the child was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents. Medical personnel notified the sheriff's office that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect.

The Medical Examiner determined the child's manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition. Investigators interviewed family members and later executed a search warrant at a mobile home park. Working with the Florida Department of Children and Families, authorities placed two other children living in the home in a safe environment.

The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said the investigation remains active as the case moves through the judicial process.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's communications officer killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
cards.teaser: Elizabeth Ortega, a communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office who served in emergency communications for nearly 25 years, was killed Saturday night in Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office announced Monday that Elizabeth Ortega, a communications officer who served in emergency communications for nearly 25 years, was killed in what investigators say was a murder-suicide in Port St. Lucie over the weekend. Port St. Lucie police responded around 7:40 p.m. Saturday to the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance. Investigators identified the suspect as 50-year-old Ralph Varela Sr. and confirmed Ortega was also 50 years old. Police said the two had been in a long-term domestic relationship, lived together with their adult son and were in the process of separating.

Police believe Varela used an AR-style .223-caliber rifle to shoot Ortega inside the home. Investigators said Ortega attempted to flee the residence, but Varela continued firing as she ran into the front yard. Home surveillance video captured portions of the shooting. Responding officers found Ortega suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. She was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she later died. Police said Varela returned inside the home after the shooting, where officers later found him dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Ortega began her emergency communications career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001 and joined the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office Emergency Communications Division following the agencies' merger in February 2016. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said Ortega's son, Ralph Varela Jr., is a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue. The investigation remains active as detectives continue processing evidence and await final results from the Medical Examiner's Office.

hero.headline: Man arrested after road rage attack involving PIT maneuver sends family into fence in Stuart area
hero.body:
A 36-year-old Florida man is in jail after deputies say he used a PIT maneuver to send a North Carolina family's SUV into a barbed-wire fence during a road rage attack that began on I-95 and passed through Stuart. Michael Jeffrey Spiers was arrested and charged with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and child abuse following the Saturday evening crash near Kanner Highway and I-95, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

The attack began around 7:30 p.m. when Spiers chased a woman who was driving alone through a gas station parking lot before following her onto the highway. The woman called 911 and told dispatchers Spiers repeatedly tried to force her off the road. Her brother was following behind her in a separate car with his wife and young son. Spiers then turned his attention to the family's vehicle, throwing objects, brake checking and attempting to run it off the roadway. Witnesses reported Spiers was flailing his arms and making what appeared to be gang signs during the encounters.

The woman lost Spiers by driving the wrong way up an exit ramp to get back on I-95. Spiers continued chasing the family's SUV and eventually performed a PIT maneuver on the family's car, sending it spinning off 96th Street near Kanner Highway and crashing into a barbed-wire fence. The three family members ran out of the car and into the brush to hide until deputies arrived. Spiers drove to the nearby Sunoco gas station at Kanner Highway and 96th Street where deputies took him into custody.

No one was injured, including the child inside the family's vehicle. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said Spiers didn't know the victims but believed they were stealing his money. Spiers acted as if he was high on some type of drug or having some kind of mental episode, Budensiek said. Deputies also found a dog inside Spiers' vehicle that had allegedly been stolen in December from someone Spiers used to date. The dog has been reunited with its owner. Spiers remains jailed on charges of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, child abuse and reckless driving.
