hero.headline: Three candidates vie for Martin County Commission District 4 seat in August 18 primary
hero.body:
Three candidates are running for the District 4 Martin County Commission seat in the August 18 Primary Election. John Dial, Sarah Heard, and John Kaz Kazanjian qualified for the race.

Dial identified over-development as the most serious issue facing Martin County, citing Senate Bill 180, SB102, and new mandates from Tallahassee that remove power from local voters and leaders. He said he would go to Tallahassee as often as necessary to represent local control and push to restore the county's ability to make decisions. Dial also opposed using taxpayer money to fund Brightline, calling it a private company that is not U.S.-owned, carries roughly $2 billion in debt, and is reportedly losing more than $220 million a year. He said he would be open to a train station if a private rail company wanted to invest its own capital, or a fair market land lease at the fairgrounds provided the property would revert to the county if the company fails.

Heard said the legislature is taking decision-making out of the Board's hands and only essential services like the Sheriff and Fire Rescue can be funded with ad valorem taxes. She said even if funding only public safety, the county would not be able to fund it by the third year. Heard said she is in favor of a train station downtown but would consider the fairgrounds location if the majority of residents overwhelmingly favors it. She said she does not want to see data centers in unincorporated Martin County because they are not allowed uses on agricultural lands, and a comprehensive plan amendment would have to be approved to change the future land use, which she would oppose.

Both Dial and Heard addressed a potential referendum on raising the Homestead exemption and cutting ad valorem property tax income. Dial said he would protect essential services first including fire protection, law enforcement, waste management, and education while reviewing non-essential programs and discretionary spending for reductions. He also suggested exploring ways to turn costly county assets like Sailfish Splash, the golf course, and the cafe on the beach into revenue-producing opportunities by leasing them to private operators. On the Business Development Board's annual $450,000 funding, which District 1 Commissioner Eileen Vargas opposed on June 23, Dial said he supports the BDB in its current role but that every use of taxpayer dollars must be examined carefully if spending cuts are forced. Heard agreed that the BDB is too dependent on government funding.
hero.article_text: John Dial John ‘Kaz’ Kazanjian Sarah Heard The Hometown News sent the same list of questions below to each qualified candidate in the August 18 Primary Election for the District 4 Martin County Commission Seat. Question 1: What do you view as the most serious issue facing Martin County and how would you propose addressing that if elected? Question 2: There will be a referendum this year on raising the Homestead exemption and potentially cutting ad valorem property tax income significantly to municipalities. If you are elected and that passes, what areas of the county budget would you suggest trimming or cutting out altogether if need-be? Question 3: Where do you stand on Martin County’s current plan to fund the Brightline train station and potentially relocating that to the county fairgrounds site? Question 4: Do you think the County Commission should address the lack of affordable housing, and if so, in what way? Question 5: On June 23, the County Commission majority voted to approve the Business Development Board’s annual $450,000 funding as part of the Consent Agenda. District 1 Commissioner Eileen Vargas cast the lone opposing vote, insisting the BDB become self-sufficient like the Economic Development Council of Martin County and potentially merge with that entity. If elected, would you support the BDB’s current funding or side with Commissioner Vargas? Question 6: The possibility of data center applications, particularly in the Indiantown area, have been very divisive. Have you studied this issue yourself, and if so, how do you think it should be addressed if you’re elected? Question 7: If elected, how would you work to improve the quality of life for Martin County voters? The most serious issue facing our county right now is over-development, and that problem has only gotten worse with Senate Bill 180, as well as SB102 and the new mandates coming from Tallahassee. These state actions take power away from local voters and leaders and make it harder for Martin County residents to control the kind of growth in their own communities. If I am elected, I will fight to take that authority back. I will go to Tallahassee as often as necessary to represent local control and push to restore the county’s ability to make decisions for itself. Without a repeal or major reform of this law, we will remain trapped in a cycle of over-development no matter what the people of Martin County want. In my view, we should have been more vocal, more organized, and more aggressive in standing up against these state changes before they were passed. We cannot afford to make that mistake again. The consequences for local government budgets are significant, and we must be prepared to act responsibly if it is approved. Like the families and taxpayers we serve, government must learn to live within its means. Over the past several years, citizens have been forced to make tough choices as housing costs, rent, groceries, and electric bills have continued to rise. If this measure passes, I will work to protect essential services first – fire protection, law enforcement, waste management and education – while carefully reviewing non-essential programs and discretionary spending for reductions. We must make sure taxpayer dollars are directed to priorities that truly serve the public. I also believe new development should pay its fair share and not shift additional burdens onto existing taxpayers. In addition, we should explore ways to turn costly county assets – Sailfish Splash, the golf course and the café on the beach – into revenue-producing opportunities. Facilities such as these could potentially be leased to private operators, allowing the county to reduce losses and create income. Every budget should be scrutinized, including the discretionary spending available to the five commissioners. I support a “use it or lose it” policy so that unused funds are returned to the general fund and put toward real needs in the districts. We should closely evaluate every dollar going to 501(c)(3) organizations to ensure there is a measurable return for the community, and we should look for better public-private partnerships where appropriate. I do not support using taxpayer money to fund a private company, especially one that is not U.S.-owned, carries roughly $2 billion in debt and is reportedly losing more than $220 million a year. That said, I would be open to a train station or stop in our county if a private rail company or a qualified buyer emerging from bankruptcy proceedings wanted to invest their own capital here. I would also consider a fair market land-lease for a smaller-scale facility at the fairgrounds or another appropriate location, provided the arrangement protects the public interest. If the company fails or goes out of business, the property should immediately revert to the county, and taxpayers should face zero financial risk. Yes, I do support it, either with non-profits such as Love And Hope In Action or if a developer is seeking to market a project as affordable housing or workforce housing. They should be required to deliver real affordability for the community. That means negotiating firm standards so that a defined percentage of the total units must be reserved at an affordable or workforce price-point. Permits should be made contingent on compliance with those terms. Affordable housing should serve working families, young people, teachers, first responders, and seniors. This is about fairness, accountability, and making sure that growth actually helps the people who live and work here. I support the Business Development Board in its current role. It plays an important part in helping Martin County grow by attracting quality jobs, strengthening our economic base and recruiting the kind of industries that support long-term prosperity. At the same time, if we are forced to make spending cuts, every use of taxpayer dollars must be examined carefully. No public funding should be automatic or off limits. That said, the BDB has a real value to our county. It helps position Martin County to compete for manufacturing opportunities, workforce recruitment, marine industry expansion, aeronautical jobs and other businesses that bring good-paying employment and responsible growth to our community. I am continuing to study this issue and will keep reviewing new information as it becomes available. If elected to the County Commission, I will give this matter my full attention and direct county staff resources toward gathering the facts before taking a position in support of or opposition to it. This is ultimately a decision for the Village of Indiantown, and whatever course they choose, the county should be prepared to assist and support them appropriately. At this time, I do not believe there is enough reliable information for me to make a final judgment. Protecting our natural resources must remain a top priority. I will work to improve water quality in both our fresh and saltwater systems and address the pollution sources that threaten them. I will also work to preserve agricultural lands, defend our development boundaries and review every available option to strengthen our comprehensive plan and restore appropriate limits on urban service expansion. At the same time, I will keep traffic concerns front and center, because growth must never outpace infrastructure. Within the laws and regulations I inherit, I will do everything possible to protect the character of Martin County and make sure our growth policies reflect the interests of current residents and not just future development pressure. Avoid allowing urban development to occur outside the Urban Services Boundary. The legislature is taking that decision-making out of the Board’s hands. Only essential services are allowed to be funded with ad valorem taxes, which means public safety – the Sheriff and Fire Rescue. All other public services are deemed non-essential. Even if funding only public safety, we would not be able to fund public safety by the third year. I am in favor of a train station here. At present the site is downtown. If the majority of residents overwhelmingly favors a fairgrounds location, I would consider it. We do through partnerships with the state and federal agencies, and we partner with Habitat for Humanity. We should continue to evaluate land trusts. I agree that the BDB is far too dependent on government funding. I don’t want to see data centers in unincorporated Martin County. They are not allowed uses on agricultural lands, so a comprehensive plan amendment would have to be approved to change the future land use. I would oppose such an amendment. My priorities have always been to clean up our water, stop over-development and keep our taxes low. Those remain my priorities. hero.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office communications officer killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
hero.body:
The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office announced Monday that Elizabeth Ortega, a communications officer who served in emergency communications for nearly 25 years, was killed in a murder-suicide in Port St. Lucie Saturday night. Ortega, 50, was shot by her longtime partner, Ralph Varela Sr., 50, at their home in the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace.

Port St. Lucie police responded around 7:40 p.m. Saturday after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance. Investigators said Varela used an AR-style .223-caliber rifle to shoot Ortega inside the home. Ortega attempted to flee the residence, but Varela continued firing as she ran into the front yard. Home surveillance video captured portions of the shooting. A neighbor found Ortega lying in the front yard unresponsive suffering from gunshot wounds. Responding officers airlifted her to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she later died. Varela returned inside the home after the shooting, where officers later found him dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Ortega began her emergency communications career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001 and joined the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office Emergency Communications Division following the agencies' merger in February 2016. Police said the two had been in a long-term domestic relationship, lived together with their adult son and were in the process of separating. Investigators said the couple's adult son had left the home around 7:30 p.m. to pick up dinner and detectives found no indication of an argument or disturbance before he left.

The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said Ortega's son, Ralph Varela Jr., is a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue. The investigation remains active as detectives continue processing evidence and await final results from the Medical Examiner's Office. Funeral arrangements are pending.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce woman arrested for drug possession after Walmart theft investigation
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce woman accused of stealing from Walmart was arrested Sunday after officers found narcotics and drug paraphernalia in her vehicle at a gas station on Orange Avenue.
cards.body:
Marrissa Bailey, 29, was arrested Sunday for grand theft, possession of cocaine and possession of drug paraphernalia after Fort Pierce police located her vehicle at a MAX gas station on Orange Avenue. Officers were called to 1228 Orange Avenue in reference to an investigation involving a white GMC Acadia that was connected to a late-July theft at Walmart.

Bailey was identified as the suspect in the Walmart theft. The Fort Pierce Police Department said narcotics and drug paraphernalia were also found during the investigation. Bailey was brought to the St. Lucie County Jail without incident.

cards.headline: Property tax increases push Treasure Coast man to relocate to Puerto Rico
cards.teaser: A Treasure Coast man said rising property taxes in Florida pushed him to leave the state and buy a home in Puerto Rico, where he pays nothing in property taxes.
cards.body:
Jock Tate now lives in Salinas, Puerto Rico, in a 3-bedroom home he purchased for $95,000. As a disabled veteran, he qualifies for exemptions that eliminate his property tax bill entirely. Tate said rising property taxes in Florida drove him to relocate.

According to a Florida Tax Watch study, property taxes rose 146.2% in St. Lucie County between 2014 and 2024. Other Treasure Coast counties saw similar increases including 90.1% in Indian River County and 90.1% in Martin County. Florida voters will have a chance to weigh in on property taxes this November. A referendum on the ballot would raise the Homestead Exemption, lowering property tax bills for Florida homeowners.
cards.article_text: A Treasure Coast man said rising property taxes in Florida pushed him to leave the state and buy a home in Puerto Rico, where he pays nothing in property taxes. WATCH BELOW: 'The price of housing here is much less than Florida,' Jock Tate tells WPTV's Consumer Reporter Matt Sczesny "The property taxes are going up and up and I'm like I just can't afford it," Jock Tate said. Tate now lives in Salinas, Puerto Rico, in a 3-bedroom home he purchased for $95,000. As a disabled veteran, he qualifies for exemptions that eliminate his property tax bill entirely. "The price of housing here is much less than Florida, especially South Florida," Tate said. His move comes as Florida homeowners face rising property tax burdens across the state. According to a Florida Tax Watch study, property taxes rose 146.2% in St. Lucie County between 2014 and 2024. Other Treasure Coast counties saw similar increases — 131.5% in Okeechobee County, 99.4% in Palm Beach County, 90.1% in Indian River County and 90.1% in Martin County. Florida voters will have a chance to weigh in on property taxes this November. A referendum on the ballot would raise the Homestead Exemption, lowering property tax bills for Florida homeowners. Many city and county officials have warned that rolling back property taxes would lead to budget cuts and force local governments to raise other fees and taxes to offset lost revenue. hero.headline: Fort Myers man arrested after PIT maneuver sends North Carolina family's SUV into fence near Stuart
hero.body:
A Fort Myers man used a police pursuit tactic to force a North Carolina family's SUV off the road and into a barbed-wire fence near Stuart during a road rage attack that began on I-95 Saturday night. Michael Jeffrey Spiers, 36, faces charges of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and child abuse following the crash near Kanner Highway and I-95 around 7:30 p.m., according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

The incident began when Spiers chased a woman driving alone through a gas station parking lot before following her onto the highway, where he repeatedly tried to force her off the road. The woman called 911 while her brother, who was following behind with his wife and young son, tried to help. Spiers then turned his attention to the family's vehicle, throwing objects, brake checking and attempting to run it off the roadway. Witnesses reported Spiers flailing his arms and making what appeared to be gang signs during the encounters. The woman escaped by driving the wrong way up an exit ramp to get back on I-95.

Spiers continued pursuing the family's SUV and eventually performed a PIT maneuver, a tactic typically used by law enforcement to stop fleeing vehicles. The impact sent the family's vehicle spinning off 96th Street near Kanner Highway and crashing into a barbed-wire fence. The three family members ran from the car and hid in the brush until deputies arrived. Body camera footage shows the family emerging from the woods where they had been hiding.

Spiers drove to the nearby Sunoco gas station at Kanner Highway and 96th Street where deputies arrested him. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said Spiers told deputies he believed the victims were stealing his money, though the family had no role in any confrontation before they were targeted. No one was injured, including the child inside the family's vehicle. Deputies found a dog inside Spiers' vehicle that had allegedly been stolen in December from someone Spiers used to date. The dog has been reunited with its owner. Spiers remains jailed on charges of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, child abuse and reckless driving.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's dispatcher killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
hero.body:
A Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office communications officer was shot and killed Saturday evening in Port St. Lucie in what investigators are calling a murder-suicide. Elizabeth Ortega, 50, was identified Monday as the victim. She worked in emergency communications for nearly 25 years.

Port St. Lucie police responded around 7:40 p.m. Saturday to the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance. Investigators identified the suspect as 50-year-old Ralph Varela Sr. Police said the two had been in a long-term domestic relationship, lived together with their adult son and were in the process of separating. The couple's adult son had left the home around 7:30 p.m. to pick up food. Detectives found no indication of an argument or disturbance before he left.

Police believe Varela used an AR-style .223-caliber rifle to shoot Ortega inside the home. Investigators said Ortega attempted to flee the residence, but Varela continued firing as she ran into the front yard. Home surveillance video captured portions of the shooting. Responding officers found Ortega suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. She was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she later died. Police said Varela returned inside the home after the shooting, where officers later found him dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Ortega began her emergency communications career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001 and joined the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office Emergency Communications Division following the agencies' merger in February 2016. Ortega's son, Ralph Varela Jr., is a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue. The sheriff's office said Ortega was known for her kindness, compassion and warm smile. Funeral arrangements are pending. The investigation remains active as detectives continue processing evidence and await final results from the Medical Examiner's Office.

hero.headline: Indian River County property taxes rose 90% in 10 years as Florida homeowner flees to Puerto Rico
hero.body:
A Treasure Coast man relocated to Puerto Rico after rising property taxes in Florida made homeownership unaffordable, part of a trend affecting Indian River County and neighboring areas. Jock Tate now lives in Salinas, Puerto Rico, in a three-bedroom home he purchased for $95,000. As a disabled veteran, he qualifies for exemptions that eliminate his property tax bill entirely.

Property taxes rose 90.1% in Indian River County between 2014 and 2024, according to a Florida Tax Watch study. St. Lucie County saw the largest increase on the Treasure Coast at 146.2%, followed by Martin County at 90.1% and Palm Beach County at 99.4%. Okeechobee County property taxes rose 131.5% during the same period.

Tate said escalating property tax bills forced his decision to leave Florida. He said the price of housing in Puerto Rico is much less than Florida, especially South Florida. He said property taxes in Florida kept going up and he could not afford it.

Florida voters will decide on a referendum this November that would raise the Homestead Exemption and lower property tax bills for homeowners. Many city and county officials have warned that rolling back property taxes would lead to budget cuts and force local governments to raise other fees and taxes to offset lost revenue.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office dispatcher killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
hero.body:
Elizabeth Ortega, a 50-year-old communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, was shot and killed Saturday evening in Port St. Lucie by her longtime partner Ralph Varela Sr., 50, who then took his own life. Port St. Lucie police responded around 7:40 p.m. Saturday to the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting gunshots and a domestic disturbance.

Investigators said Ortega and Varela had been in a long-term domestic relationship, lived together with their adult son, and were in the process of separating. The couple's adult son had left the home around 7:30 p.m. to pick up dinner, and detectives found no indication of an argument or disturbance before he left. Police believe Varela used an AR-style .223-caliber rifle to shoot Ortega inside the home. Ortega attempted to flee the residence, but Varela continued firing as she ran into the front yard. A neighbor found Ortega lying unresponsive in the front yard suffering from gunshot wounds. Home surveillance video captured portions of the shooting.

Responding officers airlifted Ortega to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she later died. Police found Varela dead inside the home from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Ortega began her emergency communications career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001 and joined the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office Emergency Communications Division following the agencies' merger in February 2016. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said Ortega was a respected and cherished part of the PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room.

The sheriff's office said Ortega's son, Ralph Varela Jr., is a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue, and asked the community to keep both agencies in their thoughts. The investigation remains active as detectives continue processing evidence and await final results from the Medical Examiner's Office. Funeral arrangements are pending. Port St. Lucie police extended their condolences to Ortega's family and loved ones.

hero.headline: Martin County considers changes to shark fishing rules on beaches after state directive
hero.teaser: Martin County is weighing changes to its local shark fishing ordinance after the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission directed the county to align its rules with state regulations. The move has drawn significant public concern.
hero.body:
The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission asked Martin County to bring its ordinance in line with state law, which preempts counties from regulating saltwater fishing. Assistant County Attorney Melissa Petrick said a state statute has preempted the powers from the county to regulate saltwater fishing that includes shark fishing. State law requires a saltwater fishing license and a special permit for shark fishing and allows shark fishing within 1,000 feet of a guarded beach at all hours.

Jessica Veatch, whose then-3-year-old daughter Violet was attacked by a bull shark on Bathtub Beach in Martin County 9 years ago, is among those opposing the changes. Veatch said she noticed some young men that were spearfishing on the reef and believes that provoked the attack on her daughter. Indian River Keeper Jim Moir raised concerns about the potential impact of the changes at the Tuesday commission meeting, saying attracting more sharks to the coast is bad for human safety, bad for angling, bad for public awareness and bad for the sharks.

County attorneys suggested the ordinance does not need to be eliminated entirely and can be reworked to reference the illegality of things under state law instead of eliminating everything. County commissioners voted to table the discussion, directing staff to review concerns raised by the community and commissioners and draft new ordinance language.
hero.article_text: Martin County is weighing changes to its local shark fishing ordinance after the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission directed the county to align its rules with state regulations. It's a move that has drawn significant public concern. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission asked the county to bring its ordinance in line with state law, which preempts counties from regulating saltwater fishing. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: "There is a state statute that has essentially preempted the powers from the county to regulate salt water fishing that includes shark fishing. Preemption meaning the state says, 'county you can't control this anymore,'" Assistant County Attorney Melissa Petrick said. State law requires a saltwater fishing license and a special permit for shark fishing. It also allows shark fishing within 1,000 feet of a guarded beach at all hours. Among those opposing the changes is Jessica Veatch, whose then-3-year-old daughter Violet was attacked by a bull shark on Bathtub Beach in Martin County 9 years ago. "I hear a scream that goes Mommy," Veatch said. "I come up out of the water and all I can see is the blood filling the water and I lifted her up out of the water and saw what was left of her leg." Veatch said she believes nearby fishing activity may have lead to the attack.. "We noticed some young men that were spearfishing on the reef," Veatch said. "That is what provoked the attack on my daughter." Veatch said she was alarmed to learn the county may now be forced to eliminate its local shark fishing regulations. "They're currently treating our shoreline like a Pavlov's dog experiment with an apex predator and I don't think that's going to work out in anybody's best interest," Veatch said. Indian River Keeper Jim Moir raised concerns about the potential impact of the changes at the Tuesday commission meeting. "These animals are incredibly important to our ecosystems. The angler offshore are complaining bitterly daily about how many of their caught fish are being depraved by sharks. Attracting more sharks to the coast is not only bad for human safety, but it's bad for angling, its bad for our public awareness, it's bad for the sharks," Moir said. County attorneys suggested the ordinance does not need to be eliminated entirely. "We can rework the ordinance and then instead of eliminating everything we can just reference the illegality of things under state law," Petrick said. County commissioners voted to table the discussion, directing staff to review concerns raised by the community and commissioners and draft new ordinance language. hero.headline: Florida Attorney General threatens Catholic school scholarship funding over vaccine exemption policies
hero.body:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is challenging the state's Catholic bishops, warning that church-run schools must honor parents' religious vaccine exemptions under state law or risk losing access to state scholarship funding. In a letter to Catholic school leaders, Uthmeier argues state law requires schools to accept religious vaccine exemptions even if church leaders disagree. He also cites Vatican teaching on individual conscience in making his case.

The financial stakes are significant. More than 525,000 Florida students use state scholarship programs, including roughly 92 percent of Catholic school students. Uthmeier has warned that schools could lose access to those programs if they do not comply. Existing policies at some Catholic schools, including one in Orlando, state that vaccines are not against Catholic teaching and that allowing exemptions could endanger students and staff.

The clash follows Governor Ron DeSantis' broader campaign against vaccine mandates. Lawmakers rejected proposals this year to eliminate Florida's remaining school vaccine requirements or create a broader conscience exemption. Medical and religious opt-outs remain available. The Florida Conference of Catholic Bishops has not yet answered the argument directly. Michele Taylor of the Florida Conference of Catholic Bishops said the organization is reviewing the letter and will respond to the Attorney General by his requested date of August 7.

State Democrats are calling the attorney general's demands a distraction. Rep. Daryl Campbell, a Fort Lauderdale Democrat, pointed to what he called more pressing concerns facing Floridians. Campbell said affordability has been the crisis of this generation. The bishops have until Friday to respond to Uthmeier's letter. For now, his scholarship threat remains a warning, not a funding cutoff.

cards.headline: Rising property taxes drive Florida residents to relocate to Puerto Rico
cards.teaser: A Treasure Coast man who relocated to Puerto Rico said rising property taxes in Florida pushed him to leave the state and buy a home where he pays nothing in property taxes.
cards.body:
Jock Tate now lives in Salinas, Puerto Rico, in a 3-bedroom home he purchased for $95,000. As a disabled veteran, he qualifies for exemptions that eliminate his property tax bill entirely. Tate said property taxes in Florida were going up and he could not afford it. He said the price of housing in Puerto Rico is much less than Florida, especially South Florida.

His move comes as Florida homeowners face rising property tax burdens across the state. According to a Florida Tax Watch study, property taxes rose 146.2 percent in St. Lucie County between 2014 and 2024. Other Treasure Coast counties saw similar increases: 131.5 percent in Okeechobee County, 99.4 percent in Palm Beach County, 90.1 percent in Indian River County and 90.1 percent in Martin County.

Florida voters will have a chance to weigh in on property taxes this November. A referendum on the ballot would raise the Homestead Exemption, lowering property tax bills for Florida homeowners. Many city and county officials have warned that rolling back property taxes would lead to budget cuts and force local governments to raise other fees and taxes to offset lost revenue.

hero.headline: Space Coast Symphony Orchestra brings Landscapes & Legends concert to Vero Beach
hero.body:
The Space Coast Symphony Orchestra will perform Landscapes Legends on Sunday, August 10, at the Community Church of Vero Beach, 1901 23rd Street. The concert features works exploring magic and myth, with guest conductor Patrick Phillips leading the performance.

The program opens with Dukas' The Sorcerer's Apprentice, the 11-minute orchestral tone poem famously depicted in Disney's Fantasia. The concert includes the world premiere performance of Kenneth Fuchs' Cloud Slant, a work capturing light, motion and atmosphere. Fuchs won the 2018 GRAMMY Award for Best Classical Compendium for an album recorded with the London Symphony Orchestra for Naxos.

Vero Beach music and arts leader Dr. Jacob Craig will perform Edward MacDowell's Piano Concerto No. 2, a deeply romantic and expressive three-movement work composed in 1885. The work holds the distinction of being the first major piano concerto written by an American. Renowned pianist Van Cliburn chose MacDowell's Piano Concerto No. 2 at age 18 for his professional orchestral debut.

The concert concludes with Pines of Rome, the 1924 orchestral tone poem by Italian composer Ottorino Respighi. The 22-minute work dramatically depicts four different locations around Rome framed by iconic pine trees. Tickets cost $35 through www.SpaceCoastSymphony.org or at Marine Bank Trust branches, and $40 at the door. Concertgoers aged 18 and under or with a college ID are admitted free. For more information, call 855-252-7276.

Guest conducted by Brevard music educator Patrick Phillips, the vivid, 11-minute orchestral tone poem musically narrates a tale of magic gone wrong. The world premiere performance of Kenneth Fuchs’ Cloud Slant shifts the focus inward, capturing light, motion and atmosphere. A Fuchs album recorded with the London Symphony Orchestra for Naxos won the 2018 GRAMMY Award for Best Classical Compendium. Landscapes Legends continues when Vero Beach music and arts leader, Dr. Jacob Craig joins the orchestra for Edward MacDowell’s Piano Concerto No. 2, a deeply romantic and expressive work in three-movements. Composed in 1885, the work has the distinction of being the first major piano concerto written by an American. Renowned pianist, Van Cliburn chose MacDowell’s Piano Concerto No. 2 at age 18 for his professional orchestral debut. Landscapes Legends concludes with Pines of Rome, the world famous 1924 orchestral tone poem by Italian composer, Ottorino Respighi. Lasting about 22 minutes, it dramatically depicts four different locations around Rome framed by iconic pine trees. Ancient streets, distant echoes, and the sound of a nightingale are sculpted into one of the greatest works of the orchestral repertoire. $35 tickets for Landscapes Legends are available through the orchestra website at www.SpaceCoastSymphony.org or at Marine Bank Trust branches. Tickets at the door are $40. Concertgoers aged 18 and under or with a college ID are admitted free to every SCSO concert. For more information about Landscapes Legends, call 855-252-7276 or visit www.SpaceCoastSymphony.org . Collins, Conductor and Artistic Director for the Space Coast Symphony Orchestra, describes what makes the Landscapes Legends concert special. “A good orchestral concert can make the invisible feel real,” said Collins. “The works on this program aren’t just pretty melodies with dramatic flourishes – they create places, characters, atmospheres, and emotional landscapes for a truly one-of-a-kind musical experience.” Concertgoers aged 18 and under or with a college ID are admitted free to every SCSO concert. hero.headline: St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware named Florida State League Pitcher of the Week
hero.body:
St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware has been named the Florida State League Pitcher of the Week for the week of July 20-26, Minor League Baseball announced. Ware made two appearances last week at Clover Park in Port St. Lucie against Fort Myers, one start on Tuesday and one relief outing on Sunday.

The southpaw combined to pitch 7.0 scoreless innings. He scattered three hits, walked two and struck out 12. The Mets won both games with Ware getting credit for the win on Sunday.

Ware, 22, was drafted by the Mets in the 15th round out of LSU in 2025. He made his pro debut with St. Lucie in April and has been with the team all season.

This is the first FSL Pitcher or Player of the Week award for the Mets this season.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's communications officer killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
hero.body:
A Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office communications officer was shot and killed Saturday night in Port St. Lucie in what investigators are calling a murder-suicide. Elizabeth Ortega, 50, was killed by her longtime partner Ralph Varela Sr., 50, at their home in the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace. The couple had been in a long-term domestic relationship and were in the process of separating.

Port St. Lucie police responded around 7:40 p.m. Saturday after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance. Investigators said the couple's adult son had left the home around 7:30 p.m. to pick up food. Police said Varela used an AR-style .223-caliber rifle to shoot Ortega inside the home. Surveillance video showed Ortega attempted to flee the residence, but Varela continued firing as she ran into the front yard, where a neighbor found her suffering from multiple gunshot wounds.

Ortega was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she later died. Officers found Varela dead inside the home from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Ortega served in emergency communications for nearly 25 years, beginning her career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001 and joining the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office Emergency Communications Division in February 2016 following the agencies' merger.

The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said Ortega's son, Ralph Varela Jr., is a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue. The investigation remains active as detectives continue processing evidence and await final results from the Medical Examiner's Office. Port St. Lucie police said anyone experiencing domestic violence should not be afraid to speak up and ask for help.

Lucie police extended their condolences to Ortega's family and loved ones.The department said anyone experiencing domestic violence should not be afraid to speak up."We encourage anyone who is experiencing domestic violence, or knows someone who is experiencing domestic violence to ask for help, seek help," Holly said. "That's what we're here for."

cards.headline: Fort Myers man arrested after road rage PIT maneuver crashes family's SUV into fence on I-95 in Martin County
cards.teaser: A Fort Myers man is charged with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and child abuse after deputies say he performed a PIT maneuver on a North Carolina family's vehicle during a road rage incident near Stuart.
cards.body:
Michael Jeffrey Spiers, 36, was arrested Saturday night after he allegedly used a PIT maneuver to send a North Carolina family's SUV into a barbed-wire fence during a road rage attack near Kanner Highway and I-95. The crash happened around 7:30 p.m. Saturday. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the incident involved a woman traveling alone and her brother, his wife, and their young son following in another vehicle while on vacation from North Carolina.

Investigators said Spiers first went after the woman, chasing her through a gas station parking lot before following her onto the highway and repeatedly trying to force her off the road. The woman called 911, and Spiers then turned his attention to the family's vehicle. Witnesses reported Spiers was flailing his arms and making what appeared to be gang signs during the encounters. Spiers intentionally performed a PIT maneuver on the family's car, sending the SUV spinning off 96th Street near Kanner Highway and crashing into a barbed-wire fence. The three family members ran from the car and hid in the brush until deputies arrived.

Spiers drove to the nearby Sunoco gas station at Kanner Highway and 96th Street where deputies took him into custody. Deputies found a dog inside Spiers' vehicle that had allegedly been stolen in December from someone Spiers used to date. The dog has been reunited with its owner. Spiers remains jailed on charges of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, child abuse and reckless driving.
cards.article_text: A Fort Myers man was arrested after an apparent road rage incident Saturday night on I-95 in Martin County that caused a family’s vehicle to crash into a barbed wire fence and left them hiding in the woods. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the incident involved a woman traveling in her own vehicle and her brother, his wife, and their young son following in another vehicle while on vacation from North Carolina. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "He tries to run the sister off the road, makes multiple attempts to run her off the road, brake checks her a couple of times. She starts panicking, calling her brother and saying there is something going on, I'm not sure what it is," Budensiek said. He said the brother caught up to the suspect, identified as Michael Spires, who then targeted his vehicle. At one point, Spires performed a pit maneuver, causing the family’s vehicle to spin off the road and crash into a barbed wire fence. Body camera footage shows the family emerging from the woods where they had been hiding after fleeing their vehicle. "The family at that point is extremely alarmed. They think he may be armed; they know he's not thinking clearly, so they jump out of the car, and they flee and they're hiding in the woods," Budensiek said. Spires drove to a nearby gas station and stayed there before speaking with investigators. "I got out of the car, and this blue car ran into me," Spires said. Spires, who is from Fort Myers, was taken into custody and appeared before a judge Monday afternoon. Officials said he had a dog in his vehicle at the time of the incident, which they later learned was stolen from his ex-boyfriend. The dog has since been returned. The sheriff said no one was injured during the incident. "The sister had driven about a few miles further up the road. She came back to the scene to tell her story. They're all safe, but only by the grace of God they are safe because this could have been so much worse," the sheriff said. Detectives said Spires was arrested and charged with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and child abuse. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

hero.headline: Property tax increases push Treasure Coast resident to relocate to Puerto Rico
hero.body:
A Treasure Coast man said rising property taxes in Florida pushed him to leave the state and buy a home in Puerto Rico, where he pays nothing in property taxes. Jock Tate now lives in Salinas, Puerto Rico, in a 3-bedroom home he purchased for $95,000. As a disabled veteran, he qualifies for exemptions that eliminate his property tax bill entirely.

Tate said the price of housing in Puerto Rico is much less than Florida, especially South Florida. He said property taxes were going up and he could not afford it anymore.

His move comes as Florida homeowners face rising property tax burdens across the state. According to a Florida Tax Watch study, property taxes rose 146.2% in St. Lucie County between 2014 and 2024. Other Treasure Coast counties saw similar increases: 131.5% in Okeechobee County, 99.4% in Palm Beach County, 90.1% in Indian River County and 90.1% in Martin County.

Florida voters will have a chance to weigh in on property taxes this November. A referendum on the ballot would raise the Homestead Exemption, lowering property tax bills for Florida homeowners. Many city and county officials have warned that rolling back property taxes would lead to budget cuts and force local governments to raise other fees and taxes to offset lost revenue.

hero.headline: Funeral set for Indian River County firefighter Geoffrey Lang after off-duty death
hero.body:
Indian River County Fire Rescue will hold a funeral service at 11 a.m. Tuesday at Community Church in Vero Beach for firefighter and paramedic Geoffrey Lang, who died off duty. The department is asking community members to attend the service virtually to ensure family members and fellow firefighters can attend in person.

The livestream will be available on the church's YouTube channel. Deputy Chief Richard Marini is coordinating attendance for outside agencies and can be reached at 772-226-1976 or rmarini@indianriver.gov.

Indian River County Fire Rescue did not release details about the circumstances of Lang's death. The department identified him as both a firefighter and paramedic who served the county.

The department asked the public to keep Lang's family and friends in their thoughts and prayers as they honor his life and service. Community Church is located in Vero Beach.

cards.headline: Four candidates compete for Indian River County Commission District 2 seat in August primary
cards.teaser: Three Republican candidates and one Democrat answered questions about the Indian River Lagoon, affordable housing, agricultural land preservation and property tax reform ahead of the Aug. 18 primary election.
cards.body:
Four candidates seeking the District 2 Indian River County Commission seat responded to questions from the Hometown News about county issues. Republicans Bob McPartian, Jennifer Pippin and Daniel Brooks Robinson will compete in the Aug. 18 primary election, with Democrat Robert Hardingham facing the winner in November.

McPartian, who served 15 years on the Sebastian City Council, said managing growth while protecting infrastructure and the Indian River Lagoon is the most serious issue facing the county. Pippin said she would prioritize responsible spending and review the $3.7 million in county funding for nonprofits and the $1.4 million paid to the sheriff for school resource officers if Amendment 3 passes and reduces property tax revenue. Robinson said the county should manage growth responsibly while protecting private property rights and neighborhood character.

Hardingham said the Indian River Lagoon is one of the most serious issues and called for speeding up the septic-to-sewer initiative to reduce pollution. All four candidates addressed affordable housing, with McPartian supporting partnerships with nonprofits like Habitat for Humanity to develop housing on county-owned property, Pippin emphasizing private sector solutions and streamlined permitting, Robinson supporting a range of housing opportunities with county government focused on responsible planning, and Hardingham advocating for affordable housing for nurses, teachers, police and working families.
cards.article_text: The Hometown News sent the same list of questions below to each qualified candidate in the Aug. 18 Republican Primary Election for the District 2 Indian River County Commission seat. The only qualified Democratic candidate in the race also agreed to participate, although he won’t face the winner of the primary until Nov. Question 1 What do you view as the most serious issue facing Indian River County and how would you propose addressing that if elected? Question 2 There will be a referendum this year on raising the Homestead Exemption and potentially cutting ad valorem property tax income significantly to municipalities. If you are elected and that passes, what areas of the county budget would you suggest trimming or cutting out altogether if need-be? Question 3 Do you think the County Commission should address the lack of affordable housing, and if so, in what way? Question 4 There have recently been calls from some citizens to stop the rezoning of agricultural lands for housing and to do more to encourage the return to citrus groves. If elected, how would you respond to such requests? Question 5 If elected, how would you work to improve the quality of life for Indian River County voters? Candidate Bob McPartian 1. The most serious issue is managing growth in a way that protects our quality of life, infrastructure and the Indian River Lagoon. If elected, I will push for better coordination between cities and the county so development is tied to available roads, utilities and environmental capacity. My 15 years on the Sebastian City Council have shown me that early planning and strong interlocal agreements prevent problems before they start. I support tax reform, but I do not support this particular amendment as written. It was developed quickly without a full analysis of its impact, and there is no clear backup plan if it creates significant revenue shortfalls. If it passes, I would protect public safety and core infrastructure first. Then, I would look to reduce non-essential spending, improve efficiency and prioritize programs that deliver clear results for residents rather than across-the-board cuts. Yes, the County Commission should address housing affordability in practical ways. I support streamlining permitting, encouraging a mix of housing types where infrastructure already exists, and working with cities and private partners. Partnering with nonprofits such as Habitat for Humanity to develop housing on existing county-owned property is one concrete step that can help without overextending government resources. Property owners have the right to request zoning changes, and those requests should be evaluated fairly. At the same time, I respect citizens who want to protect agricultural land and encourage citrus. Growth should be directed first to areas already planned for development and served by infrastructure. Any rezoning must be carefully reviewed for impacts on roads, water resources and the Lagoon. I would focus on the basics that matter most to residents: protecting the Indian River Lagoon, maintaining safe roads and reliable infrastructure, supporting public safety, keeping taxes reasonable through disciplined budgeting, and ensuring cities and the county work together. After 15 years of local service, I know steady, practical leadership improves daily life more than flashy promises. Candidate Jennifer Pippin 1, If Amendment 3 is approved by Florida voters, it will provide meaningful property tax relief for homesteaded residents. As a county commissioner, I will work to ensure the county budget reflects that change by prioritizing responsible spending, eliminating waste where possible and protecting essential services without shifting the burden back onto taxpayers through other means. Government must live within its means while providing the core services our residents expect. If the referendum passes, I believe the County Commission has a responsibility to carefully review every line of the budget before asking taxpayers to bear the burden. I would begin by evaluating discretionary spending, including the $3.7 million in funding provided to non-profit organizations and the administrative costs associated with distributing those funds. I would also review the current funding arrangement for school resource officers. Public education is a School District responsibility, and I believe the District should fund the sheriff’s $1.4 million budget currently paid by the county for SROs. Additionally, I would implement a vacancy review process so that when positions become vacant through retirement or resignation, they are evaluated to determine whether the workload can be absorbed more efficiently. I would also review and reduce consulting contracts wherever county staff can perform the work in-house. Finally, I would look for ways to increase revenue from tourism so the burden on local homeowners is reduced. I believe affordable housing is primarily driven by the private sector, not government mandates. The County Commission’s role should be to create an environment where businesses can thrive, which in turn brings better-paying jobs and more opportunities for residents. By reducing unnecessary regulations, streamlining permitting and encouraging responsible development, we can help increase the supply of housing and make it more attainable. I also support measures like Amendment 3, which will allow residents to keep more of their own money and better support their families. I want to keep oranges growing and cows grazing on agricultural land. Once farmland is developed, we can never get it back. I support protecting our agricultural heritage while respecting private property rights. I will work to ensure agricultural land remains agricultural and that development is responsible, planned and supported by the infrastructure needed to protect our quality of life. Improving our quality of life means preserving the things that make this county so special while planning responsibly for the future. When elected, I will work to keep taxes as low as possible through responsible budgeting, support our Sheriff’s Office and first responders, protect our agricultural heritage and ensure growth never outpaces our roads, infrastructure and public safety. I want future generations to enjoy the same safe, beautiful and welcoming Indian River County that my family has been blessed to call home. Candidate Daniel ‘Brooks’ Robinson 1, Our greatest challenge is managing growth responsibly. We need to ensure our roads, utilities, public safety and infrastructure keep pace with growth while protecting the quality of life that makes Indian River County such a great place to live. We don’t have to choose between growth and preservation: We can achieve both through thoughtful planning. The county should begin by reviewing every department, project and expenditure to identify efficiencies and eliminate non-essential spending. My priorities would be protecting public safety, maintaining essential infrastructure and preserving the core services residents rely on every day. I would not commit to cutting specific departments or positions without first conducting a comprehensive review. The county should encourage a range of housing opportunities that meet the needs of our workforce and families while protecting neighborhood character and ensuring infrastructure keeps pace with growth. I believe the private market should lead, with county government focused on responsible planning, efficient permitting and sound infrastructure investment. Agriculture is an important part of Indian River County’s history, economy and identity, and we should do what we can to support our agricultural community. At the same time, every rezoning request should be evaluated on its own merits and be consistent with the county’s comprehensive plan, infrastructure capacity and the long-term interests of our community. My focus will be on managing growth responsibly, protecting private property rights and ensuring development improves our community. Quality of life is why so many of us choose to live in Indian River County. As commissioner, I will work to keep our community safe, manage growth responsibly, protect our natural resources, strengthen our local economy and be a good steward of taxpayer dollars. My goal is to preserve what makes Indian River County special for future generations. Democratic Candidate Robert (Robbie) D. Hardingham While Hardingham is not actually running in the August Primary Election, he agreed to participate at the Hometown News’ request. I feel that the Indian River lagoon is one of the most serious issues facing IRC out of many. The stormwater runoff and pollution from nitrates, phosphorus and algae blooms are causing an ecological disaster. The septic-to-sewer initiative will help with that, but we need to find solutions to speed up the cleaning of the Lagoon. I would find ways of reducing the pollutants from going into the lagoon. 2, Hopefully that referendum will not pass because it will be bad for schools, businesses and renters. The savings that homeowners would get from this policy will not outweigh the loss of tax revenue. hero.teaser: The Florida Department of Environmental Protection extended Fort Pierce's deadline to Sept. 15 to review a consent order resolving state fines tied to docks at Little Jim Bait & Tackle that were allegedly built on state-owned land without authorization.

The city has filed a motion to dismiss Keene's amended complaint. Broderick said the city is planning to hire a real estate manager to oversee development decisions and prevent future situations.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office employee killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
cards.body:
Elizabeth Ortega, a 50-year-old communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, was killed in a domestic violence incident at her Port St. Lucie residence on Saturday, Aug. 2. Her partner, Ralph Varela Sr., 50, shot her with an AR-style rifle before taking his own life, according to Port St. Lucie police.

Officers responded around 7:40 p.m. to the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace, west of U.S. 1 and near HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital, after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting gunshots and a domestic disturbance. Investigators determined that Ortega and Varela had been in a long-term cohabitation relationship and were in the process of separating. Their adult son had left the residence to pick up dinner when Varela began shooting Ortega inside the home. Surveillance video shows Ortega attempting to flee into the front yard while Varela continued firing before she collapsed. She was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she was pronounced dead. Officers later found Varela dead inside the home from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Ortega began her emergency communications career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001. When the Greenacres Police Department and its communications unit merged with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office in February 2016, she continued her work there. The sheriff's office said Ortega was a respected and cherished part of the PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion and a warm smile. Her son, Ralph Varela Jr., is a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue.

According to Palm Beach Clerk records, Varela Sr. was convicted in 2014 of discharging a firearm in public and sentenced to 192 days in jail. In 2017, he was convicted of possession of cocaine, reckless driving, driving while his license was not active and refusal to submit to a chemical or physical test, and was sentenced to 20 days in jail. The investigation remains active as detectives continue processing evidence and await the final results from the Medical Examiner's Office.

cards.headline: Two sharks spotted off St. Lucie and Palm Beach County coasts
cards.teaser: A 12-foot shark was hooked by fishermen on Normandy Beach on Hutchinson Island in St. Lucie County on Friday, and a dead hammerhead shark washed up south of the Jupiter Beach Resort the same day.
cards.body:
Two sharks were spotted along the Atlantic Ocean shore on Friday, with video sent to WPBF. Jensen Beach resident Kathy Green was walking along Normandy Beach on Hutchinson Island in St. Lucie County when she filmed a group of fishermen struggling with a 12-foot shark they had hooked. The fishermen unhooked the shark and released it back into the water. Shark expert and conservationist Jim Abernethy believes it was a great white shark by looking at the video.

Also Friday, a hammerhead shark was spotted dead just south of the Jupiter Beach Resort. Christopher Ray, a musician, submitted video to WPBF. Later that day, Fish Wildlife removed the shark. Shark Week 2026 ran from July 26 to Saturday on the Discovery Channel.

Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission has ordered Martin County, which also includes Hutchinson Island, to follow rules about people fishing for fish or sharks from the beach or shoreline. Shark fishing requires a state saltwater fishing license to fish within 1,000 feet of the guarded beach boundaries at any time. Under the current county ordinance, shark fishing is prohibited within 1,000 yards of the county's four guarded beaches: Jensen, Stuart, Bathtub and Hobe Sound. On Tuesday, commissioners postponed making a decision and asked attorneys to review the law.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie police investigate domestic shooting that killed woman, left man dead
cards.teaser: Officers responded around 7:40 p.m. Saturday to the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace after multiple 911 calls reported gunshots and a domestic disturbance.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie Police Department is investigating what the agency says appears to be a domestic-related shooting Saturday night that left a man and a woman dead. At approximately 7:40 p.m., officers responded to the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace, west of U.S. 1 and near HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital, after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance.

Officers found a woman suffering from a gunshot wound. She was airlifted to a local hospital, where she was pronounced deceased. Police also located a man who was deceased from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound. Police said the incident appears to be an isolated domestic-related shooting, and there is no known threat to the public.

The house remains an active crime scene as investigators continue to process evidence and conduct interviews. Residents should expect a heavy police presence in the area of Southeast Triumph Road and Southeast Veterans Memorial Parkway. Drivers are urged to avoid the area and use alternate routes if possible to allow first responders and investigators to safely conduct their work.

hero.headline: Honduran national convicted in Fort Pierce federal court for firearms trafficking to Honduras
hero.body:
A federal jury in Fort Pierce convicted a Honduran national for operating a firearms-trafficking network that purchased guns in South Florida through straw buyers and smuggled them to Honduras. Luis Matute Figueroa, 33, of Lake Worth, was found guilty of conspiracy and possession of a firearm by an illegal alien, the U.S. Department of Justice announced Monday.

Matute Figueroa overstayed a tourist visa in 2017 and remained in the United States without lawful status. WhatsApp messages recovered during the investigation showed that Matute Figueroa provided co-conspirators with firearm inventories, pricing information and shipping instructions for weapons destined for Honduras. The messages also contained a photograph and a video of Matute Figueroa in possession of a distinctive gold Colt 1911 pistol. U.S. Attorney Markenzy Lapointe said the defendant exploited his unlawful presence in the United States to help traffic American firearms to Honduras.

Court records and trial evidence showed that Matute Figueroa conspired with Gerson Eliu Padilla-Figueroa, Juan Matute Figueroa, Ariel Henriquez-Padilla, and William Mendoza to acquire firearms in the United States through straw purchases and illegally export them to Honduras. Straw purchases involve using individuals with clean records to buy firearms on behalf of those prohibited from owning them.

Matute Figueroa faces up to five years in federal prison on the conspiracy count and up to 15 years in prison on the firearm possession count. A federal district court judge will determine the sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. The ATF Miami Field Office and Homeland Security Investigations Miami investigated the case with assistance from the Broward Sheriff's Office, the Martin County Sheriff's Office, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Attorney Suzanne Huyler is prosecuting the case.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware named Florida State League Pitcher of the Week
hero.body:
St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware has been named the Florida State League Pitcher of the Week for the week of July 20-26, Minor League Baseball announced. Ware made two appearances last week at Clover Park against Fort Myers, one start on Tuesday and one relief outing on Sunday.

The southpaw combined to pitch 7.0 scoreless innings. He scattered three hits, walked two and struck out 12. The Mets won both games with Ware getting credit for the win on Sunday.

Ware, 22, was drafted by the Mets in the 15th round out of LSU in 2025. He made his pro debut with St. Lucie in April and has been with the team all season.

This is the first FSL Pitcher or Player of the Week award for the Mets this season.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce gets 90-day extension on $16,000 in state fines for Little Jim's dock violations
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Environmental Protection has given Fort Pierce until Sept. 15 to review a proposed consent order resolving nearly $16,000 in state fines tied to docks at Little Jim Bait & Tackle, extending the city's deadline by 90 days. Emails obtained by WPTV from FDEP show city commissioners have not yet formally accepted or rejected the state's enforcement terms. City staff have been negotiating with FDEP to reduce or resolve the penalties.

The enforcement action stems from FDEP allegations that the city has been operating docks at Little Jim's on state-owned submerged land without authorization. City Commissioner Michael Broderick acknowledged the allegation July 6, saying his information indicated the accusation was true.

The FDEP action is one of several legal pressures surrounding the historic waterfront property. In early July, Fort Pierce city commissioners voted unanimously to reject a settlement offer in a lawsuit filed by local resident Kevin Keene, who alleged years of waterfront mismanagement tied to Little Jim's. Under the proposed settlement terms, Keene would have dropped the case if the city halted any new plans for Little Jim until the FDEP permit issues were resolved and allowed a public vote on future waterfront land decisions. Keene said his motivation is only to protect the publicly owned waterfront property and ensure major decisions are not made without enough transparency.

The dispute traces back to the Fort Pierce landmark of nearly 80 years facing an uncertain future after its lease expired. The city offered the land lease to bidders, drawing an outcry from residents. Restaurant co-owner Donna Qvarnstrom said their biggest fear was the location changing to a chain restaurant or big box store. After community support, the city kept the restaurant open month to month. Despite five formal proposals submitted including one from current operators, the city said none met the criteria and scrapped plans to select a new tenant. Broderick said the city is planning to hire a real estate manager to oversee development decisions and prevent future situations.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Planning & Zoning Board recommends Miracle Mile extension for former Doctors Clinic site
cards.teaser: The Vero Beach Planning & Zoning Board unanimously recommended the City Council change the land use of a seven-acre parcel at 2300 5th Ave. from residential to commercial for mixed-use development.
cards.body:
The Vero Beach Planning & Zoning Board unanimously recommended July 16 that the City Council change the land use of a seven-acre parcel from residential to commercial so a developer can repurpose the property at 2300 5th Ave. for mixed-use development as part of a northern extension of the Miracle Mile Business District. The applicant, 2300 5th Avenue LLC, has purchased an office building known locally as the Doctors Clinic. Through redevelopment, the site is planned to become integrated into the Miracle Mile area.

Principal Planner Cheri Fitzgerald said the request would change the future land use map from residential medium to commercial. The property is currently an office and pre-school. The amendment would extend the Miracle Mile commercial district to the north, which would allow mixed-use residential and commercial uses that could better align with more recent development trends. Fitzgerald based her recommendation of approval on the application's compliance with city code.

Contracted Land Planner Rebecca Grohall said the site was originally the Doctors Clinic specialized in healthcare, but many specialty medical practices eventually migrated toward the hospital. Today, it is generally utilized as office and a pre-school and faces vacancy rates and under-utilization. Grohall said the site plan has not been started because the Commercial Land Use designation is needed first. Possibilities include a hotel, multifamily units, and a true mixed-use development with ground-floor retail and upper floor residential uses. The Planning & Zoning Board voted 4-0 to recommend approval.
cards.article_text: The aerial map of a seven-acre parcel located at 2300 5th Ave., where a developer proposed to construct a mixed-use commercial and residential development on the property home to the old Doctors’ Clinic Building. The location map of a seven-acre parcel located at 2300 5th Ave., where a developer proposed to construct a mixed-use commercial and residential development on the property home to the old Doctors’ Clinic Building. VERO BEACH – The members of the Vero Beach Planning Zoning Board unanimously recommended July 16 that the City Council change the land use of a seven-acre parcel from residential to commercial so a developer can repurpose the property at 2300 5th Ave. for mixed-use development as part of a northern extension of the Miracle Mile Business District. Planning Development Director Jason Jeffries provided a brief introduction that afternoon for the three related agenda items, of which the last for the rezoning had already been withdrawn. “The applicant, 2300 5th Avenue LLC, has purchased an office building just north of the Miracle Mile Business District,” he said. “Many people locally know this property as the Doctors’ Clinic. Through redevelopment, they’re looking for this site to become integrated into the Miracle Mile area. That required three separate applications: One is the future land use map amendment, the first hearing; then a text amendment to update one of the figures in the map series, which designates the commercial districts; and the rezoning. Most of the presentation is going to occur in the first hearing.” Principal Planner Cheri Fitzgerald then kicked off that presentation. “The request is to change the future land use map from the existing residential medium to the proposed commercial,” she said. “The property is just north of the Miracle Mile commercial district [and] is currently an office/pre-school. To the north is an office complex, and the land use is residential medium; To the south is the Miracle Mile area; to the east is a multifamily residential apartment complex; and to the west is a pre-school/daycare. The amendment is to extend the Miracle Mile commercial district to the north, which would allow mixed-use residential and commercial uses that could better align with more recent development trends.” Fitzgerald based her recommendation of approval on the application’s compliance with city code. “The future land use map amendment is found to be consistent with the standards for review in Section 6525 of the land development regulations,” she explained. “It is compatible with the surrounding area in terms of existing uses and future land-use designations.” Board Member Samantha Irvin was the first to question what the future development might contain. “Do we know yet what type of commercial businesses are going to go there?” she asked. Jeffries tackled that inquiry. “It depends on what’s been submitted to staff,” he replied. That is one of the reasons why our recommendation was not to approve the zoning so that we would get a more specific development plan or some further updates that we’re working on with the B-4 Zoning to ensure it is pedestrian oriented.” Vice-Chairman Thomas “TP” Kennedy then asked about potential traffic impacts but discovered it was probably too early in the process to get clear answers on that concern as well. “Does making it more pedestrian friendly decrease the traffic?” he asked. “Is that what you guys are looking for in the B-4 Zoning?” “Because they say it’s going to be pedestrian oriented, they say there’s more internal capture in the modeling,” Jeffries answered. “Again, this goes back to making sure in the zoning you actually get the pedestrian-oriented development. I think on Indian River Boulevard... some intersection improvements are needed.” Fitzgerald offered her insight as well. “At this level like Jason explained, it’s more theoretical,” she said. “You do the overall analysis and you look at the most practical case with those assumptions, and that’s what the traffic impact analysis did. Once you get a project-specific development, the traffic report will be specified to that site plan.” After more Board member questions related to both traffic and the pedestrian-friendly focus, the applicant’s contracted developer Keith Kyte and contracted Land Planner Rebecca Grohall both came to the podium. “The reason we’re here today is we need the Commercial Land Use Designation to answer those questions,” Kyte said. “We’re aligning it with the city’s 2005 Vision Plan.” Grohall then provided details on the current status of the property and the ideas for repurposing it. “This was originally the Doctors’ Clinics specialized in heathcare,” she said. “A lot of specialty medical practices eventually migrated toward the hospital and opening their own facilities. Today, it’s generally utilized as office and a pre-school and it does face vacancy rates and under-utilization.” Grohall emphasized that the site plan was in limbo until the Commercial Land Use is approved. “The site plan hasn’t even been started because we need to put the foundation in place,” she explained. “Possibly one of those pieces could be a hotel. We’re looking at multifamily units, a true mixed-use development where there’s ground-floor retail and upper floor residential uses. You’ll see the map of how this interfaces with the neighborhood. This is a visualization, and this would be a non-vehicular pedestrian connection that would bring you into the Miracle Mile shopping plaza.” After much further discussion, Vice-Chairman Kennedy wondered why the Parc24 office building currently under construction by Kimley-Horn wasn’t included since it sits just north of the 2300 5th Avenue LLC property. “When I read through this over the past week, I thought for uniformity it might be better for Kimley-Horn to come in too,” he said. “Was there any conversation there with them?” The answer according to Jeffries was cut and dry. “That was staff’s recommendation, but they decided not to become part of this application,” he said. The Planning Zoning Board then voted 4-0 to recommend approval, with Board Member Bethany Fortunato and Chairman Jeb Bittner Absent. They also recommend amending the Miracle Mile Corridor element of the city’s comprehensive plan. Your comment has been submitted. Reported There was a problem reporting this.
