cards.headline: Indian River County Commission District 2 candidates outline priorities ahead of Aug. 18 primary
cards.teaser: Four candidates for the Indian River County Commission District 2 seat answered questions on issues ranging from property tax reform to affordable housing and agricultural land preservation.
cards.body:
The Hometown News sent the same list of questions to each qualified candidate in the Aug. 18 Republican Primary Election for the District 2 Indian River County Commission seat. The only qualified Democratic candidate in the race also agreed to participate, although he will not face the winner of the primary until November. Candidates answered questions about the most serious issue facing Indian River County, a referendum on raising the Homestead Exemption and potentially cutting ad valorem property tax income, affordable housing, rezoning of agricultural lands, and improving quality of life.

Republican candidate Bob McPartlan, who served 15 years on the Sebastian City Council, said the most serious issue is managing growth in a way that protects quality of life, infrastructure and the Indian River Lagoon. He does not support the property tax amendment as written, saying it was developed quickly without a full analysis of its impact. Republican candidate Jennifer Pippin said if the amendment passes, she would begin by evaluating discretionary spending, including $3.7 million in funding provided to non-profit organizations and the $1.4 million budget for school resource officers currently paid by the county. Republican candidate Daniel Brooks Robinson said the greatest challenge is managing growth responsibly and ensuring roads, utilities, public safety and infrastructure keep pace.

Democratic candidate Robert (Robbie) D. Hardingham said the Indian River Lagoon is one of the most serious issues facing the county. He said the stormwater runoff and pollution from nitrates, phosphorus and algae blooms are causing an ecological disaster. He said the septic-to-sewer initiative will help but solutions are needed to speed up the cleaning of the Lagoon. Hardingham said he hopes the property tax referendum will not pass because it will be bad for schools, businesses and renters.
cards.article_text: The Hometown News sent the same list of questions below to each qualified candidate in the Aug. 18 Republican Primary Election for the District 2 Indian River County Commission seat. The only qualified Democratic candidate in the race also agreed to participate, although he won’t face the winner of the primary until Nov. Question 1 What do you view as the most serious issue facing Indian River County and how would you propose addressing that if elected? Question 2 There will be a referendum this year on raising the Homestead Exemption and potentially cutting ad valorem property tax income significantly to municipalities. If you are elected and that passes, what areas of the county budget would you suggest trimming or cutting out altogether if need-be? Question 3 Do you think the County Commission should address the lack of affordable housing, and if so, in what way? Question 4 There have recently been calls from some citizens to stop the rezoning of agricultural lands for housing and to do more to encourage the return to citrus groves. If elected, how would you respond to such requests? Question 5 If elected, how would you work to improve the quality of life for Indian River County voters? Candidate Bob McPartian 1. The most serious issue is managing growth in a way that protects our quality of life, infrastructure and the Indian River Lagoon. If elected, I will push for better coordination between cities and the county so development is tied to available roads, utilities and environmental capacity. My 15 years on the Sebastian City Council have shown me that early planning and strong interlocal agreements prevent problems before they start. I support tax reform, but I do not support this particular amendment as written. It was developed quickly without a full analysis of its impact, and there is no clear backup plan if it creates significant revenue shortfalls. If it passes, I would protect public safety and core infrastructure first. Then, I would look to reduce non-essential spending, improve efficiency and prioritize programs that deliver clear results for residents rather than across-the-board cuts. Yes, the County Commission should address housing affordability in practical ways. I support streamlining permitting, encouraging a mix of housing types where infrastructure already exists, and working with cities and private partners. Partnering with nonprofits such as Habitat for Humanity to develop housing on existing county-owned property is one concrete step that can help without overextending government resources. Property owners have the right to request zoning changes, and those requests should be evaluated fairly. At the same time, I respect citizens who want to protect agricultural land and encourage citrus. Growth should be directed first to areas already planned for development and served by infrastructure. Any rezoning must be carefully reviewed for impacts on roads, water resources and the Lagoon. I would focus on the basics that matter most to residents: protecting the Indian River Lagoon, maintaining safe roads and reliable infrastructure, supporting public safety, keeping taxes reasonable through disciplined budgeting, and ensuring cities and the county work together. After 15 years of local service, I know steady, practical leadership improves daily life more than flashy promises. Candidate Jennifer Pippin 1, If Amendment 3 is approved by Florida voters, it will provide meaningful property tax relief for homesteaded residents. As a county commissioner, I will work to ensure the county budget reflects that change by prioritizing responsible spending, eliminating waste where possible and protecting essential services without shifting the burden back onto taxpayers through other means. Government must live within its means while providing the core services our residents expect. If the referendum passes, I believe the County Commission has a responsibility to carefully review every line of the budget before asking taxpayers to bear the burden. I would begin by evaluating discretionary spending, including the $3.7 million in funding provided to non-profit organizations and the administrative costs associated with distributing those funds. I would also review the current funding arrangement for school resource officers. Public education is a School District responsibility, and I believe the District should fund the sheriff’s $1.4 million budget currently paid by the county for SROs. Additionally, I would implement a vacancy review process so that when positions become vacant through retirement or resignation, they are evaluated to determine whether the workload can be absorbed more efficiently. I would also review and reduce consulting contracts wherever county staff can perform the work in-house. Finally, I would look for ways to increase revenue from tourism so the burden on local homeowners is reduced. I believe affordable housing is primarily driven by the private sector, not government mandates. The County Commission’s role should be to create an environment where businesses can thrive, which in turn brings better-paying jobs and more opportunities for residents. By reducing unnecessary regulations, streamlining permitting and encouraging responsible development, we can help increase the supply of housing and make it more attainable. I also support measures like Amendment 3, which will allow residents to keep more of their own money and better support their families. I want to keep oranges growing and cows grazing on agricultural land. Once farmland is developed, we can never get it back. I support protecting our agricultural heritage while respecting private property rights. I will work to ensure agricultural land remains agricultural and that development is responsible, planned and supported by the infrastructure needed to protect our quality of life. Improving our quality of life means preserving the things that make this county so special while planning responsibly for the future. When elected, I will work to keep taxes as low as possible through responsible budgeting, support our Sheriff’s Office and first responders, protect our agricultural heritage and ensure growth never outpaces our roads, infrastructure and public safety. I want future generations to enjoy the same safe, beautiful and welcoming Indian River County that my family has been blessed to call home. Candidate Daniel ‘Brooks’ Robinson 1, Our greatest challenge is managing growth responsibly. We need to ensure our roads, utilities, public safety and infrastructure keep pace with growth while protecting the quality of life that makes Indian River County such a great place to live. We don’t have to choose between growth and preservation: We can achieve both through thoughtful planning. The county should begin by reviewing every department, project and expenditure to identify efficiencies and eliminate non-essential spending. My priorities would be protecting public safety, maintaining essential infrastructure and preserving the core services residents rely on every day. I would not commit to cutting specific departments or positions without first conducting a comprehensive review. The county should encourage a range of housing opportunities that meet the needs of our workforce and families while protecting neighborhood character and ensuring infrastructure keeps pace with growth. I believe the private market should lead, with county government focused on responsible planning, efficient permitting and sound infrastructure investment. Agriculture is an important part of Indian River County’s history, economy and identity, and we should do what we can to support our agricultural community. At the same time, every rezoning request should be evaluated on its own merits and be consistent with the county’s comprehensive plan, infrastructure capacity and the long-term interests of our community. My focus will be on managing growth responsibly, protecting private property rights and ensuring development improves our community. Quality of life is why so many of us choose to live in Indian River County. As commissioner, I will work to keep our community safe, manage growth responsibly, protect our natural resources, strengthen our local economy and be a good steward of taxpayer dollars. My goal is to preserve what makes Indian River County special for future generations. Democratic Candidate Robert (Robbie) D. Hardingham While Hardingham is not actually running in the August Primary Election, he agreed to participate at the Hometown News’ request. I feel that the Indian River lagoon is one of the most serious issues facing IRC out of many. The stormwater runoff and pollution from nitrates, phosphorus and algae blooms are causing an ecological disaster. The septic-to-sewer initiative will help with that, but we need to find solutions to speed up the cleaning of the Lagoon. I would find ways of reducing the pollutants from going into the lagoon. 2, Hopefully that referendum will not pass because it will be bad for schools, businesses and renters. The savings that homeowners would get from this policy will not outweigh the loss of tax revenue. Many services like public safety, education/public schools and infrastructure will be detrimentally affected. I would have to look at the budget, if elected, to see where service can be trimmed. Yes, the county should have affordable living properties either single-family homes or apartment buildings for our community members like nurses, teachers, police, working families and un-housed citizens. I would work with the Affordable Housing Advisory Committee to find the best ways for our community to develop affordable housing. I agree that we shouldn’t be using agricultural land to develop single-family-home gated communities. I would like to see our citrus industry return, but I’m not sure that’s a viable option. I think more land should remain as green space for the local ecology. I would look for ways to improve affordable housing and affordable healthcare for everyone, especially seniors; rental and utility assistance programs; and clean up the Lagoon because a healthy Lagoon makes a healthy IRC. Most of all, I want to hear from the community on how I can help improve the quality of life for all of IRC. Your comment has been submitted. Reported There was a problem reporting this. hero.headline: Vero Beach keeps millage flat at 2.98 mills, adds $410,000 to budget for police positions
hero.body:
The Vero Beach City Council set a preliminary millage rate for the 2026-27 fiscal year at the current 2.9816 mills during a July 22 budget workshop, approving a $37,352,589 budget that includes $410,000 transferred from the General Fund's unassigned fund balance to cover salaries for three vacant police officer positions. City Manager Monte Falls told the council the city holds a strong financial position with a total General Fund balance of $54 million, including $17.7 million in unassigned funds and $35.56 million in committed reserves.

Falls recommended using $435,160 from the unassigned balance to offset the city's Other Post Employee Benefit trust payment, which would allow the vacant police positions to be filled. For a Vero Beach homeowner with a property assessed at $300,000, a $50,000 Homestead Exemption and a Save Our Homes 3 percent increase, the current millage rate would result in about $25 a year in additional ad valorem tax, Falls said.

Vice Mayor Linda Moore and Councilmember Taylor Dingle raised concerns about funding recurring positions with non-recurring money, particularly with Amendment 3 on the November ballot potentially creating a $1.3 million budget hole. Mayor John Cotugno said Vero Beach would fare better than other Florida communities if Amendment 3 passes because the city has four enterprise funds and a diversified tax base including industrial, residential and commercial revenue sources.

After debate, the council approved adding the $410,000 to the budget by offsetting capital expenses already included in the operating budget. Falls told Hometown News on Sept. 27 that the new police officer salaries would actually cost the city an extra $300,000. The council will return in September to set the final millage rate and adopt the budget.
hero.article_text: VERO BEACH — The City Council hashed out its preliminary 2026-27 fiscal year budget July 22, keeping the tentative millage rate at the current 2.9816 mills while approving several fee increases and a $410,000 transfer from the General Fund’s unassigned fund balance to cover salaries for three vacant police officer positions. City Manager Monte Falls launched the discussion and set its parameters. “At the conclusion of the workshops, we have to address the retiree benefits and set a not-to-exceed millage rate,” he said. “We’ll come back later in September and set the final millage rate and adopt the budget. Our audit was submitted on time, and based on that audit, we’re in a very strong financial position. The General Fund has a total fund balance of $54 million, and of that $54 million, 17.7 million is listed as unassigned. The committed fund balance of $35.56 million includes reserves of $5 million for storms. The unfunded pension reserve was $5.3 [million] and the Other Post Employee Benefit reserve of 6.8 million.” While emphasizing that the proposed $36.9 million budget was balanced at the tentative millage rate, Falls also recommended some tweaks to fill previously approved but still vacant police officer positions. “I would like to have a philosophical discussion about the budget, which, as presented, is balanced,” he continued. “It includes additional revenues from fees in the amount of $370,000 and holds three vacancies open in the Police Department. We recommend using $435,160 of the unassigned balance on your sheet of that $5 million to offset the contribution to the OPEB trust. That offset would allow us to fill the Police Department vacancies.” Falls then translated that into terms a city resident with a home assessed at $300,000 could understand. “With a $50,000 Homestead Exemption and a Save Our Homes 3 percent increase, the current millage rate would result in about $25 a year in additional ad valorem tax,” he explained. “What I’d like to zero in on is what would the Council like to do. We brought you the budget balanced with the existing millage and those additional revenues, with the three positions open. We would recommend making that OPEB payment out of the unassigned fund balance that isn’t held out for reserves. That would allow us to then fill those vacancies in the Police Department.” Vice-Mayor Linda Moore was the first to pose a clarification question afterwards. “Is that OPEB a recurring cost?” she asked. “It is a liability we have set aside,” Falls responded. “We have an annual payment on it, but we have had this policy looked at by our outside accounting firm. They concur with us that it is an OPEB liability that can be paid for out of that amount. If you look at the revenue portion of your budget on Page 22, the OPEB trust is that $435,000. So that money would come out of the unfunded reserves to cover that.” Both Moore and Councilmember Taylor Dingle wondered, however, how the city would continue to fund those new positions in next year’s budget. The vice-mayor particularly worried that Amendment 3 on this year’s ballot might severely impact the collection of future ad valorem property taxes needed for that funding. “We are facing the possibility of a $1.3 million hole in the budget,” Moore said. “I feel like it would be irresponsible to fund more staff this year out of money that’s not even technically recurring, and then next year we’re even in a bigger situation. We’re all reading articles in the paper about how this community might have to fire firefighters. I don’t want to fire anybody, so I’m trying to be very, very cautious.” Councilmember John Carroll chimed in with his own clarification question. “How long have these positions been vacant?” he asked. While Vice-Mayor Moore reminded him that they’d been approved since last year, Mayor John Cotugno emphasized the fluid nature of the Vero Beach Police force. “They have been fully staffed at one time,” he explained. “They’ve been down four, they’ve been down two [and] they’re down three now. It’s all over the place.” Mayor Cotugno also pointed that Vero Beach would not suffer the fate of most Florida communities if Amendment 3 passes because the city has a more varied income stream. “We are lucky that we have revenue sources no other municipality has in this county,” he said. “We have a diversified tax base so that we’re not as affected by the property tax referendum if it does pass. We have four enterprise funds; we have an industrial base; and we have residential and commercial.” Even so, Councilmember Aaron Vos worried about tapping the unassigned fund balance to pay for the new officers and hinted at postponing the decision until after November. “I hate raiding our savings piggy bank,” he said. “We have unusual circumstances here [and] a cycle of attrition in our Police Department. They’re in the pipeline, so maybe we could wait until we get Police Chief [David] Currey in here and go through the Police budget. If we move forward with a plan to allocate the funds and – depending on the outcome of the election – we’d back out. We’d have the option to just not hire.” Falls, however, pointed out that the referendum would only affect the 2027/2028 Fiscal Year Budget and not the one currently under review. “If we approve the number of positions, we budget as if we’re going to have those,” he explained. “Throughout the year, we always have some funds that aren’t expanded because we’re not always fully staffed. If we would authorize those positions and then after the election go back, we’d have to have direction from Council as a budget amendment to not hire whatever vacancies you didn’t want to hire.” Because Councilman Vos still feared those new officer salaries would put the city in financial bind, Falls offered another budgetary solution. “There’s a different way we could look at that money that comes out of the unassigned reserves,” he said. “I used the OPEB trust liability because it’s one of the things that the policy says can be used, but it also says it can be used for capital and construction. In this budget, there’s $410,000 of capital in the operating budget below the operating expense line because it’s not an operating expense. If it gave you a better comfort level to say we’ll offset that with some funds from that unassigned, then you’re not paying for a recurring expense.” Vice-Mayor Moore liked that idea, and after much further debate, the City Council approved the addition of that $410,000 to the budget, resulting in a proposed $37,352,589 budget for the 2026/2027 Fiscal Year. Falls told the Hometown News on Sept. 27 that the new police officer salaries would actually only set the city back an extra $300,000. Your comment has been submitted. cards.headline: Senior Resource Association and FPL deliver hurricane meal kits to Indian River County seniors
cards.teaser: Florida Power Light Company partnered with Senior Resource Association to distribute hurricane preparedness meal kits to seniors in Indian River County as the Atlantic hurricane season continues.
cards.body:
Senior Resource Association worked with Florida Power Light Company to distribute hurricane preparedness meal kits to seniors in Indian River County during the six-month Atlantic hurricane season. The effort, also in partnership with the Florida Council on Aging, provides vital supplies to vulnerable seniors in the communities the companies serve.

Each kit includes three days of shelf-stable food, water and snacks for seniors who may not be able to leave their homes or receive home-delivered meals immediately after a storm. The kits also include a hurricane preparedness guide with tips and resources. Volunteers from FPL and SRA distributed the kits to help ensure seniors have the resources they need to stay safe.

Senior Resource Association President and CEO Karen Deigl said FPL has been an incredible partner to the organization. FPL External Affairs Manager Michele Murrell said the company is committed to ensuring vulnerable customers have the necessary resources to weather any storm. FPL has worked with local community nonprofits to deliver thousands of hurricane kits to help seniors prepare for storm season since 2016.
cards.article_text: FPL employees delivering meal kits to local seniors. FPL SRA and Meals on Wheels staff and volunteers ready to deliver shelf stable meal kits. INDIAN RIVER COUNTY – With the six-month Atlantic hurricane season underway, Senior Resource Association (SRA) worked with Florida Power Light Company (FPL) to distribute hurricane preparedness meal kits to seniors in Indian River County. This effort, also in partnership with the Florida Council on Aging, provides vital supplies to vulnerable seniors in the communities the companies serve. Each kit, courtesy of FPL, includes three days of shelf-stable food, water and snacks for seniors who may not be able to leave their homes or receive home-delivered meals immediately after a storm. The kits also include a hurricane preparedness guide with tips and resources. Volunteers from FPL and SRA distributed the kits, helping ensure seniors have the resources they need to stay safe. “FPL has been an incredible partner to our organization, and we’re grateful for their continued commitment to the seniors we serve,” said Senior Resource Association President and CEO Karen Deigl. “Preparing for hurricane season can be stressful, especially for older adults living alone.” “We’re committed to powering strong communities – ensuring our most vulnerable customers have the necessary resources to weather any storm,” said FPL External Affairs Manager Michele Murrell. “By working with Senior Resource Association, seniors in our community are now better prepared for hurricane season.” Since 2016, FPL has worked with local community nonprofits to deliver thousands of hurricane kits to help seniors prepare for storm season. For more information on how customers can prepare, including tips, checklists and more, they can visit FPL.com/storm . Your comment has been submitted. Reported There was a problem reporting this. hero.headline: Fort Pierce gets 90-day extension to pay state fines for Little Jim's dock violations
hero.teaser: The Florida Department of Environmental Protection extended the city's deadline to Sept. 15 to review a proposed consent order resolving nearly $16,000 in state fines tied to docks at Little Jim Bait & Tackle.
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Environmental Protection gave Fort Pierce until Sept. 15 to review, approve and submit a proposed consent order resolving nearly $16,000 in state fines tied to docks at Little Jim Bait & Tackle. The state agency extended the city's deadline by 90 days, meaning city commissioners have not yet formally accepted or rejected the state's enforcement terms. City staff have been negotiating with FDEP to reduce or resolve the thousands of dollars in penalties.

The enforcement action follows allegations that the city has been operating docks at Little Jim's on state-owned submerged land without authorization. FDEP says the city never had permission to use the land. City Commissioner Michael Broderick acknowledged the allegation on July 6.

The FDEP action is one of several legal and regulatory pressures surrounding the historic waterfront property. In early July, Fort Pierce city commissioners voted unanimously to reject a settlement offer in a lawsuit filed by local resident Kevin Keene, who alleged years of waterfront mismanagement tied to Little Jim's. The city has filed a motion to dismiss Keene's amended complaint. Keene said he will continue to pursue litigation. Broderick said the city is planning to hire a real estate manager to oversee development decisions and prevent future situations.
hero.article_text: The Florida Department of Environmental Protection has given Fort Pierce until Sept. 15 to review, approve and submit a proposed consent order resolving nearly $16,000 in state fines tied to docks at Little Jim Bait & Tackle.Emails obtained by WPTV from FDEP show the state agency extended the city's deadline by 90 days, meaning city commissioners have not yet formally accepted or rejected the state's enforcement terms. City staff have been negotiating with FDEP to reduce or resolve the thousands of dollars in penalties.The enforcement action follows WPTV's reporting that revealed FDEP alleges the city has been operating docks at Little Jim's on state-owned submerged land without authorization — land the agency says the city never had permission to use.City Commissioner Michael Broderick previously acknowledged the allegation."My information is that accusation is actually true, that there was an extension of the existing docks," Broderick said July 6. Broderick said it remains unclear whether the city or the Little Jim's tenant was responsible for extending the docks without the required permits."Keep in mind that the city of Fort Pierce owns that real estate, so ultimately, in the day, the city of Fort Pierce is the responsible party," Broderick said.The FDEP action is one of several legal and regulatory pressures now surrounding the historic waterfront property. In early July, Fort Pierce city commissioners voted unanimously to reject a settlement offer in a separate lawsuit filed by local resident Kevin Keene, who alleged years of waterfront mismanagement tied to Little Jim's.Under the proposed settlement terms, Keene would have dropped the case if the city halted any new plans for Little Jim until the FDEP permit issues were resolved and allowed a public vote on future waterfront land decisions. The city has filed a motion to dismiss Keene's amended complaint, and Keene said he will continue to pursue litigation."My motivation is only to protect the publicly owned waterfront property and to make sure that major decisions are not being made without enough transparency, caution, and public awareness," Keene said. "This was never about money or personal gain for me."The dispute traces back to WPTV's reporting that the Fort Pierce landmark of nearly 80 years was facing an uncertain future after its lease expired. The city offered the land lease to bidders, drawing an outcry from residents."Our biggest fear is we don't want this to change and be a chain restaurant or a big box store," restaurant co-owner Donna Qvarnstrom said. "It's local and the people love local."After an outpouring of community support, the city kept the restaurant open month to month. Despite five formal proposals submitted to the city — including one from the current operators — the city said none met the criteria and scrapped plans to select a new tenant.Keene argues the handling of Little Jim's is part of a broader pattern of poor waterfront stewardship, pointing to two other controversial city projects: Fisherman's Wharf, where state records show the city promised land it didn't own, and King's Landing, where a developer claims the city promised buildable property that contained 1,500 tons of old power plant concrete. The Fisherman's Wharf situation led to a current multi-million dollar lawsuit filed by that project's developer and threats of a lawsuit from the King's Landing developer.Broderick said the city's management of leased properties needs to change."In my opinion, the handling of city-owned real estate that we subsequently lease out to tenants is — it's not being managed. I will not rest until I get to the bottom of this issue," Broderick said.When asked how the city plans to fix the problem, Broderick said a comprehensive review is needed."This is going to take a top down, bottom up approach to look at the entirety of the portfolio of the city of Fort Pierce and fix this one asset at a time," Broderick said.Broderick also said the city is planning to hire a real estate manager to oversee development decisions and prevent future situations.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman shot multiple times in front yard, suspect died of self-inflicted wound
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie Police Department responded to multiple 911 calls reporting gunshots and a domestic disturbance around 7:40 p.m. Saturday in the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace. Officers found 50-year-old Elizabeth Ortega suffering from multiple gunshot wounds in the front yard. She was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she was pronounced dead. Officers also found 50-year-old Ralph Varela Sr. inside the residence, dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Investigators determined Varela and Ortega had been in a long-term domestic relationship and lived together with their adult son. The couple was in the process of separating. Around 7:30 p.m. Saturday, the adult son left the residence to pick up dinner from a local restaurant. Investigators determined there was no known argument or disturbance inside the home before his departure.

At some point after the son left, investigators believe Varela used an AR-style .223 caliber rifle and began shooting Ortega inside the residence. Ortega fled the home in an attempt to escape, while Varela continued firing. Investigators recovered home surveillance video that shows Ortega attempting to flee into the front yard while Varela continued to fire at her before she collapsed. After the shooting, Varela returned inside the residence, where he later died.

The investigation remains active as detectives continue processing evidence and awaiting final results from the Medical Examiner's Office. Varela resided in West Palm Beach before moving to Port St. Lucie. On April 23, 2014, he was convicted of discharging a firearm in public and sentenced to 192 days in jail. On June 12, 2017, he was convicted of possession of cocaine, reckless driving reduced from DUI, driving while license was not active and refusal to submit to chemical or physical test. He was sentenced to 20 days in jail.

hero.headline: Martin County weighs shark fishing rule changes after state directive
hero.body:
Martin County is weighing changes to its local shark fishing ordinance after the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission directed the county to align its rules with state regulations. The state agency asked the county to bring its ordinance in line with state law, which preempts counties from regulating saltwater fishing. Assistant County Attorney Melissa Petrick said state statute has preempted the county's powers to regulate salt water fishing, including shark fishing.

State law requires a saltwater fishing license and a special permit for shark fishing. It also allows shark fishing within 1,000 feet of a guarded beach at all hours. Among those opposing the changes is Jessica Veatch, whose then-3-year-old daughter Violet was attacked by a bull shark on Bathtub Beach in Martin County 9 years ago. Veatch said she believes nearby fishing activity may have led to the attack, noting that some young men were spearfishing on the reef at the time.

Indian River Keeper Jim Moir raised concerns about the potential impact of the changes at the Tuesday commission meeting. He said attracting more sharks to the coast is bad for human safety, angling, public awareness, and the sharks themselves. He noted that anglers offshore are complaining daily about how many of their caught fish are being deprived by sharks.

County attorneys suggested the ordinance does not need to be eliminated entirely. Petrick said the county can rework the ordinance and instead of eliminating everything can just reference the illegality of things under state law. County commissioners voted to table the discussion, directing staff to review concerns raised by the community and commissioners and draft new ordinance language.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie police identify couple in murder-suicide on Southeast Oxmoor Terrace
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police identified the victim and suspect in a domestic-related murder-suicide that occurred Saturday night at a residence in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. Elizabeth Ortega, 50, was killed and Ralph Varela Sr., 50, died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound. The investigation revealed that Varela and Ortega had been involved in a long-term cohabitation domestic relationship and resided together with their adult son, and the couple was in the process of separating.

Officers responded at approximately 7:40 p.m. Saturday after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance. Investigators learned the couple's adult son left the residence to pick up dinner from a local restaurant. Investigators determined there was no known argument or disturbance inside the home before his departure. At some point after the son left, investigators believe Varela utilized an AR-style .223 caliber rifle and began shooting Ortega inside the residence.

Ortega fled the home in an attempt to escape, while Varela continued firing. Investigators recovered home surveillance video that shows Ortega attempting to flee into the front yard while Varela continued to fire at her before she collapsed. After the shooting, Varela returned inside the residence. Responding officers located Ortega with multiple gunshot wounds. She was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she was later pronounced deceased. Varela was later observed inside the home, where he appeared to have died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Varela resided in West Palm Beach before moving to Port St. Lucie. On April 23, 2014, he was convicted of discharging a firearm in public and was later sentenced to 192 days in jail with all time served credited, according to Palm Beach Clerk records. On June 12, 2017, he was convicted of possession of cocaine, reckless driving reduced from DUI, driving while license wasn't active and refusal to submit to chemical or physical test. He was sentenced to 20 days in jail, which was served. The three-bedroom home sold for $160,000 in 2018. The investigation remains active as detectives continue processing evidence and are awaiting the final results from the Medical Examiner's Office.

hero.teaser: The St. Lucie County Sheriffs Office is searching for a suspect wearing a tropical shirt dominated by a giant pink flamingo who allegedly burglarized a residence twice on July 28.
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriffs Office is searching for a suspected burglar dressed in a tropical shirt dominated by a giant pink flamingo, now known across St. Lucie County as the Flamingo Bandit. Investigators said the suspect entered a residence on July 28 and stole a laptop, miscellaneous food and a key to the home.

Deputies allege he then returned later that same day and used the stolen key to get inside a second time. The sheriffs office shared an image of the suspect, hoping his difficult-to-miss wardrobe will help someone identify him.

Anyone who recognizes the man or has information about the case is asked to call the St. Lucie County Sheriffs Office at 772-462-7300 or email Deputy V. Ancewicz at PatrolTips@stluciesheriff.com.

cards.headline: Elizabeth Ortega killed, Ralph Varela Sr. dead in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide on SE Oxmoor Terrace
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie Police have identified Elizabeth Ortega and Ralph Varela Sr., both 50, as the victim and suspect in a domestic-related murder-suicide that occurred Saturday evening at a home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. Officers responded around 7:40 p.m. Saturday after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance.

Investigation revealed that Varela and Ortega were involved in a long-term cohabitation domestic relationship and lived together with their adult son. The couple was in the process of separating. On Saturday, the adult son left the residence to pick up dinner from a local restaurant. Investigators said there was no known argument or disturbance inside the home before he left.

Investigators believe that at some point after the son left the home, Varela began shooting Ortega with an AR-style .223 caliber rifle inside the home. Home surveillance video obtained by police shows that Ortega was trying to flee from the house into the front yard while Varela continued to fire at her before she collapsed. The video shows that after the shooting, Varela went back into the house.

Responding officers found Ortega suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. She was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce, where she was later pronounced deceased. Varela was found inside the house, where he appeared to have died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound. The investigation remains active as detectives continue processing evidence and awaiting the final results from the Medical Examiners Office. Police said the incident appears to be isolated and there is no known threat to the public.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware named Florida State League Pitcher of the Week
hero.body:
St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware has been named the Florida State League Pitcher of the Week for the week of July 20-26, Minor League Baseball announced. Ware made two appearances last week at Clover Park against Fort Myers, one start on Tuesday and one relief outing on Sunday.

The southpaw combined to pitch 7.0 scoreless innings. He scattered three hits, walked two and struck out 12. The Mets won both games with Ware getting credit for the win on Sunday.

Ware, 22, was drafted by the Mets in the 15th round out of LSU in 2025. He made his pro debut with St. Lucie in April and has been with the team all season.

This is the first FSL Pitcher or Player of the Week award for the Mets this season.

hero.headline: Martin County hoarding case grows to 108 rescued animals as adoptions begin
hero.body:
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast continues to receive animals from a Martin County hoarding case that has now yielded 108 rescued dogs and cats. More than a dozen animals from the case have already found forever homes, but new animals arrive at the shelter daily from the same case.

Sarah Fisher of the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast said the shelter needs community support to keep up with the growing number of animals. Staff perform spay and neuter surgeries, microchip animals, and clear them for adoption medically every day as donations pour in to support the effort.

The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast recommends checking their website for the most up to date adoption listings. People interested in adopting can call or visit the shelter for a meet and greet with the animals.

Fisher said the shelter can use all the help it can get as animals continue to come forth from the same case. The organization did not release the location of the hoarding case or provide details about the property owner.

hero.body:

Officers responded around 7:40 p.m. Saturday after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance.

When officers arrived, they found an adult woman suffering from a gunshot wound. She was airlifted to a local hospital, where she was later pronounced dead. Officers also found an adult man dead at the scene. Investigators said he appeared to have died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

The scene remains an active crime scene as detectives continue processing evidence and interviewing witnesses. Based on the preliminary investigation, police believe the incident was an isolated, domestic-related shooting and said there is no known threat to the public.

Residents should continue to expect a heavy police presence in the area of SE Triumph Road and SE Veterans Memorial Parkway while investigators remain on scene. Motorists are encouraged to avoid the area and use alternate routes whenever possible. Detectives cautioned that the facts and circumstances surrounding the case remain subject to change as the investigation continues.

cards.headline: 86-year-old woman dies after Port St. Lucie intersection crash
cards.teaser: Marie R. Martin died after her Hyundai Elantra was struck by a Honda HR-V at Southwest Savona Boulevard and Southwest Lawndale Avenue Thursday afternoon.
cards.body:
An 86-year-old woman died after police said she pulled into the path of an SUV and was struck in a Port St. Lucie intersection Thursday afternoon. The crash happened at about 2:30 p.m. at Southwest Savona Boulevard and Southwest Lawndale Avenue, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.

Investigators said Marie R. Martin was driving a 2006 Hyundai Elantra west on Lawndale Avenue when she entered the intersection from near a stop sign and failed to yield to a northbound 2026 Honda HR-V. The Honda, driven by a 17-year-old boy, struck the drivers side of Martins car, police said. Martin had to be extricated from the Hyundai before she was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with critical injuries, police said. She later died despite efforts to save her.

The teenage driver of the Honda was not injured. The Police Departments Traffic Homicide Unit continues to investigate the crash.

hero.headline: Woman killed, man dead in apparent domestic shooting in Port St. Lucie
hero.body:
A woman was killed and a man was found dead following an apparent domestic-related shooting in a Port St. Lucie neighborhood Saturday evening. Port St. Lucie Police Department officers responded around 7:40 p.m. to the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace, west of U.S. 1 and near HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital, after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance.

When officers arrived, they found an adult woman suffering from a gunshot wound. She was airlifted to a local hospital, where she was later pronounced dead. During the response, officers also found an adult man dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Detectives remain at the scene processing evidence and conducting interviews as they work to determine the circumstances leading up to the shooting. Police said the incident appears to be isolated and domestic-related, and there is no known threat to the public at this time.

Residents can continue to expect a heavy law enforcement presence in the area of SE Triumph Road and SE Veterans Memorial Parkway while investigators remain on scene. Motorists are encouraged to avoid the area and use alternate routes whenever possible. The investigation remains active.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware named Florida State League Pitcher of the Week
hero.body:
St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware has been named the Florida State League Pitcher of the Week for the week of July 20-26. Minor League Baseball announced the award Tuesday.

Ware made two appearances last week at Clover Park against Fort Myers, one start on Tuesday and one relief outing on Sunday. The southpaw combined to pitch 7.0 scoreless innings. He scattered three hits, walked two and struck out 12. The Mets won both games with Ware getting credit for the win on Sunday.

Ware, 22, was drafted by the Mets in the 15th round out of LSU in 2025. He made his pro debut with St. Lucie in April and has been with the team all season.

This is the first FSL Pitcher or Player of the Week award for the Mets this season.

hero.headline: Education Foundation of Martin County launches programs to support classrooms ahead of Aug. 10 school year
hero.body:
The Education Foundation of Martin County is inviting residents, civic groups, nonprofits and businesses to help meet classroom needs through three online programs as Martin County students prepare to return to school Aug. 10. Adopt-A-Class allows supporters to adopt a specific classroom or school program with a donation of $100 or more. Classrooms and programs may be adopted multiple times, and the foundation hopes to have every classroom adopted at least once during the school year. Through Fund-A-Project, teachers can post requests for classroom projects designed to support student learning, and donors can select and fund specific educational projects.

Bulletin Board Listings connect community members with nonmonetary classroom needs. Participants may volunteer their time or donate materials, gently used equipment, books, magazines, shoe boxes and other reusable supplies. Community members also may offer subject-matter expertise or advisory board support. The foundation said 100 percent of donations go directly toward classroom needs because program sponsors cover administrative costs.

Lead sponsors include Napoli Orthodontics, the Kelley Decowski Team at RE/MAX of Stuart, Tami Karol Insurance, Diagnostic Radiology Center of the Treasure Coast, Seacoast Bank, and Rosenthal, Levy, Simon Sosa Injury Lawyers. Other sponsors include Precision Site Contracting, Stuart Pediatric Dentistry, Sullivan Electric Pump, Searcy Law, New Wave Compass Sara Crombie, Ampersand Graphics, JoAnna Oster, RE/MAX of Stuart, Pinders Nursery, All Jetting Technologies, Elegant Entries, Lesser Landy Smith Siegel PLLC, SwissMango and Sals Air.

Chanda Leon, a pre-AICE biology teacher at Martin County High School and the Education Foundation's 2025-2026 Martin County Teacher of the Year, said too often classroom ideas never become reality because of cost. Adopt-a-Classroom and Fund-a-Project have helped to remove financial barriers, allowing me the opportunity to convert creative solutions into meaningful learning experiences for my students, she said. Lisa Rhodes, executive director of the Education Foundation of Martin County, said every adopted classroom, funded project and donated resource sends a powerful message to teachers and students that this community believes in them. To adopt a classroom, fund a project, respond to a classroom need or learn more, visit www.EducationFoundationMC.org or call 772-600-8062.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce residents petition against plan to convert Museum Pointe Park into mega-yacht marina
hero.body:
A petition with nearly 800 signatures opposes a proposal to transform Fort Pierce's Museum Pointe, a public waterfront park along the Indian River Lagoon, into a mega-yacht marina. The Port of Fort Pierce's updated 2026 Master Plan calls for redeveloping Museum Pointe, which currently includes a history center, public waterfront access, fishing piers, and green space, into a facility featuring floating docks, a multi-story marina, an event center, a waterfront restaurant, and a clubhouse.

Terry Howard, a volunteer at the History Center at Museum Pointe Park, said the plan amounts to giving public land to private interests. The master plan's renderings place the proposed marina clubhouse exactly where the museum stands today. For more than 50 years, the museum has preserved artifacts from Florida's Native American tribes, Spanish shipwrecks, and other historical items.

St. Lucie County spokesperson Erick Gill said the museum's future is not in jeopardy if the project moves forward. Gill said the county has been talking for years about better locations for the history center because it sits on a barrier island in a flood zone. The master plan is designed to expand economic development, create jobs, and generate county revenue, Gill said.

Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the city will have the final say on whether the project moves forward. Broderick said commissioners will have to weigh economic benefits against preserving waterfront access. St. Lucie County leaders are scheduled to discuss the proposal and its current status at a 9 a.m. meeting at St. Lucie County Commission Chambers.

hero.headline: Los Angeles man sentenced to life in federal prison for fentanyl sale that killed Vero Beach resident
hero.body:
A Los Angeles man was sentenced to life in federal prison for selling fentanyl that caused the death of a Vero Beach man in May 2023, then continuing to traffic the deadly drug just two days later. U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon imposed the sentence on Alfonso Guerrero, 39, of Los Angeles, after a federal jury convicted him in May 2026 of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute fentanyl resulting in death and distribution of fentanyl resulting in death.

Guerrero sold fentanyl in Indian River County on May 16, 2023, exchanging 0.1 gram of fentanyl for another controlled substance known as molly. The drug transaction was captured on a doorbell camera. Hours later, David Eller was found dead inside his Vero Beach home. Investigators recovered drug paraphernalia, including a small piece of burnt aluminum foil that Eller used to receive the fentanyl from Guerrero on his front porch, near his body.

Two days later, on May 18, 2023, Guerrero was arrested and found in possession of additional quantities of fentanyl intended for distribution. U.S. Attorney Reding Quiones for the Southern District of Florida said a tenth of a gram of fentanyl, about the size of a small pinch of salt, was enough to kill Eller.

Guerrero's extensive criminal history included documented gang membership and prior convictions for attempted robbery with a firearm in California, aggravated assault in Georgia, and cocaine and fentanyl possession offenses in Florida. Federal prosecutors said they will trace fatal doses back to dealers who sold them and hold those dealers fully accountable.

hero.headline: 86-year-old woman dies after Port St. Lucie intersection crash
hero.body:
An 86-year-old woman died after she pulled into the path of an SUV and was struck in a Port St. Lucie intersection Thursday afternoon. Marie R. Martin was driving a 2006 Hyundai Elantra west on Southwest Lawndale Avenue when she entered the intersection at Southwest Savona Boulevard from near a stop sign and failed to yield to a northbound 2026 Honda HR-V at about 2:30 p.m., according to Port St. Lucie police.

The Honda, driven by a 17-year-old boy, struck the drivers side of Martin's car. Body-camera video recorded after the crash shows the Hyundai off the roadway near a cluster of palm trees, with visible damage to its drivers side and emergency crews working around the vehicle. The Honda also came to rest on the grass nearby, close to vegetation and a roadside sign.

Martin had to be extricated from the Hyundai before she was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with critical injuries. She later died despite efforts to save her. The teenage driver of the Honda was not injured.

Port St. Lucie police officers and St. Lucie County Fire District personnel responded to the scene, with fire engines, rescue vehicles and traffic cones blocking part of the intersection. The Police Department's Traffic Homicide Unit continues to investigate the crash.

cards.headline: Sanctuary at Winterlakes residents in Port St. Lucie report unanswered maintenance requests, mold
cards.teaser: Residents at Sanctuary at Winterlakes Apartments in Port St. Lucie said they have been living with unresolved maintenance issues including mold and that their requests for help are being ignored.
cards.body:
Residents at Sanctuary at Winterlakes Apartments in Port St. Lucie said they have been living with unresolved maintenance issues and that their requests for help are being ignored. Alison Malio showed what she believes is structural damage in her bedroom and described rot near the foundation. She also said her freezer seal was damaged and has cost her over $1,500 in lost food in the last year and a half to two years.

Malio showed a cockroach problem inside her apartment and building. She said pest control only comes once every 13 weeks. Malio said she and her neighbors submit maintenance requests through an online portal, but she claims those requests go unanswered or get deleted and are sometimes marked complete even when no work has been done.

Neighbor Cheryl Jones said her air conditioning was out for nine weeks. Jones said maintenance eventually fixed the air conditioning, but mold had grown inside her apartment. Jones sent a report from a company that tested her unit and found evidence of mold, recommending that drywall, insulation and other materials be removed. Property management sent a statement saying they are looking into the issues and that they prioritize the safety and well-being of their tenants.

hero.headline: Martin County considers changes to shark fishing rules after state directive
hero.body:
Martin County is weighing changes to its local shark fishing ordinance after the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission directed the county to align its rules with state regulations. The state law preempts counties from regulating saltwater fishing, meaning the county can no longer control shark fishing independently. Assistant County Attorney Melissa Petrick explained that state law requires a saltwater fishing license and a special permit for shark fishing and allows shark fishing within 1,000 feet of a guarded beach at all hours.

Jessica Veatch, whose then-3-year-old daughter Violet was attacked by a bull shark on Bathtub Beach nine years ago, opposes the changes. Veatch said she believes nearby spearfishing activity may have provoked the attack on her daughter. She expressed alarm that the county may be forced to eliminate its local shark fishing regulations. Indian River Keeper Jim Moir raised concerns at the Tuesday commission meeting about attracting more sharks to the coast, warning it could harm human safety, angling, and the sharks themselves.

County attorneys suggested the ordinance does not need to be eliminated entirely. Petrick said the county can rework the ordinance and reference the illegality of certain activities under state law instead of eliminating everything. County commissioners voted to table the discussion, directing staff to review concerns raised by the community and commissioners and draft new ordinance language.

The directive from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission stems from a state statute that preempts local control over saltwater fishing regulations. State law currently governs shark fishing requirements across Florida, including licensing and permitting standards. cards.teaser: David Allen Kingsley Jr., 31, fled a Stuart Police officer during a traffic stop on July 28, leading law enforcement on a chase that ended in Martin County.
cards.body:
David Allen Kingsley Jr., 31, was arrested July 28 after fleeing a Stuart Police officer during a traffic stop and leading law enforcement on a chase into Martin County. Kingsley was stopped by a Stuart Police officer on an equipment violation the evening of July 28. After the officer discovered that Kingsley's driver's license was revoked, Kingsley took off, leading officers on a brief pursuit within the City of Stuart and striking another vehicle before continuing out of the city.

Kingsley drove recklessly into Martin County jurisdiction, where deputies with the Martin County Sheriff's Office and troopers with the Florida Highway Patrol assisted in the pursuit. He was charged with two counts of fleeing eluding law enforcement and one count each of leaving the scene of a crash involving property damage, failure to obey an officer's order to stop, reckless driving, and driving while license suspended or revoked. He was in the Martin County Jail as of July 30 on a $40,000 bond.

hero.headline: Martin County weighs shark fishing rule changes after state directive
hero.body:
Martin County is weighing changes to its local shark fishing ordinance after the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission directed the county to align its rules with state regulations. The state says a statute has preempted the powers from the county to regulate saltwater fishing including shark fishing. State law requires a saltwater fishing license and a special permit for shark fishing and allows shark fishing within 1,000 feet of a guarded beach at all hours.

Jessica Veatch, whose then-3-year-old daughter Violet was attacked by a bull shark on Bathtub Beach in Martin County 9 years ago, opposes the changes. Veatch said she noticed young men spearfishing on the reef before the attack and believes nearby fishing activity may have led to it. She said she was alarmed to learn the county may now be forced to eliminate its local shark fishing regulations.

Indian River Keeper Jim Moir raised concerns about the potential impact at the Tuesday commission meeting. Moir said attracting more sharks to the coast is bad for human safety, angling, public awareness, and the sharks themselves. County attorneys suggested the ordinance does not need to be eliminated entirely and can be reworked to reference the illegality of things under state law.

County commissioners voted to table the discussion, directing staff to review concerns raised by the community and commissioners and draft new ordinance language. Assistant County Attorney Melissa Petrick said the county can rework the ordinance and instead of eliminating everything can reference the illegality of things under state law.

hero.headline: Los Angeles man sentenced to life in prison for fentanyl sale that killed Vero Beach resident
hero.body:
A federal jury convicted Alfonso Guerrero, 39, of Los Angeles, in May 2026 of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute fentanyl resulting in death and distribution of fentanyl resulting in death. U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon sentenced Guerrero to life in federal prison on Friday. The conviction stems from Guerrero selling fentanyl in Indian River County that caused the death of David Eller, a Vero Beach resident, and then continuing to traffic fentanyl just two days later.

On May 16, 2023, Guerrero exchanged 0.1 gram of fentanyl for another controlled substance known as molly in a drug transaction captured on a doorbell camera. Hours later, Eller was found dead inside his Vero Beach home. Investigators recovered drug paraphernalia near his body, including a small piece of burnt aluminum foil that Eller used to receive the fentanyl from Guerrero on his front porch.

Two days later, on May 18, 2023, Guerrero was arrested and found in possession of additional quantities of fentanyl intended for distribution. U.S. Attorney Markenzy Lapointe for the Southern District of Florida said a tenth of a gram of fentanyl, about the size of a small pinch of salt, was enough to kill Eller. Guerrero sold the fentanyl that killed his friend and just two days later was caught carrying more fentanyl for distribution.

Guerrero's criminal history included documented gang membership and prior convictions for attempted robbery with a firearm in California, aggravated assault in Georgia, and cocaine and fentanyl possession offenses in Florida. U.S. Attorney Lapointe said federal prosecutors will trace fatal doses back to the dealers who sold them and hold those dealers fully accountable.

hero.headline: 86-year-old woman dies after Port St. Lucie intersection crash
hero.body:
An 86-year-old woman died after she pulled into the path of an SUV and was struck in a Port St. Lucie intersection Thursday afternoon. Marie R. Martin was driving a 2006 Hyundai Elantra west on Southwest Lawndale Avenue when she entered the intersection at Southwest Savona Boulevard from near a stop sign and failed to yield to a northbound 2026 Honda HR-V, according to Port St. Lucie police. The crash happened at about 2:30 p.m. The Honda, driven by a 17-year-old boy, struck the drivers side of Martin's car.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce residents fight plan to turn Museum Pointe Park into mega-yacht marina
cards.teaser: A petition with nearly 800 signatures opposes a Port of Fort Pierce proposal to redevelop Museum Pointe, a public waterfront park along the Indian River Lagoon, into a facility featuring floating docks, a multi-story marina, an event center, a waterfront restaurant, and a clubhouse.
cards.body:
A petition with nearly 800 signatures is mounting against a proposal that could transform Fort Pierce's Museum Pointe into a mega-yacht marina. The proposal is part of the Port of Fort Pierce's updated 2026 Master Plan. It calls for redeveloping Museum Pointe, which is currently home to a history center, public waterfront access, fishing piers, and green space, into a facility featuring floating docks, a multi-story marina, an event center, a waterfront restaurant, and a clubhouse.

Terry Howard, a volunteer at the History Center at Museum Pointe Park, said the loss of public waterfront access is a concern but his biggest worry is the fate of the museum. For more than 50 years, the museum has preserved artifacts from Florida's Native American tribes, Spanish shipwrecks, and more. The master plan's renderings place the proposed marina clubhouse exactly where the museum stands today.

St. Lucie County spokesperson Erick Gill said the museum's future is not in jeopardy if the project moves forward. Gill said the museum and its collection would be preserved and relocated if the project proceeds. He added that the master plan is designed to expand economic development, create jobs, and generate county revenue. Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the city will have the final say on whether the project moves forward. St. Lucie County leaders are scheduled to discuss the proposal and its current status at a 9 a.m. meeting Tuesday at the St. Lucie County Commission Chambers.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie officer resigns after allegations he left scene where man later died by suicide
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie police officer resigned in April following allegations of neglect during a March incident at the Treasure Coast Church of God Worship Center on Savona Boulevard.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police officer Mathew Brown resigned in April following allegations of neglect during a March incident at the Treasure Coast Church of God Worship Center on Savona Boulevard, according to an internal affairs report. The report alleged Officer Brown came across a car with a man inside, looked, and then immediately left the scene.

Fifteen minutes later, another officer spotted the same car and discovered the man inside had died by suicide. Officer Brown arrived as backup but allegedly did not inform anyone about his earlier encounter with the vehicle and later claimed he did not see anything.

hero.headline: Los Angeles man sentenced to life in prison for fentanyl sale that killed Vero Beach resident
hero.body:
A federal judge sentenced a Los Angeles man to life in prison for selling fentanyl that caused the death of a Vero Beach resident and then trafficking the drug two days later. U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon imposed the sentence on Alfonso Guerrero, 39, of Los Angeles, after a federal jury convicted him in May 2026 of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute fentanyl resulting in death and distribution of fentanyl resulting in death.

Guerrero sold fentanyl in Indian River County on May 16, 2023, exchanging 0.1 gram of fentanyl for another controlled substance known as molly. The drug transaction was captured on a doorbell camera. Hours later, David Eller was found dead inside his Vero Beach home. Investigators recovered drug paraphernalia, including a small piece of burnt aluminum foil that Eller used to receive the fentanyl from Guerrero on his front porch, near his body.

Two days later, on May 18, 2023, Guerrero was arrested and found in possession of additional quantities of fentanyl intended for distribution. U.S. Attorney Markenzy Lapointe for the Southern District of Florida said a tenth of a gram of fentanyl, about the size of a small pinch of salt, was enough to kill Eller.

Guerrero's extensive criminal history included documented gang membership and prior convictions for attempted robbery with a firearm in California, aggravated assault in Georgia, and cocaine and fentanyl possession offenses in Florida. Lapointe said federal prosecutors will trace fatal doses back to the dealers who sold them and hold those dealers fully accountable.

hero.body:
An 86-year-old woman who failed to yield at a Port St. Lucie intersection Thursday afternoon and was struck by an SUV driven by a 17-year-old boy later died from her injuries at HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. Marie R. Martin was driving a 2006 Hyundai Elantra westbound on Southwest Lawndale Avenue when she entered the intersection with Southwest Savona Boulevard near a stop sign at approximately 2:30 p.m. Thursday.

The preliminary investigation by the Port St. Lucie Police Department determined that Martin failed to yield the right of way to a 2026 Honda HR-V traveling northbound on Southwest Savona Boulevard, east of Interstate 95. The Honda struck the driver's side of the Hyundai, causing the Honda to T-bone Martin's vehicle.

St. Lucie Fire Rescue extricated Martin from the Hyundai before transporting her to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with critical injuries. Martin later succumbed to her injuries. The 17-year-old driver of the Honda was not injured in the crash.

The Port St. Lucie Police Department Traffic Homicide Unit continues to investigate the crash. Body camera video recorded after the crash shows the Hyundai off the roadway near a cluster of palm trees with visible damage to its driver's side, while the Honda came to rest on the grass nearby close to vegetation and a roadside sign.

cards.headline: King's Landing development in Fort Pierce advances with luxury villas nearing completion
cards.teaser: Construction of villas 9 and 10 at the King's Landing development in downtown Fort Pierce is nearly complete, with the foundation already in place for villas 7 and 8 and two residences already sold.
cards.body:
The King's Landing development project in downtown Fort Pierce is advancing with construction milestones on ten luxury villas, condos, retail spaces, restaurants, a parking garage, and a Marriott Hotel. Brooke Harris, Team Lead of the Beachfront Brooke Team powered by Keller Williams Realty, said construction on villas 9 and 10 is almost done, the foundation has already been installed for villas 7 and 8, and two residences have been sold and are nearing completion.

The project is located in the waterfront district near the city marina and historic downtown. Harris said the development is waterfront and connects downtown to Edgartown, providing walkability to shopping, restaurants, and retail, with boat storage available at the marina. Michelle Chaffee Cavalcanti, executive director of Main Street Fort Pierce, said the development has the potential to impact local businesses by bringing in visitors and providing a place for families to stay.

Business owners are optimistic about having more residents in the downtown area with most amenities within walking distance. Chaffee Cavalcanti said walkability means people can visit a restaurant and then walk to another business to shop, creating an experience rather than just a singular destination. The estimated completion date is November 2029.

hero.headline: King's Landing development in Fort Pierce advances with luxury villas nearing completion, Marriott Hotel planned for 2029
hero.body:
The King's Landing development project in downtown Fort Pierce is advancing with construction milestones on ten luxury villas, condos, retail spaces, restaurants, a parking garage, and a hotel. Brooke Harris, Team Lead of the Beachfront Brooke Team powered by Keller Williams Realty, said construction is nearly complete on Villas 9 and 10, with foundations already in place for Villas 7 and 8. Two residences have been sold and are nearing completion. A Marriott Hotel will be part of the development after the company signed an agreement.

The project sits in the waterfront district near the city marina and historic downtown Fort Pierce. Harris said the location connects downtown to Edgartown and provides walkability to shopping, restaurants, and retail. Residents with boats can store them at the marina.

Michelle Chaffee Cavalcanti, executive director of Main Street Fort Pierce, said the development could have significant impact on local businesses by bringing in visitors and giving residents a place for their families to stay. She said the downtown area will become an experience where people can walk, shop, live, and play.

Business owners said having more residents downtown will benefit the area because most amenities are within walking distance. Chaffee Cavalcanti said people can walk to a restaurant and then go to another business to shop and get information. Officials said the estimated completion date is November 2029.

hero.headline: Los Angeles man sentenced to life in prison for fentanyl sale that killed Vero Beach resident
hero.body:
A federal judge sentenced a Los Angeles man to life in prison for selling fentanyl that caused the death of a Vero Beach resident and then trafficking the drug two days later. U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon imposed the sentence on Alfonso Guerrero, 39, of Los Angeles, after a federal jury convicted him in May 2026 of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute fentanyl resulting in death and distribution of fentanyl resulting in death.

According to court records and evidence presented at trial, Guerrero sold fentanyl in Indian River County. On May 16, 2023, he exchanged 0.1 gram of fentanyl for another controlled substance known as molly. The drug transaction was captured on a doorbell camera. Hours later, David Eller was found dead inside his Vero Beach home. Investigators recovered drug paraphernalia, including a small piece of burnt aluminum foil that Eller used to receive the fentanyl from Guerrero on the victim's front porch, near his body.

Two days later, on May 18, 2023, Guerrero was arrested and found in possession of additional quantities of fentanyl intended for distribution. U.S. Attorney Markenzy Lapointe for the Southern District of Florida said in a statement that a tenth of a gram of fentanyl, about the size of a small pinch of salt, was enough to kill Eller. Guerrero sold the fentanyl that killed his friend and, just two days later, was caught carrying more fentanyl for distribution, Lapointe said.

Guerrero's criminal history included documented gang membership and prior convictions for attempted robbery with a firearm in California, aggravated assault in Georgia, and cocaine and fentanyl possession offenses in Florida. Federal prosecutors said the life sentence is the consequence of that deadly conduct and his long record of violence and crime.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man caught on video stealing thousands of dollars worth of tequila from Martin County store
cards.teaser: The Martin County Sheriff's Office released surveillance video showing a Port St. Lucie man stuffing bottles of tequila into a backpack and walking out with three cases without paying.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office released surveillance video that investigators say shows a Port St. Lucie man stealing thousands of dollars worth of tequila from a liquor store. Michael Ruiz, 31, was caught on camera stuffing bottles of tequila into a backpack while inside the store. The video also shows Ruiz entering a storage room, grabbing three cases of tequila and walking out without paying.

Ruiz was later arrested in St. Lucie County on unrelated charges after police said he was driving under the influence. Investigators believe Ruiz may be connected to several other recent tequila thefts reported across the area and are continuing to look into those cases. The Martin County Sheriff's Office is asking anyone with information about similar incidents to contact law enforcement.

hero.headline: 86-year-old woman dies after Port St. Lucie intersection crash
hero.body:
An 86-year-old woman died after pulling into the path of an SUV at a Port St. Lucie intersection Thursday afternoon. The crash happened at about 2:30 p.m. at Southwest Savona Boulevard and Southwest Lawndale Avenue.

Marie R. Martin was driving a 2006 Hyundai Elantra west on Lawndale Avenue when she entered the intersection from near a stop sign and failed to yield to a northbound 2026 Honda HR-V, according to Port St. Lucie police investigators. The Honda, driven by a 17-year-old boy, struck the drivers side of Martin's car. Body camera video recorded after the crash shows the Hyundai off the roadway near a cluster of palm trees, with visible damage to its drivers side and emergency crews working around the vehicle. The Honda also came to rest on the grass nearby, close to vegetation and a roadside sign.

Martin had to be extricated from the Hyundai before she was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with critical injuries. She later died despite efforts to save her. The teenage driver of the Honda was not injured.

The Police Department's Traffic Homicide Unit continues to investigate the crash. Port St. Lucie police officers and St. Lucie County Fire District personnel responded to the scene, along with fire engines, rescue vehicles and traffic cones blocking part of the intersection.

hero.headline: Martin County school district cuts 3 bus routes, saving $255,000 with no impact to students
hero.body:
The Martin County School District has approved a consolidation of bus routes that officials say will save $255,000 without affecting students or eliminating any driver positions. The school board voted Tuesday unanimously to reduce the number of bus routes by 3, bringing the total from 58 to 55 ahead of the upcoming school year. District officials say all bus stops will remain the same and students will not be impacted by the change.

Superintendent Michael Maine said the district has 55 routes and roughly 56 drivers, meaning all routes are covered. The $255,000 in savings reflects a reduced transportation budget and will not be redirected to a specific expense, according to the school district. Parents have mixed reactions. Marino Reyes and Tiffany Gugumuck expressed support for the financial decision. Ken Winstanley wondered where the money will go.

Michael Skinner, the President of the local AFSCME labor union chapter, voiced concerns during public comment on behalf of the bus drivers. He said feedback from bus drivers indicated their routes or buses are always full and cutting routes is not a good idea. Transportation Director Ruth Spires pushed back on that concern, noting that the buses hold a maximum of 77 passengers and are not operating at capacity.

Spires confirmed that no drivers were let go as part of the consolidation. The district was already challenged with a shortage last year, so the drivers were already covering the routes that were merged, Spires said. Drivers will be paid for any additional hours they work as a result of the consolidation. The district said it is confident it will maintain the same level of service with fewer buses on the road.

hero.headline: Los Angeles man sentenced to life in prison for fentanyl sale that killed Vero Beach resident
hero.body:
A federal judge sentenced Alfonso Guerrero, 39, of Los Angeles, to life in federal prison for selling fentanyl that caused the death of Vero Beach resident David Eller and continuing to traffic the deadly drug just two days after the fatal sale. U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon imposed the sentence after a federal jury convicted Guerrero in May 2026 of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute fentanyl resulting in death and distribution of fentanyl resulting in death.

According to court records and evidence presented at trial, Guerrero sold fentanyl in Indian River County on May 16, 2023. He exchanged 0.1 gram of fentanyl, commonly known as a point, for another controlled substance known as molly. The drug transaction was captured on a doorbell camera. Hours later, Eller was found dead inside his Vero Beach home. Investigators recovered drug paraphernalia, including a small piece of burnt aluminum foil that Eller used to receive the fentanyl from Guerrero on the victim's front porch, near his body.

Two days later, on May 18, 2023, Guerrero was arrested and found in possession of additional quantities of fentanyl intended for distribution. U.S. Attorney Markenzy Lapointe for the Southern District of Florida said in a statement that a tenth of a gram of fentanyl, about the size of a small pinch of salt, was enough to kill Eller. Lapointe said the sentence reflects that Guerrero sold the fentanyl that killed his friend and was caught carrying more fentanyl for distribution just two days later.

Guerrero's extensive criminal history included documented gang membership and prior convictions for attempted robbery with a firearm in California, aggravated assault in Georgia, and cocaine and fentanyl possession offenses in Florida. Federal prosecutors said they will trace fatal doses back to the dealers who sold them and hold those dealers fully accountable.
